teile.einleitung: A blacksmith is a craftsman who shapes glowing metal with a hammer and muscle power. For thousands of years blacksmiths have made tools, weapons, horseshoes and decorative railings. In doing so they use what chemistry knows about metals: heat makes iron soft and easy to shape.
wichtigste: A blacksmith shapes glowing metal, usually iron or steel.
His workshop is called a forge.
The metal is made red-hot in the forge fire, the hearth, so that it becomes soft and easy to shape.
With bellows the blacksmith blows air into the fire so that it burns hotter.
He holds the glowing iron with tongs and hammers it on the heavy anvil.
A farrier shoes horses with horseshoes.
The common surname Schmid comes from the trade of the blacksmith.

abschnitte.text: The heart of every **forge** is the **hearth**, a fireplace in which mainly charcoal used to burn and later coal. With **bellows** or an electric blower, air is blown into the fire. The extra oxygen makes the embers much hotter. Iron gets so hot that it glows red, orange or even yellowish white. From the glowing colour, the blacksmith can tell roughly how hot the metal is.

The **anvil** is a heavy block of iron or steel on which the metal is hammered. It has a flat face and a pointed horn, over which iron can be bent round. With the **tongs** the blacksmith holds the glowing piece, because it would be impossible with bare hands. The hammer stretches, upsets, bends and splits the metal. Because the iron cools quickly while it is being worked, it has to go back into the fire again and again.

Heated iron becomes softer because the metal atoms can slide past each other more easily. If the blacksmith quickly plunges glowing steel into water or oil, it becomes hard; this process is called **hardening**. After that the steel is often warmed again moderately so that it is not too brittle; this is called **tempering**. On the hot surface, the iron reacts with the oxygen in the air. A dark layer of iron oxide forms, the **scale**, which flies off during hammering.

A **farrier** fits horseshoes exactly to a horse’s hooves and nails them on. This does not hurt the horse, because the outer edge of the hoof, like a fingernail, has no feeling. An **artistic blacksmith** makes decorated railings, gates, banisters and lanterns. Other smiths make knives, tools or bells. Today large machines in factories also forge metal parts automatically.

In Central Europe the **Iron Age** began about 2800 years ago. The Celts were skilled smiths; famous are the many iron finds from **La Tène** on Lake Neuchâtel, after which a whole era is named. In the Middle Ages almost every village had its own forge, because farmers needed ploughshares, scythes and horseshoes. That is why the blacksmith was an important and respected man in the village. In legends there are even gods of smithing, such as Hephaestus among the ancient Greeks.

Many surnames go back to the trade, in Switzerland for example **Schmid**, one of the most common names in the country. In English the name is Smith, in French Lefèvre. Sayings also recall the craft: “Strike while the iron is hot” means you should use a good opportunity straight away. In open-air museums such as Ballenberg you can sometimes watch blacksmiths at work.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fireplace in the forge where the metal is heated.
A heavy iron block on which the glowing metal is hammered.
Heating steel strongly and cooling it quickly so that it becomes hard.
A dark layer of iron oxide that forms on hot iron.
A smith who shoes horses with horseshoes.

gewusst: A good anvil can weigh over a hundred kilograms so that it does not jump about during hammering.
The hissing when glowing steel is plunged into water happens because the water turns into steam in an instant.
The German saying “Jeder ist seines Glückes Schmied”, “everyone is the smith of their own fortune”, is also named after the blacksmith.

teile.einleitung: The acid dissociation constant Ka is a number that shows how strong an acid is in water. The larger it is, the more protons the acid gives up to the water. It can be used to compare acids and to calculate the pH of a solution.
wichtigste: The acid dissociation constant describes the equilibrium HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻.
It is calculated as Ka = c(H₃O⁺) · c(A⁻) / c(HA).
The concentration of water does not appear in the expression, because it is practically constant in dilute solutions.
For a particular acid in water, Ka depends only on temperature.
The larger the Ka value, the stronger the acid.
For bases there is a corresponding base dissociation constant Kb.
If a weak acid is diluted a lot, its degree of dissociation increases.

abschnitte.titel: What is the acid dissociation constant
abschnitte.text: If you put an acid HA into water, it gives a **proton** to a water molecule, forming H₃O⁺ ions and A⁻ ions. With weak acids this only happens partly, and a **chemical equilibrium** is set up. The acid dissociation constant is the equilibrium constant of this reaction: Ka = c(H₃O⁺) · c(A⁻) / c(HA). The concentration of water is left out, because it stays practically constant in dilute solutions.

A large Ka value means that the acid gives up protons almost completely; it is a **strong acid**. A small Ka value shows a **weak acid**, in which most molecules stay unchanged. If acid A has a Ka of 10⁻³ mol/L and acid B one of 10⁻⁶ mol/L, acid A is therefore the stronger. Hydrocyanic acid (HCN) is a very weak acid with a particularly small Ka value.

Because Ka values are often tiny numbers, people usually calculate with the **pKa value**, the negative base 10 logarithm of Ka. The smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid. Acetic acid, for example, has a pKa of about 4.76. The pKa is also important for **buffer solutions**, because a buffer works best close to this value.

For weak acids the pH can be calculated with an approximation: pH = ½ · (pKa minus log c). So an acid with Ka = 10⁻⁵ mol/L and a concentration of 0.1 mol/L has a pH of about 3. The proportion of acid molecules that give up a proton is called the **degree of dissociation**. If a weak acid is diluted a lot, this proportion increases, even though the solution as a whole becomes less acidic.

For bases there is a corresponding quantity, the **base dissociation constant** Kb, for example for the reaction B + H₂O ⇌ HB⁺ + OH⁻. For a conjugate acid-base pair in water at 25 degrees Celsius, the product of Ka and Kb is always 10⁻¹⁴. The acid dissociation constant of a particular acid in water only changes with **temperature**. That is why tables usually give the values for 25 degrees Celsius.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that gives the strength of an acid in water.
The negative logarithm of the acid dissociation constant; a small value means a strong acid.
The giving up or taking up of a proton in an acid-base reaction.
A state in which the forward and reverse reactions run equally fast.

gewusst: Between a strong acid and a very weak acid, the Ka value can differ by more than twenty powers of ten.
Water itself also gives up protons to a tiny extent, which is why pure water at 25 degrees Celsius is neutral with a pH of 7.

teile.einleitung: The pH is a number that shows how acidic or how alkaline a solution is. The usual scale runs from 0 to 14, where 7 means neutral. Whether lemon juice, soap or swimming pool water, they can all be compared using the pH.
wichtigste: The pH shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
The usual pH scale runs from 0 to 14.
Pure water has a pH of 7 at 25 °C and is neutral.
A pH below 7 means acidic, above 7 means alkaline.
Lemon juice has a pH of about 2.
With universal indicator you can find the pH easily; at pH 7 it is green.
A solution with pH 3 is 10 times more acidic than one with pH 4.

abschnitte.text: The pH measures how many **oxonium ions** H₃O⁺ there are in a solution. The more of them there are, the more acidic the solution and the smaller the pH. Pure water has the value 7 at 25 °C and is **neutral**. Values below 7 are **acidic**; values above 7 are **basic**, also called alkaline.

The pH scale is a **logarithmic scale**. This means each step corresponds to a factor of 10. So a solution with pH 3 is 10 times more acidic than one with pH 4 and 100 times more acidic than one with pH 5. The usual scale runs from 0 to 14, but very strong acids and alkalis can also go beyond it.

**Gastric juice**, with a pH of about 1 to 2, is very acidic and helps with digestion. Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, vinegar about 3 and cola about 2.5. Our blood is slightly alkaline, with a pH of about 7.4. Soapy water is at about 9 to 10, and drain cleaner can be over 13.

The easiest way to measure pH is with **universal indicator**, a mixture of dyes on paper strips or as a liquid. It turns red in acidic solutions, green at pH 7 and blue to violet in alkaline solutions. **Red cabbage juice** is also a natural indicator that changes colour depending on the pH. More precise measurements are made with an electronic **pH meter**.

In the swimming pool the water should have a pH of about 7 to 7.4 so that the chlorine works well and your eyes do not sting. Gardeners measure the pH of the soil because plants such as blueberries like acidic soil. In the past, acid rain damaged forests and lakes in Europe. The pH is also monitored regularly in Swiss lakes and rivers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solution with a pH below 7, like lemon juice.
A solution with a pH above 7, like soapy water.
Neither acidic nor alkaline, with a pH of 7.
A dye that shows by its colour whether something is acidic or alkaline.

gewusst: The pH was introduced in 1909 by the Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked in a brewery laboratory.
Hydrangeas often flower blue on acidic soil and rather pink on alkaline soil.
Our skin is slightly acidic, with a pH of about 5, which protects it from bacteria.

teile.einleitung: Non-metals are chemical elements that do not have the typical properties of metals. They include substances vital for life such as oxygen, nitrogen and carbon. In the periodic table they are at the top right, and although there are only a few of them, they make up a large part of the air and of all living things.
wichtigste: Non-metals usually do not shine and conduct electricity poorly.
Many non-metals are gases at room temperature, for example oxygen and nitrogen.
Bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Sulphur is a yellow solid that is often found at volcanoes.
Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the air.
Chlorine is used to disinfect swimming pool water.
In Switzerland iodine has been added to table salt since 1922.

abschnitte.text: The non-metals include hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulphur, the **halogens** and the **noble gases**, among others. Unlike metals, most non-metals **conduct electricity poorly** and do not shine. Solid non-metals are often brittle and break when hammered. Between metals and non-metals are the metalloids such as silicon.

Eleven non-metals are gases at room temperature, including nitrogen, which makes up about 78 per cent of the air, and oxygen. **Bromine** is the only liquid non-metal, a dark red liquid with poisonous fumes. Solid non-metals include carbon, phosphorus, iodine and sulphur. Yellow **sulphur** is often deposited at volcanoes, where hot gases stream out of the Earth.

**Chlorine** is a poisonous yellowish green gas. In small amounts it kills bacteria, which is why it is used to disinfect swimming pool water. The typical indoor pool smell, however, comes from substances formed when chlorine reacts with sweat and urine. With sodium, chlorine forms harmless **table salt**.

**Iodine** is a shiny dark violet solid. Our body needs it for the thyroid gland, and a lack of iodine can cause a **goitre**. In the past many people in Switzerland had a goitre, because the soils of the Alps contain little iodine. That is why iodine has been added to table salt in Switzerland since 1922, which made goitre almost disappear.

Living things consist mostly of non-metals, above all carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. **Phosphorus** is found in bones and in genetic material. Nitrogen is an important part of **fertiliser**. Noble gases such as neon glow in advertising tubes, and helium fills balloons because it is lighter than air.

begriffe.erklaerung: An element that does not shine and usually conducts electricity poorly.
A group of non-metals such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Non-metals such as helium and neon that hardly react with other substances.
An enlarged thyroid gland, often because of a lack of iodine.

gewusst: The name bromine comes from the Greek word for stench, because it has a sharp smell.
Graphite is an exception among the non-metals, because it conducts electricity quite well.
Sulphur burns with a blue flame, forming a sharp-smelling gas.

teile.einleitung: Sodium hydroxide solution is a solution of sodium hydroxide in water and one of the most important alkalis in chemistry. It is strongly corrosive and must be handled very carefully. Even so, you come across it in everyday life, for example in drain cleaner or when lye pretzels are baked.
wichtigste: Sodium hydroxide solution is sodium hydroxide, formula NaOH, dissolved in water.
It is a strong base and has a pH well above 7.
Dilute alkali feels soapy and slippery on the skin.
Alkalis can seriously burn the eyes, which is why safety goggles are compulsory.
When solid sodium hydroxide dissolves in water, the solution gets noticeably warm.
Sodium hydroxide solution attacks aluminium and dissolves it.
Lye pretzels are dipped in dilute sodium hydroxide solution before baking, which is why they are shiny brown.

abschnitte.text: **Sodium hydroxide** is a white solid that is often sold as small pellets or beads. If you dissolve it in water, sodium hydroxide solution is formed. A lot of heat is released, and the solution gets noticeably warm. Sodium hydroxide is **hygroscopic**: if the pellets are left open in the air, they attract water and become damp. That is why it is kept in tightly closed containers.

Sodium hydroxide solution is a strong **base** and is corrosive. It breaks down proteins and fats, which is why even dilute alkali feels soapy and slippery on the skin. It is particularly dangerous for the eyes, because alkalis can seriously burn the cornea. Anyone working with it wears safety goggles and gloves. Splashes are rinsed off immediately with plenty of water.

Lye pretzels, lye rolls and, in Switzerland, the popular **Silserli** are briefly dipped into dilute sodium hydroxide solution before baking. In the hot oven, the alkali produces the shiny brown crust and the typical taste. During baking the alkali reacts with carbon dioxide from the air, so the finished bakes are safe to eat. Even so, bakeries work with protective gloves.

abschnitte.titel: In the home and in industry
abschnitte.text: Many **drain cleaners** contain sodium hydroxide because it breaks down fats, hair and food remains. Such products must never be mixed and must be kept safely away from children. In industry, sodium hydroxide solution is needed to make soap, paper, aluminium and many chemicals. It is usually produced by electrolysis of salt solution, which also produces chlorine at the same time.

Sodium hydroxide solution attacks **aluminium** and dissolves it, producing hydrogen gas. That is why it must not be stored in aluminium containers, and aluminium pans do not belong in lye baths. If you mix sodium hydroxide solution with an acid, they cancel each other out. This reaction is called **neutralisation**, and water and a salt are formed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solution of a base in water, with a pH above 7.
A substance that can neutralise acids, the opposite of an acid.
Attracts water from the air, like a sponge.
The reaction of an acid and an alkali, in which water and a salt are formed.

gewusst: The name “natron” comes from a salt that the ancient Egyptians obtained from salt lakes.
In the past, before sodium hydroxide solution could be bought, people boiled soap from fat and an alkali made from wood ash.
A legend says that the lye pretzel came about because a baker accidentally dropped dough into an alkaline solution.

teile.einleitung: The mass fraction says what part of the total mass of a mixture consists of a particular substance. It is usually given as a percentage. Whether salt water, squash or seawater: with the mass fraction you can work out exactly how much of a substance is in it.
wichtigste: The mass fraction is the mass of a substance divided by the mass of the whole mixture.
It is given as a fraction, as a decimal or as a percentage.
The symbol for the mass fraction is usually the letter w.
It is important to divide by the mass of the whole solution and not just by the mass of the water.
Seawater has a salt mass fraction of about 3.5 per cent.
If you add water, the amount of salt stays the same, but the mass fraction falls.

abschnitte.text: The **mass fraction** describes how large the share of a substance in the total mass of a **mixture** is. It is calculated like this: mass of the substance divided by mass of the mixture. If you multiply the result by 100, you get a percentage. So a mass fraction of 10 per cent means: in 100 g of mixture there are 10 g of the substance.

If you dissolve 20 g of salt in 180 g of water, you get 200 g of solution. The mass fraction of the salt is then 20 g divided by 200 g, that is 10 per cent. A common mistake is to divide only by the 180 g of water. In the same way, 12 g of salt in 228 g of water give a solution weighing 240 g with 5 per cent salt, and 50 g of sugar in 200 g of water give 20 per cent sugar.

If you know the mass fraction, you can calculate the mass of the substance: mass of the mixture times mass fraction. 500 g of a sugar solution at 5 per cent contain 25 g of sugar. For 400 g of a **salt solution** at 15 per cent, you need 60 g of salt and 340 g of water. This is how solutions of exactly the strength required are made in the laboratory.

When **diluting**, you add more solvent, usually water. The mass of the dissolved substance stays the same; only the total mass grows. 300 g of a 10 per cent salt solution contain 30 g of salt. If you add 200 g of water, there are 30 g of salt in 500 g of solution, so only 6 per cent.

Seawater contains about 3.5 per cent salt, so there are about 70 g of salt in 2 kg of seawater. Food packaging often states how much sugar or fat there is in 100 g, which is nothing other than the mass fraction. For metal mixtures such as brass or gold jewellery, too, it is stated how much of each metal they contain. It can even be calculated for compounds: in water (H₂O), oxygen makes up about 89 per cent of the mass, because an oxygen atom is 16 times heavier than a hydrogen atom.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something made by mixing two or more substances, for example salt water.
A mixture in which a substance is spread so finely in the water that you can no longer see it.
Means “out of a hundred”. 10 per cent is 10 out of 100 parts.
Adding more solvent so that a solution becomes weaker.

gewusst: The number on a gold chain, for example 750, means that 750 out of 1000 parts of the mass are pure gold, that is 75 per cent.
In the Dead Sea the salt content is almost ten times higher than in normal seawater.
Although hydrogen supplies twice as many atoms as oxygen in the water molecule, it makes up only about 11 per cent of the mass.

teile.einleitung: The pKa value is a number that shows how strong an acid is. The smaller the pKa, the more readily an acid gives up its protons. With it you can easily compare acids such as vinegar, lemon juice or hydrochloric acid.
wichtigste: The pKa is the negative base 10 logarithm of the acid dissociation constant Ka.
A small pKa means a strong acid, a large one a weak acid.
Acetic acid has a pKa of 4.76 at 25 °C.
If two pKa values differ by 2, the Ka values differ by a factor of 100.
For an acid-base pair at 25 °C: pKa plus pKb equals 14.
Polyprotic acids such as phosphoric acid have several pKa values.
The structure of a molecule decides how easily it gives up a proton.

abschnitte.text: An **acid** gives up protons in water, that is positively charged hydrogen ions. How readily it does this is described by the **acid dissociation constant** Ka. Because Ka values are often tiny numbers with many zeros, the negative base 10 logarithm is taken. So a Ka of 0.001 becomes a pKa of 3. This is similar to pH, which is also a logarithm.

The smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid. Hydrochloric acid has a negative pKa and gives up its protons almost completely. **Acetic acid** in vinegar has 4.76 and is a weak acid. Because it is a logarithm, a difference of 1 means a factor of 10. So an acid with a pKa of 3 has a Ka value 100 times larger than an acid with a pKa of 5.

abschnitte.titel: Acids and bases as a pair
abschnitte.text: When an acid gives up a proton, it becomes its **conjugate base**. For such a pair at 25 °C: pKa plus pKb equals 14. The ammonium ion has a pKa of 9.25, so ammonia has a pKb of 4.75. The stronger the acid, the weaker its base. Polyprotic acids such as phosphoric acid give up their protons one after another; their first pKa is 2.16, the second 7.21, because the second proton has to leave a negatively charged ion.

The strength depends on the structure of the molecule. **Hydrofluoric acid** HF is only weak despite the very electronegative fluorine, because the H-F bond is very strong. Phenol, with a pKa of about 10, is much more acidic than ethanol, at about 16, because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by **resonance**. Formic acid is somewhat stronger than acetic acid, because the methyl group of acetic acid pushes electrons and makes the acetate ion less stable.

With pKa values you can predict whether a reaction between an acid and a base will take place. They help in making **buffer solutions**, which keep the pH stable, for example in medicines or in the blood. In the laboratory they are used to choose the right colour indicator for a titration. They also play a part in food chemistry, for example with citric acid in drinks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how strongly an acid gives up protons in water.
A way of calculating that turns very large or very small numbers into handy ones.
A positively charged hydrogen ion that acids give up.
A solution that keeps its pH almost the same, even when a little acid or alkali is added.

gewusst: The “p” in pKa and in pH stands for the negative base 10 logarithm.
Hydrofluoric acid is a weak acid, yet it is one of the most dangerous chemicals in the laboratory because it passes through the skin.
Buffers keep our blood almost always at a pH of about 7.4.

teile.einleitung: A period is a horizontal row in the periodic table of the elements. All the elements in a period have the same number of electron shells. If you know the periods, you can read a lot about the size and behaviour of an atom.
wichtigste: Today’s periodic table has 7 periods.
The number of the period gives the number of occupied electron shells.
In the first period there are only 2 elements, hydrogen and helium.
The second period has 8 elements, from lithium to neon.
From the second period on, each period begins on the left with an alkali metal.
Each period ends on the far right with a noble gas.
Within a period, the atomic radius decreases from left to right.

abschnitte.text: The **periodic table** arranges all the chemical elements by their atomic number, that is by the number of protons in the nucleus. The horizontal rows are called **periods**, and the vertical columns are called groups. The number of the period reveals how many **electron shells** an atom has. Potassium, for example, is in period 4 and therefore has four occupied shells.

The first period is very short and contains only hydrogen and helium. The second and third periods each have 8 elements. The fourth and fifth each have 18 elements, and the sixth and seventh as many as 32 each. Because the long periods do not fit on the page, the **lanthanides** and **actinides** are usually placed in two extra rows below the table.

Every period from the second on begins with an **alkali metal** such as lithium, sodium or potassium. Then come metals, metalloids and non-metals. At the end there is always a **noble gas** such as neon or argon, whose outermost shell is full. So the properties of the elements change step by step within a period.

From left to right in a period, the number of protons in the nucleus increases. As a result the nucleus pulls the electrons more strongly, even though no new shell is added. That is why the **atomic radius** decreases within a period. At the same time more energy is needed to remove an electron from the atom.

In 1869 the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev** published a periodic table, leaving gaps in it for elements that were still unknown. At almost the same time the German Lothar Meyer was working on a similar arrangement. The seventh period has only been fully named since 2016, when elements 113, 115, 117 and 118 received their names. The last of them is called **oganesson**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.
A region around the atomic nucleus where electrons are found.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus; it determines the element.
A very unreactive element at the end of each period.
A measure of the size of an atom.

gewusst: Helium is on the far right, but it has only two electrons and a single shell.
Mendeleev predicted properties of elements that were only discovered years later, for example gallium and germanium.

teile.einleitung: The reaction rate says how fast a chemical reaction takes place. Some reactions take years, like a bicycle rusting; others happen in fractions of a second, like an explosion. The speed can be influenced by temperature, surface area and concentration.
wichtigste: The reaction rate shows how much an amount of substance changes per unit of time.
At higher temperatures the particles collide more often and more violently.
A rule of thumb says: 10 degrees more doubles to quadruples the rate.
In the fridge, food goes off more slowly because cold slows reactions down.
A larger surface area makes substances react faster, which is why wood shavings burn faster than a log.
Magnesium reacts faster in more concentrated acid.
Finely spread flour dust can explode because of its huge surface area.

abschnitte.text: The **reaction rate** describes how fast starting substances are used up or products are formed. To measure it, you find out how much an amount of substance or a concentration changes in a certain time. When marble reacts with hydrochloric acid, carbon dioxide is produced, and you can measure the **amount of gas per minute**. At the beginning the reaction is usually fastest, because there is still most starting substance there.

For particles to react, they must collide; this is how the **collision theory** describes it. Not every collision leads to a reaction: the particles need enough energy, the so-called **activation energy**. The more often and more violently the particles collide, the faster the reaction goes. So anything that increases the number of effective collisions speeds up the reaction.

When it gets warmer, the particles move faster and collide more often and more violently. According to the **RGT rule**, the reaction rate rises to about two to four times as much with 10 degrees more. The other way round, cold slows reactions down, which is why food stays fresh longer in the **fridge**. This is also used in cooking: at high heat, food cooks faster.

The more finely a substance is divided, the larger its **surface area** and the more particles can react at the same time. That is why wood shavings burn faster than a whole log. Finely spread flour or wood dust in the air can even explode, which is dangerous in mills and joiners’ workshops. A higher **concentration** also speeds things up; magnesium, for example, reacts more violently in more concentrated hydrochloric acid.

A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. It lowers the activation energy so that more collisions lead to a reaction. In a car, a catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. In our body, **enzymes** work as catalysts and make digestion possible at body temperature, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: The minimum energy particles need for a reaction.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
How much of a substance there is in a particular amount of solution.
The explanation that particles must collide in order to react.

gewusst: Without enzymes, some reactions in the body would run millions of times more slowly.
Flour dust explosions have destroyed whole mills in the past.

teile.einleitung: Soured milk is milk that has become sour and thick through lactic acid bacteria. It tastes tangy and refreshing and is one of humanity’s oldest milk products. Quark and many other foods are also made from it.
wichtigste: Lactic acid bacteria make milk sour.
In the process, lactic acid is formed from milk sugar.
Soured milk becomes thick and tastes tangy.
Milk goes sour fastest in a warm room.
Yoghurt is also made with the help of lactic acid bacteria.
If you let soured, thick milk drain, you get quark.
The yellowish liquid that separates is called whey.

abschnitte.text: Soured milk, also called **thick milk**, is milk that has been soured by **lactic acid bacteria**. It is thicker than fresh milk and tastes pleasantly tangy. In the past it was made by simply leaving raw milk in a warm place. Today dairies add carefully chosen bacteria, a so-called **starter culture**, to the milk.

The lactic acid bacteria feed on the **milk sugar** in the milk. They turn it into **lactic acid**, and the milk becomes more and more acidic. The acid makes the milk protein casein curdle; it clumps together and the milk becomes thick. In warmth the bacteria multiply faster, which is why milk goes sour faster in a warm room than in the fridge.

If you let thick soured milk drain in a cloth, a white, firm mass is left behind, the **quark**. The yellowish green liquid that runs off is called **whey**. Whey contains water, milk sugar, minerals and a little protein. In Switzerland whey is made into drinks, for example, or fed to pigs.

**Yoghurt**, buttermilk, kefir and sour cream are also made with lactic acid bacteria. Depending on the kind of bacteria and the temperature, they taste different. For yoghurt, for example, the milk is kept warm at about 40 degrees. The acid makes these products keep longer, because many harmful germs grow poorly in acidic conditions.

Milk from the shop is usually pasteurised or heated to a high temperature, which kills most bacteria. Such milk often does not go nicely sour, but is spoilt by other germs and can smell bitter or rotten. Then you should not drink it any more. That is why real soured milk is best bought ready-made or made with a **starter culture**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things that turn milk sugar into lactic acid.
The acid that gives soured milk and yoghurt their tangy taste.
The liquid left over when quark or cheese is made from milk.
Heating milk briefly to kill germs.

gewusst: Sauerkraut and pickled gherkins are also preserved with lactic acid bacteria.
Lactic acid is also produced in our muscles when they work hard.

teile.einleitung: Smoke is produced when something burns and consists of hot gases and tiny particles. You often smell it before you see a fire. In a fire, the smoke is usually more dangerous than the flames themselves.
wichtigste: Smoke consists of gases and tiny solid or liquid particles.
In a fire, you often smell the smoke first.
In a house fire, the smoke is often the most dangerous thing.
In a smoke-filled room you crawl along the floor, because there is less smoke there.
Smoke makes your eyes sting and water.
Smoke from a chimney shows that a fire is burning in the stove.
If the stairwell is full of smoke, you keep the flat door shut and call for help.

abschnitte.text: Smoke is a mixture of hot **combustion gases** and countless tiny particles. The particles include **soot**, ash and small droplets of water and tar. The gases are, for example, carbon dioxide, water vapour and poisonous carbon monoxide. Depending on what is burning and how much air the fire gets, smoke looks white, grey or black.

If a substance burns completely, mainly invisible gases are produced. But if the fire is short of oxygen or the wood is damp, not everything burns, and a lot of smoke forms. That is why wet wood smokes particularly heavily on a campfire. Because hot air is lighter than cold air, the smoke rises, for example out of a **chimney** on the roof.

In a fire, most people do not die from the flames but from the **smoke**. Just a few breaths can make you unconscious, because the gas **carbon monoxide** stops the blood from carrying oxygen. Smoke also irritates the eyes, which sting and water, and it makes it hard to see. Because it rises, the air near the floor stays breathable for longer, which is why you should crawl in a smoke-filled room.

If the stairwell is full of smoke, you stay in the flat, keep the door shut and call the fire brigade on **118**. You can seal the gap under the door with wet cloths and make yourself noticed at the window. If there is a fire in your own flat, you leave it immediately and close the doors behind you. A **smoke alarm** gives an early warning, even when you are asleep.

abschnitte.titel: Smoke in the environment and in language
abschnitte.text: Smoke from chimneys, factories and forest fires pollutes the air with **fine particles**. Large forest fires can produce clouds of smoke that travel thousands of kilometres and make the sky hazy. In the past people also used smoke to preserve meat and fish; this is called smoking. The saying “There is no smoke without fire” means that there is usually some truth in a rumour.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invisible, odourless and very poisonous gas from fires.
Black particles of carbon produced by incomplete burning.
Tiny particles in the air that get deep into the lungs.
Preserving food with smoke.

gewusst: In a room fire, smoke can spread through a whole flat within a few minutes.
In the past, some peoples communicated over long distances with smoke signals.

teile.einleitung: A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery in which lithium ions move back and forth between two electrodes. It is found in mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and electric cars. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for its development in 2019.
wichtigste: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino for the lithium-ion battery.
In 1991 Sony brought the first commercial lithium-ion battery onto the market.
The negative electrode is usually made of graphite.
During charging, lithium ions slot in between the layers of graphite; this is called intercalation.
A typical cell with graphite and lithium cobalt oxide has a nominal voltage of about 3.6 volts.
The electrolyte contains no water, because water would be broken down at this high voltage.
Damaged cells can overheat and burn; this is called thermal runaway.

abschnitte.text: A lithium-ion battery consists of two **electrodes** with an electrolyte and a thin dividing layer, the separator, between them. During charging, lithium ions move from the positive electrode to the negative one and slot in there between the layers of the **graphite**. During discharging they move back, and at the same time electrons flow through the device and supply electricity. This slotting in and out is called **intercalation**; you can compare it to guests moving back and forth between two hotels.

The positive electrode is made of lithium metal oxides, for example lithium cobalt oxide. The material **lithium iron phosphate** is regarded as particularly safe and does without expensive cobalt. Because water would be broken down at the high cell voltage, an electrolyte made of organic solvents is used. During the first charge, a thin protective layer forms on the graphite, the **solid electrolyte interphase**, or SEI for short.

In the 1970s **Stanley Whittingham** built a first lithium battery, but it was still unsafe. In 1980 John Goodenough found a better material for the positive electrode in lithium cobalt oxide. In 1985 Akira Yoshino replaced the dangerous pure lithium with an electrode made of carbon. Sony sold the first batteries in 1991, and in 2019 the three scientists jointly received the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry.

Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy with little weight. That is why they are found in smartphones, laptops, headphones, e-bikes and electric cars. They can be charged hundreds to thousands of times, but lose **capacity** over time. Large battery storage systems also help to keep electricity from solar and wind power for later.

If a battery is damaged, overcharged or strongly heated, a short circuit can occur inside. The cell then gets hotter and hotter; this **thermal runaway** can lead to fire. That is why batteries should not be pierced, not left in blazing sun and only charged with suitable chargers. Swollen batteries must not be used any more.

Batteries never belong in the household rubbish, because they can start fires in bin lorries and plants. In Switzerland, every shop that sells batteries takes back old batteries free of charge. In **recycling**, valuable substances such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and copper are recovered. This means less new material has to be mined.

begriffe.erklaerung: A store for electrical energy that can be recharged.
A conducting part of a battery where electrons enter or leave.
The substance between the electrodes through which the ions move.
Ions slotting in between the layers of a material.
Self-reinforcing overheating of a damaged battery cell.

gewusst: John Goodenough was 97 years old at the Nobel Prize ceremony, making him the oldest Nobel Prize winner of all time.
Lithium is the lightest metal and even floats on water.
An electric car often contains thousands of individual battery cells.

teile.einleitung: The Nernst equation is an important formula in electrochemistry. It calculates how the voltage of a battery or an electrode depends on the concentration of the dissolved ions and on temperature. Without it, you could neither build pH meters nor understand why batteries get weaker over time.
wichtigste: The Nernst equation was put forward in 1889 by the German chemist Walther Nernst.
It describes how the electrode potential depends on the ion concentration.
The factor RT/(zF) contains the gas constant R, the temperature T, the charge number z and the Faraday constant F.
At 25 °C and z = 1, the potential changes by about 59 mV when the concentration falls to a tenth.
As the temperature rises, the factor becomes larger.
Even two identical half-cells with different concentrations produce a voltage; this is a concentration cell.
pH meters are based on the same principle.

abschnitte.text: **Walther Nernst** lived from 1864 to 1941 and was one of Germany’s best-known physical chemists. He put forward the equation named after him in 1889. Later he formulated the third law of thermodynamics and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1920. He also invented an electric lamp, the Nernst lamp.

Every **half-cell**, for example a silver wire in a silver salt solution, has a particular electrical potential. At a concentration of 1 mol/L it equals the **standard potential** E°, which can be found in tables. If the concentration changes, the potential changes too. The Nernst equation says exactly by how much: E = E° + (RT/zF) times ln(c). At 25 °C you can simply calculate 0.059 V divided by z times the base 10 logarithm of the concentration.

A silver half-cell with E° = +0.80 V has a potential at 0.01 mol/L silver ions of 0.80 V minus 2 times 0.059 V, that is about +0.68 V. For nickel with z = 2 and E° = -0.25 V, a concentration of 0.01 mol/L gives about -0.31 V. The **hydrogen electrode** has a potential of about -0.41 V instead of 0 V at pH 7 and 25 °C. This shows how strongly the pH affects electrochemistry.

If you connect two silver half-cells with 1 mol/L and 0.001 mol/L, a current flows, even though both are made of the same metal. This **concentration cell** produces about 0.18 V at 25 °C. The half-cell with the lower concentration forms the anode; there silver goes into solution. The cell works until both concentrations are the same.

The factor RT/(zF) becomes larger when the temperature rises, which is why you need to know the temperature for precise measurements. The equation explains why a battery slowly loses voltage as it discharges: the concentrations inside it change. **pH meters** measure a voltage and convert it into a pH value with the help of the Nernst equation. Nerve cells also use differences in ion concentration to produce electrical signals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A conductor, usually a piece of metal, through which current flows into or out of a solution.
An electrode dipping into a solution of its own ions, half of a battery.
The electric charge of one mole of electrons, about 96,485 coulombs per mole.
The electrode at which electrons are given up.

gewusst: Nernst did not receive the Nobel Prize in 1920 for his equation, but for his work on thermochemistry.
The voltage that a nerve cell builds up at rest can be estimated with an equation modelled on Nernst’s.
A concentration cell shows that electrical energy can be obtained from nothing more than a difference in the amount of salt.

teile.einleitung: Carbohydrates are natural substances such as sugar, starch and cellulose that consist mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Plants make them with the help of sunlight, and for us humans they are the most important source of energy in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes.
wichtigste: The name carbohydrates comes from the fact that many have the formula Cn(H2O)m, as if they were hydrates of carbon.
A distinction is made between simple sugars, double sugars and complex sugars.
Fructose is a ketohexose, glucose an aldohexose.
In water, glucose mostly forms a six-membered ring, the pyranose.
Cellulose and amylose both consist of glucose, but linked in different ways.
Chitin forms the outer skeleton of insects and crustaceans.
A brick-red precipitate in Fehling’s test shows a reducing sugar.

abschnitte.text: **Carbohydrates** are a large group of natural substances. Many of them have the formula Cn(H2O)m, which in the past made it look as if they were made of carbon and water. This is where the name comes from. Carbohydrates include sweet sugars as well as tasteless substances such as starch and cellulose.

**Monosaccharides** or simple sugars are the smallest building blocks, for example glucose (grape sugar) and fructose (fruit sugar). Glucose has an aldehyde group and is an aldohexose; fructose has a keto group and is a ketohexose. If two simple sugars join, a disaccharide is formed, such as table sugar, sucrose, or milk sugar, lactose. Long chains of many building blocks are called **polysaccharides**.

In water, glucose usually closes up into a ring. Mostly a six-membered ring of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom is formed, the **pyranose**. When the ring closes, a new stereocentre is created, the anomeric carbon atom. Depending on how the OH group sits on it, it is called alpha or beta glucose.

Plants store energy as **starch**, which consists of amylose and amylopectin. Amylose is an unbranched chain with alpha-1,4 bonds; amylopectin is branched by extra alpha-1,6 bonds. Cellulose forms the cell walls of plants and is built from glucose with beta-1,4 bonds, which our body cannot split. The nitrogen-containing polysaccharide chitin makes the shells of insects and crustaceans hard.

**Fehling’s test** is used to check whether a sugar is reducing. The sample is heated with a deep blue copper solution. If a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide forms, a reducing sugar such as glucose is present. Starch, on the other hand, is detected with iodine solution, which turns bluish black.

Carbohydrates provide about 17 kilojoules per gram and are the most important fuel for muscles and brain. During digestion, the body breaks starch down into glucose, which travels in the blood to the cells. The body stores surplus glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. In Switzerland sugar is obtained from sugar beet, which is processed in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple sugar, the smallest building block of carbohydrates, for example glucose.
A complex sugar made of long chains of sugar units, such as starch.
A link between two sugar units.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.

gewusst: Cellulose is the most common organic substance on Earth.
Cows and other ruminants can only digest cellulose thanks to microorganisms in their rumen.
If you chew bread for a long time, it tastes sweeter, because an enzyme in saliva splits starch into sugar.

teile.einleitung: Kurt Wüthrich is a Swiss chemist and biophysicist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. He developed a method that makes it possible to see the three-dimensional structure of protein molecules in solution. This makes him one of the best-known researchers at the ETH Zurich.
wichtigste: Kurt Wüthrich was born in Aarberg in the canton of Bern in 1938.
In 2002 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for determining the structure of biological molecules in solution by NMR.
With his method a protein does not have to be crystallised, unlike in X-ray crystallography.
He used the nuclear Overhauser effect to measure distances between hydrogen atoms in proteins.
Wüthrich taught as professor of biophysics at the ETH Zurich.
He also held a professorship at the Scripps Research Institute in California.
In 1996 his group determined the structure of the prion protein, and in 1997 it developed the TROSY technique.

abschnitte.text: **Kurt Wüthrich** was born on 4 October 1938 in Aarberg in the canton of Bern. He studied chemistry, physics and mathematics at the University of Bern and wrote his doctoral thesis in Basel. After that he did research in the USA for several years, among other places at the University of California in Berkeley. In 1969 he came to the ETH Zurich, where he later became professor of biophysics.

Wüthrich worked with **nuclear magnetic resonance**, NMR for short. Molecules are placed in a very strong magnetic field and irradiated with radio waves. The atomic nuclei, especially the hydrogen nuclei, then send out signals that reveal a lot about their neighbours. The same physical principle is used in the MRI scanner in hospital.

In the 1980s Wüthrich showed how NMR can be used to determine the three-dimensional structure of **proteins**. For this he used the **nuclear Overhauser effect**, which can measure which hydrogen atoms lie close together. From many such distances, the computer calculates the shape of the whole molecule, rather like a jigsaw puzzle. The big advantage: the protein does not have to be crystallised and can be studied in solution, much as in a living cell.

In 2002 Kurt Wüthrich received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry**. He shared it with the American John B. Fenn and the Japanese Kōichi Tanaka, who had developed methods of mass spectrometry for biological molecules. Wüthrich received half of the prize. This puts him among a whole series of Nobel Prize winners who have done research at the ETH Zurich.

In 1996 Wüthrich’s group determined the structure of the **prion protein**, which is linked to the cattle disease BSE. In 1997 his laboratory developed the TROSY technique, which makes it possible to study even very large proteins and protein complexes. Besides the ETH Zurich, he also taught at the Scripps Research Institute in La Jolla, California. His methods are used today in laboratories all over the world, for example in developing new medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A molecule made of long chains of amino acids.
Nuclear magnetic resonance, a measuring method using a magnetic field and radio waves.
A method in which crystals are X-rayed to make molecules visible.
The science that studies life processes with the methods of physics.

gewusst: With NMR you can not only determine the shape of a protein, but also watch how it moves.
The shape of a protein decides what job it can do in the body.
NMR studies need magnets that are many hundreds of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: A molecule is a tiny particle in which two or more atoms are firmly joined together. Water, oxygen and sugar are made of molecules. They are so small that a single drop of water contains more molecules than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth.
wichtigste: A molecule consists of at least two firmly joined atoms.
A water molecule H₂O consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
The oxygen we breathe in has the formula O₂.
Ozone consists of three oxygen atoms.
A carbon dioxide molecule CO₂ has three atoms.
A methane molecule CH₄ contains five atoms.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of tiny **atoms**. When several atoms stick firmly together, a **molecule** is formed. The atoms are held together by **chemical bonds**, in which they share electrons with each other. Molecules are so small that you cannot see them even with a normal light microscope.

Chemists write molecules with a **formula**. H₂O means: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. CO₂ has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, so three atoms. Methane CH₄ has one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms, so five altogether.

abschnitte.titel: Molecules of one kind of atom
abschnitte.text: Identical atoms can also join. The oxygen we breathe in consists of molecules with two atoms, that is **O₂**. **Ozone** consists of three oxygen atoms and protects us high up in the atmosphere from dangerous UV rays. Nitrogen in the air also occurs as N₂.

Some molecules consist of only two atoms. A molecule of table sugar already has 45 atoms. The genetic material **DNA** is a giant molecule with billions of atoms. Plastics also consist of very long chain molecules called **polymers**.

Because molecules are so small, **molecular models** made of balls and sticks are built in lessons. Each kind of atom has its own colour: carbon is usually black, oxygen red and hydrogen white. With special microscopes such as the **scanning tunnelling microscope**, individual atoms can be imaged. This instrument was invented in 1981 in Rüschlikon near Zurich, for which Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer received the Nobel Prize.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest building block of a chemical element.
A particle made of at least two firmly joined atoms.
A shorthand that shows which atoms and how many a molecule has.
A gas made of molecules with three oxygen atoms.

gewusst: A glass of water contains about ten million billion billion water molecules, that is a 1 with 25 zeros.
The word molecule comes from the Latin “moles” and means “small mass”.
What we smell as a scent are individual molecules that get into our nose.

teile.einleitung: A buffer solution is a liquid whose pH hardly changes when a little acid or alkali is added. It consists of a weak acid and its matching base, which complement each other. Buffers are important for laboratories and also keep our blood in the right range.
wichtigste: A buffer solution is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base.
One example is the mixture of acetic acid and sodium acetate.
If acid is added, the base mops up the protons.
The buffer capacity is greatest when acid and base are present in equal amounts.
A buffer works roughly in the range from one pH unit below to one above its pKa.
When diluted moderately with water, the pH of a buffer stays almost the same.
Inside cells, the phosphate buffer is particularly important.

abschnitte.text: A buffer solution contains a **weak acid** and its **conjugate base**, that is the particle left over after a proton has been given up. A classic example is the **acetate buffer** made of acetic acid and sodium acetate. The two partners are in equilibrium with each other. This allows the buffer to mop up both added acid and added alkali.

If you add a little hydrochloric acid to an acetate buffer, the acetate ions take up the protons and become acetic acid. If you add sodium hydroxide solution instead, the acetic acid gives up protons, which react with the hydroxide ions to form water. In both cases the ratio of acid to base changes only a little. That is why the **pH** also stays almost the same, whereas in pure water it would jump sharply.

Every buffer works within a particular **buffer range**, about one pH unit below and above the pKa of the acid. A phosphate buffer with a pKa of 7.21 therefore buffers roughly between pH 6.2 and 8.2. The **buffer capacity** says how much acid or alkali a buffer can cope with, and it is greatest with equal amounts of acid and base. If both partners are made more concentrated in the same ratio, the capacity rises without the pH changing.

Human blood has a pH of about 7.4 and may only differ from it a little. This is ensured mainly by the **carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer**. In the cells the phosphate buffer is particularly important, and proteins also help with buffering. Without these systems, even small amounts of acid from metabolism would disturb vital enzymes.

abschnitte.titel: Buffers in everyday life and the laboratory
abschnitte.text: In the laboratory, buffers are needed to calibrate **pH meters** and to carry out biological experiments at a constant pH. Many medicines, cosmetics and foods also contain buffer substances. Seawater is buffered too, mainly by dissolved carbonates. Because the oceans take up a lot of carbon dioxide, this natural buffer is slowly being strained.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
The particle formed from an acid when it gives up a proton.
The amount of acid or alkali that a buffer can mop up.
A positively charged hydrogen ion that acids give up.

gewusst: Without buffers in the blood, even intense sports training would be dangerous because of the acid produced.
A good buffer can absorb a pH jump that would amount to several pH units in pure water.

teile.einleitung: A redox flow cell is a special battery in which the energy is stored in liquids. These liquids are kept in large tanks and pumped through a stack of cells. Such batteries are well suited for storing electricity from sun and wind for later.
wichtigste: The energy is in liquid electrolytes kept in tanks.
Pumps circulate the electrolytes through the cell stack.
A membrane that lets ions through separates the two electrolytes.
The most common type is the vanadium redox flow battery.
Power and storage capacity can be increased separately.
Redox flow batteries are mainly used as large stationary storage systems.

abschnitte.text: A redox flow cell, also called a **flow battery**, is a rechargeable energy store. Unlike in a mobile phone battery, the energy is not in solid electrodes but in two liquid **electrolytes**. These liquids are kept in two separate tanks. During charging and discharging, **redox reactions** take place, in which electrons are given up and taken up.

**Pumps** move the two electrolytes from their tanks into a stack of cells. There they flow past electrodes, separated by a **membrane** that lets ions through. During discharging, one liquid gives up electrons and the other takes them up, and electricity flows through an external circuit. During charging the process is reversed with electricity, and the liquids are “filled up” again.

The most widespread type is the **vanadium redox flow battery**, which was developed in Australia in the 1980s. In both tanks the metal vanadium is dissolved, but in different oxidation states. The negative side uses the states +2 and +3, the positive side the states +4 and +5. Because the same element is on both sides, a crossing through the membrane does not destroy the electrolyte; it only costs a little energy.

The **power** depends on the size of the cell stack, the **storage capacity** on the size of the tanks. So both can be increased separately; for more energy you simply build bigger tanks. The batteries can withstand many thousands of charging cycles and hardly burn, because the electrolytes consist mostly of water. On the other hand, they store much less energy per kilogram than lithium-ion batteries and are therefore unsuitable for cars or mobile phones.

Redox flow batteries are mainly used as **large stationary storage systems**, for example next to solar and wind farms. They store electricity when a lot is being produced and release it when it is needed. In this way they help to keep the electricity grid stable. Researchers in Switzerland and Germany are also working on new electrolytes that should be cheaper and more environmentally friendly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid in which charged particles conduct electricity.
A thin dividing layer that only lets certain particles through.
A reaction in which electrons move from one substance to another.
A number that shows how many electrons an atom has given up or taken up.

gewusst: The vanadium electrolytes have different colours depending on how charged they are, for example violet, green, blue or yellow.
Some redox flow stores are as big as a sports hall and can supply whole neighbourhoods for hours.

teile.einleitung: The peptide bond is the chemical link that holds amino acids together in long chains. Without it there would be no proteins, so no muscles, no hair and no enzymes. It is, so to speak, the press stud with which nature links its protein bead chains.
wichtigste: A peptide bond joins two amino acids together.
It is formed by a condensation in which a water molecule is split off.
The carbonyl carbon of one amino acid is joined directly to the nitrogen of the other.
The bond partly behaves like a double bond and therefore cannot rotate freely.
In proteins the peptide bond is usually in the trans form.
In the cell, peptide bonds are formed at the ribosomes.
With the biuret test, peptide bonds can be detected by a violet colour.

abschnitte.text: Every amino acid has an **amino group** (NH₂) and a **carboxyl group** (COOH). In the peptide bond, the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next. The carbon atom of the carbonyl group and the nitrogen atom are joined. Chemically, the peptide bond is a special form of the **amide bond**.

When a peptide bond is formed, a molecule of water is released, which is why it is called a **condensation**. For every new bond in a chain, exactly one water molecule is formed. If you join 100 amino acids into a straight chain, 99 bonds are formed and therefore 99 water molecules. The reverse process is called **hydrolysis**; the bond is split again with water, as in digestion in the stomach and intestine.

The electrons of the peptide bond are spread over several atoms; this phenomenon is called **resonance**. As a result, the bond between carbon and nitrogen behaves a little like a double bond. The atoms involved therefore lie in one plane and cannot rotate freely against each other. The neighbours are usually in the **trans form**, that is on opposite sides, because this way they are less in each other’s way.

Two linked amino acids are called a dipeptide; short chains are called peptides and very long chains proteins. The order of the amino acids in the chain is the **primary structure** of a protein. In the cell, the **ribosomes** build the chains according to the blueprint in the genetic information. They add one amino acid after another, often several per second.

With the **biuret test**, peptide bonds can be made visible. Sodium hydroxide solution and a little copper sulphate are added to a protein solution, and the solution turns violet. Around 1901 the German chemist **Emil Fischer** was one of the first to make peptides artificially, and he coined the term peptide. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1902, though for his work on sugars and purines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block from which proteins are put together.
A reaction in which two molecules join and give off water.
Splitting a bond with the help of water.
A tiny protein factory in every cell.
The spreading of electrons over several atoms, which makes a bond more stable.

gewusst: A single protein can contain hundreds or even thousands of peptide bonds.
The peptide bond is very stable in water and without enzymes would often take years to break down by itself.

teile.einleitung: Mass spectrometry is a measuring method for finding out how heavy individual atoms and molecules are. The particles are given an electric charge and sorted by their mass, rather like a pair of scales for the tiniest particles. With it, researchers identify unknown substances, find traces of doping or study proteins.
wichtigste: In mass spectrometry, particles are first turned into ions, that is electrically charged.
The ions are separated by their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z for short.
The result is a mass spectrum with many vertical lines, the peaks.
The highest peak is called the base peak; all the others are compared with it.
Isotope patterns reveal whether a substance contains chlorine or bromine, for example.
Francis William Aston discovered many isotopes with an early mass spectrograph and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1922.
The method is used in medicine, environmental protection, doping control and research.

abschnitte.text: A **mass spectrometer** consists of three main parts: an ion source, an analyser and a detector. In the ion source the particles are charged, in the analyser they are sorted by mass, and in the detector they are counted. Because this only works without disturbing air, the instrument works in a high vacuum. Even tiny amounts of a substance, often less than a millionth of a gram, are enough for a measurement.

A classic method is **electron ionisation**: fast electrons hit the molecules and knock out an electron. As standard, an energy of 70 electronvolts is used so that the spectra can be compared with databases. Many molecules break into typical fragments that act like a fingerprint. For large, delicate biological molecules there are gentle methods such as electrospray ionisation, for which John B. Fenn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002.

There are various ways of separating the ions. In the **time-of-flight mass spectrometer**, TOF for short, all the ions are accelerated equally and then fly through a long tube. With the same charge, the lightest ions arrive at the detector first, just as a light ball flies faster than a heavy one if both are pushed equally hard. Other instruments deflect the ions in magnetic or electric fields.

In the **mass spectrum**, the x-axis shows the mass-to-charge ratio m/z and the y-axis shows how often it occurs. The molecular ion peak shows the mass of the whole molecule. A chlorine atom produces two peaks 2 units apart in a ratio of about 3 to 1, because there are the isotopes chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. With a bromine atom, the two peaks M and M+2 are about the same height. The **nitrogen rule** says: if a compound of C, H, N and O has an odd mass, it contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms.

Doping control laboratories use mass spectrometers to test urine and blood samples from athletes. In hospitals it is used to detect metabolic diseases in newborn babies or to identify bacteria. Environmental laboratories measure pollutants in drinking water, and food inspectors look for pesticides in vegetables. Space probes also carry mass spectrometers to study the gases on other planets and comets.

begriffe.erklaerung: An atom or molecule that is electrically charged because it has lost or gained electrons.
Atoms of the same element that differ in weight because they have different numbers of neutrons.
A spike or line in the spectrum showing that particles with this mass were measured.
A space from which almost all the air has been pumped out.

gewusst: Mass spectrometry proved that most chemical elements consist of several isotopes.
The space probe Rosetta used a mass spectrometer from Bern to study the gases of comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko.
A modern instrument can measure masses so precisely that the exact molecular formula of a molecule can be read from them.

teile.einleitung: Foam consists of many small gas bubbles surrounded by thin walls of liquid or solid material. It is found on a cappuccino, in the bath, in whipped cream and even in a mattress. Depending on the type, foam can be soft, firm, edible or an important extinguishing agent.
wichtigste: Foam consists of many small bubbles.
If you whisk egg white hard, you get stiffly beaten egg white.
For whipped cream, you whip cream.
The fire brigade often puts out burning petrol with firefighting foam.
Soap foam is white because the many bubbles reflect the light.
Solid foam is found in a mattress, for example.
A cappuccino has a layer of milk foam on top.
Liquid foam collapses over time.

abschnitte.text: Foam is a mixture in which many **gas bubbles** are trapped in a liquid or a solid. The bubbles are separated from each other by thin walls, called **lamellae**. If the material around the bubbles is liquid, it is called liquid foam, as with soap foam. If it is solid, solid foam is formed, as with a sponge or polystyrene.

Pure water hardly foams, because the bubbles burst immediately. Only substances such as **surfactants** in soap or protein in milk and eggs make the lamellae stable. Even so, the liquid drains downwards over time, the walls get thinner and burst. That is why foam collapses if you wait a long time. Soap foam is white because the many bubbles reflect the light in all directions.

If you whisk **egg white** hard, you get stiffly beaten egg white, from which meringues are baked, for example. Whipping cream produces whipped cream, which stays stable thanks to fat and protein. On a **cappuccino** there is a layer of milk foam, which is frothed with hot steam. Bread and cake are actually solid foams too, because their dough becomes light with gas bubbles during baking.

Mattresses, cushions and gym mats are often made of **foam material**, for example polyurethane. White polystyrene is foamed polystyrene and consists mostly of air. Such foams are light, soft or shock-absorbing and insulate well against cold and heat. There is solid foam in nature too, for example pumice, a rock from volcanoes that can even float on water.

Burning petrol or oil cannot be put out with water, because the water sinks underneath and can spatter the fire. For this the fire brigade uses **firefighting foam**, which lies over the burning liquid like a blanket. It cuts the fire off from oxygen and cools it at the same time. Because many firefighting foams used to contain long-lasting fluorine chemicals, fluorine-free foams are increasingly being used today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin wall between two foam bubbles.
A substance in soap and washing-up liquid that stabilises foam and dissolves fat.
A solid, often soft foam, for example in mattresses.
Foam with which the fire brigade smothers burning liquids.

gewusst: Polystyrene consists of about 98 per cent air.
The foam on sea waves is formed by natural substances from algae that act like soap.

teile.einleitung: Food colourings are substances used to colour food and drinks. They make sweets shine brightly, give pasta a golden yellow colour and make Easter eggs colourful. Some come from plants such as beetroot or turmeric, others are made in the laboratory.
wichtigste: Food colouring is used to colour food.
If you mix red and yellow food colouring, you get orange.
Beetroot colours food a strong red, turmeric colours it yellow.
A green colouring can be obtained from spinach.
On packaging, colourings carry numbers that begin with the letter E.
In warm water a drop of food colouring spreads faster than in cold water.
A white flower in coloured water gets coloured petals after a few days.

abschnitte.text: **Food colourings** are additives that give food colour or bring back lost colour. This is because many foods fade when they are cooked, stored or processed. Colour matters because we eat with our eyes too: a strawberry yoghurt should look pink. However, colourings change neither the taste nor the nutritional value of a food.

Many colourings come from plants. From **beetroot** you get the strong red betanin, from the spice **turmeric** the bright yellow curcumin. The green leaf pigment chlorophyll comes, for example, from spinach or nettles, and carrots provide orange carotene. Caramel colour, a brown colouring made from heated sugar, is also a natural colouring.

In Switzerland and the EU, approved additives must be listed on the packaging. For this there are **E numbers**; colourings carry the numbers from E 100. E 100, for example, stands for curcumin, E 162 for beetroot red. Artificially made colourings such as tartrazine (E 102) are often cheaper and stronger in colour, but some of them are criticised.

Food colourings can be mixed like paints. Red and yellow give orange, blue and yellow give green, and red and blue give violet. In this way confectioners can decorate cakes in every colour with just a few basic colours. At Easter many families in Switzerland dye eggs, in the past often with onion skins, today also with bought colours.

If you put a drop of colouring into warm water, it spreads faster than in cold water, because the water particles move faster. This mixing is called **diffusion**. If you put a white flower in coloured water for a few days, it sucks the water up through fine tubes in its stem, and the petals change colour. This makes it visible how plants transport water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance added to a food on purpose, for example for colour or to make it keep longer.
A label for approved additives on packaging.
Particles mixing by themselves, for example colouring in water.
A substance that gives colour, as found in plants for example.

gewusst: Some red food colourings come from tiny scale insects; this is the colouring carmine.
Farmed salmon often gets its pink colour from colourings in its feed.
Without colouring, many jelly bears would be almost colourless and see-through.

teile.einleitung: The atomic number of a chemical element shows how many protons there are in the nucleus of its atoms. It is like an identity card: every element has exactly one atomic number of its own. The elements are arranged in order in the periodic table according to it.
wichtigste: The atomic number is the number of protons in the atomic nucleus.
Every chemical element has its own atomic number.
An electrically neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
Hydrogen has the atomic number 1, neon 10, calcium 20 and iron 26.
Copper has the atomic number 29, silver 47 and gold 79.
In the periodic table the elements are arranged by increasing atomic number.
So far, elements up to atomic number 118 are known.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a nucleus of **protons** and neutrons. The number of protons is called the **atomic number** or proton number. It decides which element it is. An atom with 6 protons is always carbon, one with 8 protons always oxygen. If the number of protons changes, a different element is formed.

The lightest element, **hydrogen**, has the atomic number 1, helium has 2. Neon has the atomic number 10, sulphur 16, calcium 20 and iron 26. For the metals used to make jewellery and coins, it is 29 for copper, 47 for silver and 79 for **gold**. Uranium, with the atomic number 92, is the heaviest element found in larger amounts in nature. The heaviest known element, oganesson, has the atomic number 118.

Protons are positively charged, electrons negatively. In an electrically **neutral** atom there are therefore as many electrons as protons. So a magnesium atom with the atomic number 12 has 12 electrons. If an atom gives up or takes up electrons, it becomes an **ion**. Its atomic number stays the same, because the protons in the nucleus do not change.

In the **periodic table** the elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, row by row. In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev first arranged the elements by their mass. He left gaps for elements that were not yet known. Only later did it turn out that the atomic number decides the real order. In most versions of the periodic table, the atomic number is written small above or next to the element symbol.

In 1913 the young English physicist **Henry Moseley** studied the X-rays of different elements. He found that their wavelength changes regularly from element to element. From this he concluded that each element has its own whole number, which corresponds to the charge of the nucleus. He was even able to predict that elements were still missing at some atomic numbers. These were later actually discovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
Another name for the atomic number, because it gives the number of protons and so the positive charge of the nucleus.
A table of all the chemical elements, arranged by their atomic number.
A pure substance whose atoms all have the same atomic number.

gewusst: Elements with very high atomic numbers have been made artificially in particle accelerators and often decay in fractions of a second.
The atomic number is always a whole number, because there are no half protons.
For centuries alchemists tried to turn lead, atomic number 82, into gold, atomic number 79, without success.

teile.einleitung: Metals are substances such as iron, copper, gold or aluminium that shine and conduct electricity and heat well. Most chemical elements are metals. For thousands of years people have used metals for tools, jewellery, coins and machines.
wichtigste: All metals conduct electricity.
Metals shine, conduct heat well and can be shaped.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Iron is attracted by a magnet.
Bronze consists mainly of copper and tin.
Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon.
Aluminium is a light metal used for cans and kitchen foil.

abschnitte.text: Metals have a typical **metallic shine**. All metals **conduct electricity**, and they also conduct heat well, which is why a metal spoon in hot tea quickly gets warm. They can be bent, hammered and drawn into wire without breaking. The reason is that some of their electrons can move freely between the atoms.

**Iron** is the most widely used metal and is attracted by magnets. **Copper** conducts electricity very well and is therefore used for the electric cables in houses. Aluminium is light and is used for drinks cans, kitchen foil and aeroplanes. Gold and silver are precious metals that hardly rust and are popular for jewellery.

**Mercury** is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. In the past it was found in clinical thermometers and other thermometers. Because its vapour is poisonous, it is now banned in clinical thermometers in Switzerland. The metal with the highest melting point is **tungsten**, which only melts at over 3400 degrees.

If you mix molten metals, an **alloy** is formed, which often has better properties. **Bronze** consists mainly of copper and tin and was so important that a whole era is called the Bronze Age. Steel is an alloy of iron and a little carbon. Brass, made of copper and zinc, is used for brass instruments and door handles.

Switzerland has hardly any ore deposits of its own, but iron ore used to be mined, for example, at Gonzen near Sargans. Today the **recycling** of metals is very important. Aluminium cans and tin cans are collected and melted down in Switzerland. Recycled aluminium needs only about a twentieth of the energy needed for new aluminium.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of molten metals that becomes solid when it cools.
A substance through which electricity or heat can flow well.
A metal such as gold or silver that hardly rusts.
Rock from which metals can be obtained.

gewusst: Gallium melts at only about 30 degrees and would turn liquid in your hand.
One gram of gold can be beaten into a wafer-thin foil of about half a square metre.
The heaviest metal is osmium; a cube with sides of 10 centimetres weighs over 22 kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Leopold Ružička was a chemist who was born in Croatia and later became Swiss. He researched fragrances and terpenes and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 1939. For many years he made the ETH Zurich a world-famous centre of organic chemistry.
wichtigste: Leopold Ružička was born in 1887 in Vukovar in what is now Croatia.
He worked as an assistant to Hermann Staudinger in Karlsruhe and followed him to the ETH Zurich.
In the 1920s he did research for the Geneva fragrance company Chuit, Naef & Cie, later Firmenich.
He proved that the fragrances muscone and civetone consist of very large carbon rings.
According to his isoprene rule, terpenes are built from units with five carbon atoms.
In 1939 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on polymethylenes and higher terpenes.
His successor at the ETH, Vladimir Prelog, also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1975.

abschnitte.text: **Leopold Ružička** was born on 13 September 1887 in Vukovar, which at that time belonged to Austria-Hungary. He studied chemistry at the Technical University in Karlsruhe. There he became assistant to **Hermann Staudinger**, who later received the Nobel Prize himself. In 1912 he followed Staudinger to the ETH Zurich and became a Swiss citizen a few years later.

In the 1920s Ružička worked for the Geneva company Chuit, Naef & Cie, which is called Firmenich today and is one of the largest fragrance manufacturers in the world. He studied the valuable fragrances **muscone** and **civetone**, which were obtained from animals. He discovered that their molecules consist of unusually large rings of carbon atoms. Until then, many chemists had thought such large rings were impossible or unstable.

Ružička worked on **terpenes**, a large group of natural substances found, for example, in resins, essential oils and plant pigments. He formulated the **isoprene rule**: terpenes are built from units of five carbon atoms each. A triterpene, for example, consists of six such isoprene units and therefore has 30 carbon atoms. This rule helped to work out the structure of many natural substances.

In 1939 Ružička received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for his work on polymethylenes and higher terpenes. He shared the prize with the German chemist Adolf Butenandt. Because of the Second World War, the prizes could not be celebrated in Stockholm as usual at that time. The prize made Ružička and the ETH Zurich even better known worldwide.

From 1929 to 1957 Ružička headed the laboratory of organic chemistry at the ETH Zurich and trained many young researchers. His successor **Vladimir Prelog** also received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1975. Ružička also collected paintings by Dutch and Flemish painters, which he gave to the Kunsthaus Zurich. He died in Switzerland in 1976, and the ETH still awards a prize named after him to young chemists today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of natural substances that give plants their scent, for example.
A building block of five carbon atoms from which terpenes are built.
