A substance with a scent, used for example in perfumes.
A molecule in which atoms are joined into a closed ring.

gewusst: Today the sought-after musk fragrances are made artificially, so no animals are needed for them any more.
The scent of lemons, pine needles and peppermint comes from terpenes.
People from many different countries did research in Ružička’s laboratory at the ETH.

teile.einleitung: Sulphuric acid is a very strong, oily and highly corrosive acid. It is one of the most important chemicals in the world and is produced in huge quantities. It is needed for fertiliser, batteries and countless other products.
wichtigste: Sulphuric acid has the formula H₂SO₄.
It is a diprotic acid and can give up two hydrogen ions.
When diluting, the rule is: always pour the acid into the water, never the other way round.
Concentrated sulphuric acid removes water from other substances and turns sugar black.
An important starting material for making it is sulphur dioxide.
A large part of sulphuric acid is used for fertilisers.
Chemically, gypsum is a salt of sulphuric acid.

abschnitte.text: **Sulphuric acid** H₂SO₄ is a colourless, oily liquid that is almost twice as heavy as water. It is a **diprotic acid**, because each molecule can give up two hydrogen ions. Its salts are called sulphates. It used to be called oil of vitriol. Bottles of concentrated sulphuric acid carry the hazard symbol for corrosive substances.

If you mix concentrated sulphuric acid with water, a great deal of heat is released. That is why the rule is: always pour the acid slowly into the water, never the other way round. A memory aid is: **“Always add acid to water, never water to acid.”** If you pour water into the acid, it can boil suddenly and throw out corrosive splashes.

Concentrated sulphuric acid strongly attracts water; it is **hygroscopic**. If you pour it onto sugar, it takes the water out of it. What remains is black carbon, which grows out of the beaker as a steaming black column. For the same reason it also chars wood, paper and skin. In laboratories it is used to dry gases.

First sulphur is burnt, producing the gas **sulphur dioxide**. In the **contact process**, this is converted into sulphur trioxide with the help of a catalyst. This is passed into sulphuric acid and then diluted with water. Today the sulphur comes mainly from the purification of crude oil and natural gas.

A large part of the sulphuric acid produced worldwide is used for **fertilisers**. Every car starter battery, the **lead-acid battery**, contains dilute sulphuric acid. It is also used to make paints, detergents, synthetic fibres and medicines. A well-known salt of sulphuric acid is **gypsum**, from which wallboards and plaster casts are made.

begriffe.erklaerung: An acid that can give up two hydrogen ions per molecule.
A salt of sulphuric acid, for example gypsum or Epsom salt.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
Strongly attracts water, even from the air.

gewusst: In the past, how strong a country’s industry was used to be measured by the amount of sulphuric acid it produced.
Acid rain forms, among other reasons, because sulphur dioxide from exhaust gases turns into sulphuric acid in the air.
On Venus the clouds consist largely of droplets of sulphuric acid.

teile.einleitung: The Lewis structure is a way of writing that chemists use to show how the atoms in a molecule are joined. Lines and dots represent the outer electrons. This way you can see at a glance which electrons form a bond and which are left over as lone pairs.
wichtigste: In 1916 Gilbert Newton Lewis showed valence electrons as dots around the element symbol.
He used this to explain chemical bonding by shared electron pairs.
A single line in a Lewis structure stands for two electrons.
The Lewis structure is also called a valence line formula.
Unlike a simple structural formula, it also shows the lone pairs.
The oxygen atom in water has two lone pairs, the nitrogen atom in ammonia one.
For methane, a total of 8 valence electrons have to be distributed.

abschnitte.text: A **Lewis structure** shows how the atoms in a molecule are joined to one another. Only the **valence electrons** are shown, that is the electrons in the outermost shell, because only they take part in bonds. A line between two atoms means a shared electron pair, that is a bond. A line next to an atom stands for a **lone pair**, which does not take part in a bond.

In 1916 the American chemist **Gilbert Newton Lewis** showed valence electrons as dots around the element symbol. He explained the bond between atoms by saying that they share electron pairs. Later a pair of dots was often replaced by a line, which is why the notation is also called a valence line formula. To this day it is one of the most important tools in chemistry lessons.

Many atoms are particularly stable when they have eight electrons around them, like the noble gases. This **octet rule** helps when drawing Lewis structures. Hydrogen is an exception; two electrons are enough for it. Sometimes atoms also share two or three electron pairs; then double or triple bonds form, as in the nitrogen molecule N₂.

In the **water molecule** H₂O, the oxygen atom is joined to the hydrogen atoms by two lines and carries two lone pairs. In ammonia NH₃, the nitrogen atom has three bonds and one lone pair. In the chlorine molecule Cl₂, the atoms share one pair, and each chlorine atom carries three lone pairs. In methane CH₄, 8 valence electrons are distributed over four bonds; there are no lone pairs.

With the Lewis structure you can predict what shape a molecule has in space. Lone pairs need room and push the bonds apart, which is why the water molecule is bent. From this you can work out whether a molecule is **polar**, which explains, for example, why salt dissolves in water. Lewis structures are therefore the basis for many other topics in chemistry.

begriffe.erklaerung: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom that form bonds.
Two electrons that belong together and are drawn as a line.
An electron pair that belongs to one atom and does not form a bond.
The rule that atoms like to have eight outer electrons.

gewusst: Gilbert Newton Lewis was often nominated for the Nobel Prize but never received it.
Lewis structures can also be drawn for ions; then the charge is added.
In carbon dioxide, the carbon atom is joined to the oxygen atoms by two double bonds.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, is a colourless and odourless gas made of carbon and oxygen. We breathe it out with every breath, and plants need it to grow. In too large amounts in the air, however, it strengthens the greenhouse effect and warms the climate.
wichtigste: A CO2 molecule consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Carbon dioxide is detected by bubbling it through limewater, which then turns cloudy.
Solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice and turns directly into gas at about minus 78 °C.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects near the ground, for example in fermentation cellars.
Because it pushes away oxygen, it is suitable for putting out fires.
Dissolved in water, it forms carbonic acid.
Yeast and baking powder make dough rise with carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.text: Carbon dioxide is a natural part of the air; its share is about 0.04 per cent (as of 2025). It is produced when people and animals breathe and when wood, coal, oil or gas burn. Plants take it in during **photosynthesis** and use it with the help of sunlight to make sugar. In doing so they give off oxygen, which we need to breathe.

Carbon dioxide is about one and a half times as heavy as air. That is why you can pour it like water from one glass into another and use it to put out a candle. In a school experiment, it is recognised with **limewater**, which turns milky. It can only be liquefied under increased pressure, which is why it is stored in pressurised cylinders.

At about minus 78 °C carbon dioxide becomes solid and is then called **dry ice**. It does not melt but turns directly into gas; this is called **sublimation**. That is why nothing wet is left behind. Dry ice is used for cooling goods and for fog effects on stage.

In fermentation cellars, a lot of carbon dioxide is produced when wine ferments, and it collects near the floor. Because you can neither see nor smell it, you can suffocate in it. Winemakers therefore use a burning candle to check whether there is enough oxygen. You also have to be careful when handling dry ice in closed rooms.

Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas**: it lets sunlight through but holds back part of the Earth’s heat. Since the beginning of industrialisation its share in the air has risen sharply, mainly through burning coal, oil and natural gas. As a result the Earth is warming, and in Switzerland the glaciers are melting. Many countries, including Switzerland, therefore want to cut their CO2 emissions sharply.

In yeast dough, yeast produces carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise; baking powder does the same without yeast. Fire extinguishers with CO2 are well suited for electrical equipment because they leave no residue. In drinks, the gas provides the fizz. The Zurich company **Climeworks** has developed plants that filter carbon dioxide directly out of the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat and so warms the Earth.
The process in which plants make sugar and oxygen from CO2, water and light.
Solid carbon dioxide, very cold.
Changing directly from solid to gas.
A solution used to detect carbon dioxide, because it turns cloudy.

gewusst: An adult breathes out about one kilogram of carbon dioxide a day.
The Scot Joseph Black discovered the gas around 1750 and called it “fixed air”.
On Venus the atmosphere consists almost entirely of carbon dioxide, which is why it is over 400 °C hot there.

teile.einleitung: A condensation reaction is a chemical reaction in which two molecules join to form a larger molecule. A small molecule is split off, usually water. This is how proteins are made in our body, but also plastics such as nylon and PET.
wichtigste: In a condensation reaction two molecules join, and a small molecule such as water is split off.
When two amino acids condense, a peptide bond is formed.
Three amino acids give a tripeptide, and two water molecules are split off.
Two glucose molecules form the double sugar maltose via an alpha-1,4 bond.
The reverse of condensation is called hydrolysis.
The plastic nylon is made by polycondensation.
PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethanediol.

abschnitte.text: In a **condensation reaction**, two molecules react with each other and are linked by a new bond. A small molecule is left over, usually water, sometimes also hydrogen chloride or methanol. The name has nothing to do with steam condensing, but recalls that molecules are “compressed” together. Typically, reactive groups such as OH, COOH or NH₂ groups are involved.

In our cells, amino acids are linked into proteins by condensation. The bond between two amino acids is called a **peptide bond**. For each new bond, one water molecule is split off, so with three amino acids there are two. Sugars also join in this way: two glucose molecules form malt sugar, **maltose**, via an alpha-1,4 bond.

The reverse of a condensation is **hydrolysis**. A bond is split again with the help of water. During digestion, enzymes break down the proteins, fats and starch from food into small building blocks by hydrolysis. The body can take these into the blood and build new substances from them.

If both starting substances have two reactive groups, many molecules can join together into long chains. This **polycondensation** produces important plastics. Nylon, a polyamide, was developed in the USA in the 1930s and is used for stockings, ropes and toothbrush bristles. PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethanediol and is made into drinks bottles and textile fibres.

If you heat ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid to about 140 °C, two ethanol molecules condense to form **diethyl ether**. When a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, an ester is formed with the loss of water; many esters smell of fruit. Silicones and some resins are also made by condensation reactions. So chemistry uses this principle in many different ways.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bond between two amino acids in a protein.
Splitting a bond with water, the opposite of condensation.
Condensation of many molecules into long chains, for example in plastics.
A substance made from an acid and an alcohol, which often smells fruity.

gewusst: A single PET chain can consist of hundreds of building blocks.
When a protein of 100 amino acids is built, 99 water molecules are split off.
In the 19th century diethyl ether was one of the first anaesthetics used in operations.

teile.einleitung: Popcorn is a crunchy snack made of burst maize kernels. When the kernels are heated, they explode with a loud pop and turn into white, fluffy little clouds. Behind this there is exciting chemistry and physics with water, steam and pressure.
wichtigste: Popcorn is made from a special kind of maize, popcorn maize.
Every maize kernel contains a little water.
When heated, the water turns into steam, which bursts the hard shell.
If the shell has a crack, the steam escapes and the kernel does not pop properly.
When it pops, the kernel becomes much bigger and there is a bang.
Maize originally comes from America.
A lid on the pan stops the kernels from jumping out.

abschnitte.text: Popcorn is made from **popcorn maize**, a special kind of maize with small, hard kernels. Not every kind of maize is suitable; sweetcorn or feed maize hardly pop. The kernel has a very hard, dense shell and a lot of **starch** inside. In the middle there is a little water, which is the key to popping.

If you heat the kernels in a pan, the water inside gets hot and turns into **steam**. The steam needs much more space, but the hard shell holds it in. The pressure rises until the shell suddenly bursts at about 180 °C. You hear the typical pop. If the shell has a crack, the steam escapes slowly and the kernel does not pop properly.

When it pops, the soft, hot starch in the kernel puffs up like foam. The steam escapes, and the starch immediately sets into a light, crunchy shape. In this way the kernel becomes much bigger than before. A few kernels are almost always left over, because they are too dry or have a damaged **shell**.

**Maize** originally comes from America, from what is now Mexico. People there grew it thousands of years ago and also knew popped maize kernels. Maize only came to Europe after the voyages of Christopher Columbus. In the cinema, popcorn became popular above all in the USA from the 1930s.

You put a little oil and a layer of popcorn maize into a pan and put a **lid** on it so that the kernels do not jump out. Over a medium heat you shake the pan now and then. When the popping almost stops, you take the pan off the cooker. Then you can season it sweet with sugar or salty with a little salt. Because hot oil is dangerous, children should only do this with adults.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of maize with hard kernels that burst when heated.
A nutrient from plants found in maize, potatoes and grain.
Water that has become a gas through heat and needs much more space.
The force with which something pushes from inside against a wall.

gewusst: A popcorn kernel sometimes jumps several centimetres high when it pops.
If the kernels have been stored too dry, far fewer of them pop.
Popcorn without sugar and butter is a wholegrain food with plenty of fibre.

teile.einleitung: A Lewis acid is a particle that can accept an electron pair from another particle. This explanation comes from the American chemist Gilbert Newton Lewis and is much broader than the idea of acids as sour liquids. It can also be used to understand reactions in which no hydrogen ions occur at all.
wichtigste: According to Lewis, an acid is an electron pair acceptor.
Gilbert Newton Lewis put forward this definition in 1923.
Boron trifluoride (BF₃) is a typical Lewis acid, because its boron atom has only an electron sextet.
A Lewis base donates a lone pair, for example ammonia.
BF₃ and NH₃ form a Lewis acid-base adduct.
The proton H⁺ and metal ions such as Cu²⁺ also act as Lewis acids.
Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base.

abschnitte.text: Lewis theory does not look at hydrogen ions but at **electron pairs**. A Lewis base has a lone pair that it makes available; it is called an **electron pair donor**. The Lewis acid has a gap and takes up this pair; it is an **electron pair acceptor**. The two join together through a new shared bond.

In the BF₃ molecule, the boron atom has only six outer electrons instead of the stable eight, that is an **electron sextet**. That is why it is looking for another electron pair. Ammonia (NH₃) has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom. When the two meet, a firm compound forms, the **Lewis acid-base adduct**.

Many positively charged metal ions are Lewis acids, because they have free places for electron pairs. A **Cu²⁺ ion**, for example, attaches four ammonia molecules, forming the deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex. Such compounds are called **complexes**. The proton H⁺ is also a Lewis acid, because it can take up an electron pair into its empty orbital.

The Swede Svante Arrhenius described acids as substances that form H⁺ ions in water. In 1923 Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry defined acids as proton donors. In the same year **Gilbert Newton Lewis** went even further and spoke of electron pairs. Because every Brønsted base needs a lone pair to bind a proton, it is always a Lewis base too.

In the 1960s the chemist Ralph Pearson divided Lewis acids and Lewis bases into “hard” and “soft” particles. This **HSAB concept** says that hard acids prefer to react with hard bases, and soft acids with soft bases. Hard particles are small and strongly charged; soft ones are large and easily deformed. In this way you can predict which compounds are particularly stable.

abschnitte.titel: What Lewis acids are needed for
abschnitte.text: In the chemical industry, Lewis acids such as aluminium chloride or boron trifluoride serve as **catalysts**. They help, for example, in making plastics, dyes and medicines. In living things, too, metal ions play a part as Lewis acids, for example in some enzymes. By the way, Lewis is also known for **Lewis structures**, in which electrons are drawn as dots and lines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that can accept an electron pair.
A particle that can donate a lone pair.
Two electrons that together occupy one orbital.
A compound formed when two particles join together.
A compound of a metal ion with attached molecules or ions.

gewusst: Gilbert Newton Lewis was nominated for the Nobel Prize very often but never received it.
The definitions of Brønsted and Lewis both appeared in the same year, 1923.
According to Lewis, substances that contain no hydrogen at all can also be acids.

teile.einleitung: An oxidation is a chemical reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen. This happens when things burn, when iron rusts and even in our body. Often it happens slowly and is hardly noticed, but sometimes in a flash with fire and heat.
wichtigste: An oxidation is a reaction of a substance with oxygen.
The product of an oxidation is called an oxide.
Chemically, rust is iron oxide.
Iron only rusts when oxygen and water are present.
Copper roofs turn green over time because a patina forms.
A cut apple turns brown because substances in it react with oxygen.
If oxygen is removed from an oxide, this is called reduction.

abschnitte.text: In an **oxidation**, a substance combines with **oxygen**. A new substance is formed, which is called an **oxide**. When coal burns, for example, carbon dioxide is formed. When magnesium burns, white magnesium oxide is formed with a dazzling light.

Some oxidations happen quickly and produce flames; this is called **combustion**. Others happen slowly and without fire; this is called **slow oxidation**. Slow oxidation also takes place in our body, when the cells turn sugar and oxygen into energy. This produces carbon dioxide and water, which we breathe out.

Chemically, rust is **iron oxide**, more precisely a hydrated iron oxide. For iron to rust, **oxygen and water** are needed. Salt speeds up rusting, which is why cars rust particularly quickly in winter because of road salt. Iron is protected with paint, oil or a coating of zinc; this is called **galvanising**.

Copper roofs, as seen on many churches, turn green over time. A **patina** forms, a thin layer that protects the copper underneath. A cut apple turns brown in the air because substances in the apple react with oxygen. A few drops of **lemon juice** slow this reaction down.

If oxygen is removed from an oxide, this is called **reduction**. This is how iron is obtained from iron ore in the blast furnace: carbon takes the oxygen away from the iron oxide. Oxidation and reduction always take place together; together they are called a **redox reaction**. Today chemists understand oxidation more generally as the loss of electrons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A compound of an element with oxygen.
Reddish brown iron oxide that forms on damp iron.
A green protective layer that forms on copper.
A reaction in which oxygen is removed from an oxide.

gewusst: The Statue of Liberty in New York was originally copper brown and only turned green because of the patina.
Gold practically does not oxidise in air, which is why gold finds still shine even after thousands of years.
Aluminium immediately forms a wafer-thin oxide layer that protects it from further corrosion.

teile.einleitung: A sacrificial anode is a piece of a base metal such as zinc or magnesium that protects a more valuable part from rusting. In a way it sacrifices itself: instead of the protected iron, it is slowly eaten away itself. Sacrificial anodes are found on ships, bridges, pipelines and in hot water tanks.
wichtigste: A sacrificial anode is made of a less noble metal than the part it protects.
Zinc is often used for steel ship hulls.
Many hot water tanks contain a sacrificial anode made of magnesium.
The sacrificial anode is part of cathodic corrosion protection.
The sacrificial anode and the part must be connected so that electricity can flow.
Because it gradually dissolves, a sacrificial anode has to be replaced from time to time.
In impressed current protection, a direct current source takes over the job of the base metal.

abschnitte.text: Iron and steel rust when they come into contact with water and oxygen. This eating away of metal is called **corrosion**. A **sacrificial anode** is a block or rod of a less noble metal that is connected to the steel so that electricity can flow. Now it is no longer the steel that is attacked, but the sacrificial anode. So it sacrifices itself for the part, hence the name.

Every metal gives up electrons with a different ease, as shown by the **electrochemical series**. Base metals such as magnesium, zinc or aluminium give up electrons more easily than iron. If they are connected to iron and lie in water, a small galvanic cell is formed, similar to a battery. The base metal becomes the **anode** and dissolves; the iron becomes the **cathode** and stays protected. That is why the method is called cathodic corrosion protection.

On the hulls of ships, sacrificial anodes usually sit below the **waterline**, where salt water attacks the steel particularly strongly. They are often made of zinc or aluminium. Oil rigs, harbour walls, sheet piling and **pipelines** in the ground are also protected in this way. As early as 1824 the English chemist Humphry Davy suggested protecting the copper sheathing of warships with pieces of less noble metal. The idea is still used today.

Many homes also contain a sacrificial anode, namely in the **hot water tank**. There a long rod of magnesium is usually fitted, which protects the steel tank from rust. Over the years the rod gets thinner and thinner. That is why a specialist should check it regularly and replace it if necessary. Otherwise the tank can rust through from the inside and start to leak.

For a sacrificial anode to work, it must be **electrically connected** to the part and lie in the same water or damp soil. The protective metal must be less noble than the part. Copper would be unsuitable for an iron pipe, because copper is more noble than iron and would even speed up rusting. For very large installations, **impressed current protection** is often used. A direct current source supplies the electrons, and no metal has to be sacrificed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The destruction of a metal by a chemical reaction with its surroundings, for example rusting.
The electrode at which a substance gives up electrons; the sacrificial anode dissolves.
The electrode at which electrons are taken up, here the protected part.
A metal that gives up electrons easily and reacts quickly, for example zinc or magnesium.
Corrosion protection in which a power source is used instead of a base metal.

gewusst: Hot-dip galvanised crash barriers and garden fences are protected on a similar principle, because the zinc corrodes first.
Outboard motors of boats also often have small sacrificial anodes, which are changed after a while.
Without corrosion protection, a steel ship in seawater would get large patches of rust after only a few years.

teile.einleitung: The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer is the most important buffer system in our blood. It makes sure that the pH of the blood always stays almost the same, even when acids are produced during sport or after eating.
wichtigste: The normal value for arterial blood is between pH 7.35 and 7.45.
The buffer consists of carbonic acid, or dissolved CO₂, and hydrogen carbonate ions.
The enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds up the reaction of CO₂ with water to form carbonic acid.
At pH 7.4, hydrogen carbonate and dissolved CO₂ are in a ratio of about 20 to 1.
The buffer works so well because it is an open system: CO₂ is breathed out through the lungs.
The kidneys regulate the hydrogen carbonate concentration in the long term.
Severe hyperventilation leads to respiratory alkalosis.

abschnitte.text: A **buffer** is a solution whose pH hardly changes when a little acid or base is added. It consists of a weak acid and its matching base. In the blood these are carbonic acid and the **hydrogen carbonate** ion HCO₃⁻, also called bicarbonate. If acid is added, hydrogen carbonate mops up the hydrogen ions; if base is added, carbonic acid releases hydrogen ions.

Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into hydrogen ions and hydrogen carbonate. Without help, this step is fairly slow. The enzyme **carbonic anhydrase**, which is found mainly in the red blood cells, speeds it up enormously. The pKa of this system is about 6.1; at pH 7.4 this gives a ratio of about 20 parts hydrogen carbonate to one part dissolved CO₂.

Actually, the pKa of 6.1 is a long way from the blood pH of 7.4. Even so, the system buffers very well because it is an **open system**. The lungs can quickly breathe out excess CO₂, within minutes. The kidneys help more slowly but lastingly, by keeping back or getting rid of hydrogen carbonate and releasing acids in the urine.

If the pH falls below 7.35, this is called **acidosis**; if it rises above 7.45, alkalosis. Anyone who breathes very fast and deeply, that is hyperventilates, breathes out too much CO₂, and respiratory alkalosis results. In metabolic acidosis, for example in diabetic ketoacidosis, the body does the opposite and breathes more deeply and faster to get rid of CO₂. In this way it makes up for the excess acid in the short term.

Seawater also contains carbonic acid, hydrogen carbonate and carbonate. The oceans take up a large part of the CO₂ released by humans from the air. As a result, the pH of seawater falls; this is called **ocean acidification**. It then becomes harder for corals, mussels and snails to build their shells and skeletons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is; 7 is neutral.
A solution that keeps its pH almost constant even when acid or base is added.
The ion HCO₃⁻, also called bicarbonate, which can mop up acid in the blood.
A condition in which the blood is too acidic.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in the body.

gewusst: Even small deviations of the blood pH of a few tenths can be life-threatening.
Carbonic anhydrase is one of the fastest enzymes known.
Many Swiss mineral waters contain hydrogen carbonate, which is given on the label.

teile.einleitung: A PET bottle is a light drinks bottle made of the plastic polyethylene terephthalate, PET for short. In Switzerland, water, soft drinks and iced tea are mostly sold in such bottles. Because they are collected and recycled, old bottles are often made into new ones.
wichtigste: PET bottles are made of the plastic polyethylene terephthalate.
In Switzerland, empty PET drinks bottles go into the PET collection box in the shop.
Only drinks bottles made of PET belong in the PET collection.
Before putting it in, you squash the bottle flat so that it takes up less space.
Collected PET bottles are often made into new bottles.
Recycled PET is also made into fibres for fleece jumpers.
PET recycling saves oil and energy.

abschnitte.text: PET is short for **polyethylene terephthalate**, a plastic made of long molecular chains. It is made mainly from **crude oil**. PET is light, transparent, shatterproof and keeps the fizz in drinks well. The plastic was invented in England in 1941 and has been used for drinks bottles since the 1970s.

First a small, thick-walled blank is made that looks like a test tube with a screw thread. This **preform** is warmed and blown up with compressed air in a mould. In a few seconds a finished bottle is formed. The process is called **stretch blow moulding**.

In Switzerland there are **PET collection boxes** in almost all shops, at railway stations and in schools. Only drinks bottles made of PET belong in them, not shampoo or oil bottles. You squash the empty bottle flat and put the lid back on. The collection has been organised since 1990 by the association **PET-Recycling Schweiz**, and about 80 per cent of bottles are brought back (as of around 2023).

The collected bottles are sorted, washed and chopped into small flakes. From these flakes, new drinks bottles are often made again; this is called **bottle-to-bottle recycling**. Some of it is spun into fibres, from which fleece jumpers, sleeping bag fillings or carpets are made, for example. This saves oil and a lot of energy.

A PET bottle left lying in nature breaks down only very slowly; it can take hundreds of years. It crumbles into tiny pieces, so-called **microplastics**, which animals can eat. That is why a bottle never belongs on the ground, in the forest or in a lake. Even better for the environment is to fill tap water into a reusable drinking bottle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The abbreviation for the plastic polyethylene terephthalate.
Turning waste into new products.
Tiny plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres.
A small blank from which a PET bottle is blown up.

gewusst: An empty PET bottle weighs only a few dozen grams, even though it holds over a litre of drink.
PET is used to make not only bottles but also fibres for clothes, which are often sold under the name polyester.

teile.einleitung: Nucleic acids are huge molecules in which the genetic information of all living things is stored. The two most important are DNA and RNA. They were discovered in 1869 by the Basel doctor Friedrich Miescher.
wichtigste: Nucleic acids are built from many building blocks, the nucleotides.
A nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, a sugar and a nucleobase.
The two most important nucleic acids are DNA and RNA.
In RNA, the base uracil occurs instead of thymine.
The nucleotides are linked into a long chain by phosphodiester bonds.
Messenger RNA takes the information of a gene to the ribosomes.
The Basel doctor Friedrich Miescher discovered nucleic acids in 1869 and called them nuclein.

abschnitte.text: **Nucleic acids** are chain molecules found in every cell. They store and pass on the **genetic information**, that is the blueprint of a living thing. They get their name from the Latin nucleus, kernel, because they were first found in the cell nucleus. The best-known nucleic acid is **DNA**, deoxyribonucleic acid. Its most important partner is RNA, ribonucleic acid.

A nucleic acid is built from many **nucleotides**, much like a string of beads from beads. Each nucleotide has three parts: a phosphate group, a sugar and a **nucleobase**. In DNA the sugar is called deoxyribose, in RNA ribose. Phosphate and sugar alternate to form the backbone of the chain and are linked by **phosphodiester bonds**. The bases stick out to the side and form the actual writing of the genetic information.

In DNA there are four bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine, abbreviated A, G, C and T. In RNA, thymine is replaced by **uracil**. Adenine and guanine belong to the purines; the others are smaller pyrimidines. In DNA two strands form a **double helix**, with A always paired with T and G always with C. James Watson and Francis Crick described this structure in 1953, based on X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin.

RNA has many jobs in the cell. **Messenger RNA**, mRNA for short, copies the information of a gene and takes it to the ribosomes. There, proteins are built according to these instructions. Other kinds of RNA help to bring along the right building blocks. Some RNA molecules can even speed up chemical reactions themselves; they are called **ribozymes**.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Basel discovers nuclein
abschnitte.text: In 1869 the Basel doctor **Friedrich Miescher** studied the nuclei of white blood cells in Tübingen. He found a substance containing phosphorus, which he called **nuclein**. At that time nobody suspected that this substance carries the genetic information. Later Miescher continued his research in his home town of Basel. Only in the 20th century did it become clear how important his discovery was.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block of a nucleic acid made of phosphate, sugar and base.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, the carrier of genetic information.
Ribonucleic acid; it passes on and processes the genetic information.
The shape of DNA: two strands wound round each other like a twisted rope ladder.
An RNA molecule that speeds up a chemical reaction.

gewusst: The DNA from a single human cell would be about two metres long if stretched out.
The Covid-19 vaccines of 2020 were the first widely used vaccines based on mRNA.
Friedrich Miescher later became professor of physiology at the University of Basel.

teile.einleitung: Le Chatelier’s principle describes how a chemical equilibrium reacts when it is disturbed. The equilibrium gives way to the pressure, just as a roly-poly toy always stands itself up again. With this principle you can predict how to make more of a desired product.
wichtigste: The principle was formulated in 1884 by the French chemist Henry Le Chatelier.
It is also called the principle of least constraint.
If an equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts so that the disturbance becomes smaller.
If a starting substance is added in excess, more product is formed.
If a product is removed continuously, more of it is continuously formed.
When warmed, the direction that uses up heat, the endothermic direction, is favoured.
An increase in pressure favours the side with fewer gas particles.

abschnitte.text: Many chemical reactions run forwards and backwards at the same time. When both are equally fast, nothing changes any more; this is called **chemical equilibrium**. In 1884 **Henry Le Chatelier** (1850 to 1936) realised: if you put a constraint on such an equilibrium, it shifts so as to get away from the constraint. That is why it is also called the principle of least constraint. Shortly afterwards the German physicist Ferdinand Braun also described this behaviour.

If you add more of a substance, the equilibrium tries to use it up again. If you add more iron ions to the blood-red equilibrium Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]²⁺, the solution turns a deeper red. In the **esterification** of acetic acid with ethanol, an excess of ethanol increases the yield of ester. If a product is removed continuously, for example by distilling it off, more of it is continuously formed.

If you warm an equilibrium, the direction that uses up heat is favoured, that is the **endothermic** direction. The equilibrium N₂O₄ ⇌ 2 NO₂ is endothermic in the forward direction; when warmed, more brown NO₂ is formed and the gas gets darker. A pink cobalt chloride solution with a lot of chloride turns blue when heated, so the formation of the blue complex is endothermic. When it cools, the colour comes back.

With gases, an increase in pressure favours the side with fewer **gas particles**, because these need less space. In the equilibrium H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2 HI there are two gas particles on each side, so the position stays unchanged. If a noble gas is added at constant volume, the position does not change either, because the concentrations of the gases involved stay the same. When you open a bottle of mineral water, the pressure drops, less CO₂ stays dissolved and it fizzes.

The best-known example is the **Haber-Bosch process**, in which ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen. Because four gas particles become two, very high pressure is used. Ammonia is the most important starting material for artificial fertiliser, which today feeds a large part of humanity. The principle is also used in many other factories to obtain as much product as possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which the forward and reverse reactions run equally fast and the amounts no longer change.
A reaction that takes in heat from the surroundings.
A reaction that gives off heat to the surroundings.
How much of the desired product you actually get from a reaction.

gewusst: There is a similar principle in the body: if we get too hot, we sweat to get rid of the heat.
Without the Haber-Bosch process there would not be enough fertiliser to feed today’s world population.
A catalyst speeds up the setting of an equilibrium but does not shift its position.

teile.einleitung: Laboratory safety covers all the rules and equipment that protect people from accidents when experimenting in the laboratory. In chemistry lessons you work with acids, alkalis, gases and open flames, so there are clear rules of behaviour. Anyone who knows and follows them can experiment safely and with enjoyment.
wichtigste: Long hair is tied back in the laboratory.
Eating and drinking are forbidden in the chemistry laboratory.
When diluting a concentrated acid, you first pour the water into the container and then add the acid.
You carefully waft the smell of a substance towards you with your hand.
Substances that give off poisonous or sharp fumes are handled in the fume cupboard.
If a chemical splashes into the eye, you rinse it immediately for a long time with plenty of water.
In case of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse can be reached on 145.

abschnitte.text: In the laboratory you always wear **safety goggles**, because even a small splash can seriously injure the eye. A cotton **lab coat** protects skin and clothing. For corrosive substances, suitable protective gloves are added. Long hair is tied back so that it does not get into a flame or into chemicals.

In the laboratory there is no eating, no drinking and no running. You never taste chemicals, even if they look harmless. You never suck liquids into a **pipette** with your mouth, but use a pipette filler. You check smells by carefully wafting the fumes towards you with your hand.

When a concentrated acid is diluted, a lot of heat can be produced. If you pour water into the acid, it can suddenly boil and throw out corrosive splashes. That is why the rule is: always add acid to water, never water to acid. So the acid is poured slowly into the water and not the other way round.

On bottles of chemicals, red-bordered diamonds with black pictures show what danger a substance poses. These **hazard pictograms** are the same worldwide. A flame warns of flammable substances, a skull of poisonous ones and a damaged hand of corrosive ones. Anyone who reads a label before opening a bottle knows how careful they need to be.

Substances that give off poisonous or sharp fumes are handled in the **fume cupboard**. This is a workplace with a glass screen from which a fan sucks out the air. Leftover chemicals are not simply poured down the sink. They go into special collection containers and are disposed of properly.

If something splashes into the eye, you rinse it immediately for at least ten minutes at the **eyewash station** or with plenty of water. If a person’s clothing catches fire, you smother the flames with the **fire blanket** or under the emergency shower. In case of poisoning, in Switzerland you can reach Tox Info Suisse on 145, the fire brigade on 118 and the ambulance on 144. You report every accident to the teacher immediately.

begriffe.erklaerung: A workplace in the laboratory with extraction, for substances with dangerous fumes.
Goggles that protect the eyes from splashes and splinters.
A warning symbol on chemicals that shows the kind of danger.
A fireproof blanket used to smother small fires.
The Swiss advice centre for poisoning, emergency number 145.

gewusst: Tox Info Suisse in Zurich answers questions about poisoning around the clock, including when a child has swallowed something it should not have.
Most laboratory accidents do not happen in dangerous experiments, but through carelessness, for example working without safety goggles.

teile.einleitung: Corrosion protection includes all the measures that keep metals from being destroyed by rust and other chemical attacks. From a simple film of oil on a tool to a zinc block on a ship’s hull, there are many clever methods.
wichtigste: Corrosion is the destruction of a metal by a chemical reaction with its surroundings.
Iron needs water and oxygen to rust.
Rust is loose and flakes off, while the oxide layer on aluminium is dense and protective.
A thin film of oil or anti-rust paint keeps water and air away from iron.
A sacrificial anode made of a base metal corrodes instead of the ship’s hull.
In anodising, the protective layer of aluminium is strengthened electrically.
The greenish patina on copper roofs protects the copper underneath.

abschnitte.text: **Corrosion** destroys metals through reactions with their surroundings. Iron rusts as soon as water and oxygen come together. Rust is loose, flakes off and exposes more and more iron, until a part has rusted right through. Corrosion protection is therefore meant to keep bridges, vehicles, pipes and tools in good condition for as long as possible.

The simplest method is to shield the metal from air and water. Bare tools are rubbed with a thin **film of oil**, and an iron garden gate is given a coat of anti-rust paint. Cars are painted several times, and steel girders are dipped into liquid zinc in **hot-dip galvanising**. Coatings of chromium, nickel or plastic also protect the metal underneath.

For ships, pipelines and hot water tanks, a trick from electrochemistry is used. The iron is connected to a piece of a less noble metal such as zinc or magnesium, the **sacrificial anode**. This metal gives up electrons more easily and therefore corrodes instead of the iron. When the sacrificial anode is used up, it is simply replaced.

Some metals protect themselves. Aluminium forms a dense oxide layer in air, which can be strengthened with electricity in **anodising** and can even be coloured. Over time copper becomes covered with a greenish **patina**, which preserves the metal underneath. Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms an invisible, self-renewing protective layer.

The green dome of the Federal Palace in Bern gets its colour from the patina on the copper. Crash barriers on Swiss roads are usually hot-dip galvanised and therefore silvery grey. Many hot water tanks in Swiss houses contain a sacrificial anode made of magnesium, which should be checked regularly. Bicycles and garden furniture also last longer if they are stored dry and looked after.

begriffe.erklaerung: A special paint that shields iron from water and oxygen.
A piece of base metal that corrodes instead of the part being protected.
An electrical process that strengthens the protective layer of aluminium.
A greenish layer on copper that forms over time and protects it.
Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc.

gewusst: The Statue of Liberty in New York was originally copper brown and only turned green through its patina.
The Eiffel Tower in Paris is repainted about every seven years to protect it from rust.
Zinc still protects iron even when the zinc layer has a scratch.

teile.einleitung: In a neutralisation, an acid reacts with an alkali, and the two cancel out each other’s effect. Water and a salt are formed. We come across neutralisations everywhere, from remedies for heartburn to lime on the fields.
wichtigste: In neutralisation, an acid reacts with an alkali to form a salt and water.
Oxonium ions and hydroxide ions combine to form water.
Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution form table salt, that is sodium chloride.
Heat is released during neutralisation, and the container gets warm.
If there are equal numbers of acid and alkali particles, the pH afterwards is about 7.
A titration is used to find out how much acid or alkali there is in a solution.
Bicarbonate of soda helps against mild heartburn because it neutralises stomach acid.

abschnitte.text: **Acids** such as lemon juice or vinegar taste sour and have a pH below 7. **Alkalis** such as soapy water feel slippery and have a pH above 7. If you mix the two in the right amounts, a **neutral** solution with a pH of 7 is formed. Water and a salt are produced. This process is called neutralisation, from the Latin neuter, neither of the two.

Every acidic solution contains **oxonium ions**, every alkali **hydroxide ions**. In neutralisation, one oxonium ion and one hydroxide ion combine each time to form two water molecules. The other ions stay in the solution and together form a salt. With hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution, **sodium chloride**, that is table salt, is formed in this way. If you let the water evaporate, the salt crystals are left behind.

During neutralisation, **energy** is released; this is called an exothermic reaction. If you mix hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution in a beaker, you can feel the glass getting warm. With concentrated acids and alkalis the solution can even get very hot and spit. That is why in the laboratory you work with safety goggles and dilute solutions. You should never simply pour strong acids and alkalis together.

With a **titration** you can find out how much acid there is in a solution. An **indicator** is added to the acid, a dye that changes colour depending on the pH. Then alkali is slowly dripped in from a measuring tube, the burette. As soon as the indicator changes colour, the acid has been neutralised. From the amount of alkali used, the amount of acid can be calculated.

Farmers sometimes spread **lime** on their fields to neutralise soil that is too acidic. Many crops grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil. For mild heartburn you can take **bicarbonate of soda**, that is sodium hydrogen carbonate, which neutralises some of the stomach acid. Industrial waste water is also neutralised before it goes to the sewage treatment plant. In our body, the pancreas neutralises the acidic food pulp coming from the stomach.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that forms oxonium ions in water and has a pH below 7.
A solution with hydroxide ions and a pH above 7.
A dye that changes colour depending on the pH.
A measuring method in which alkali is dripped into an acid until the indicator changes colour.
A reaction is exothermic if heat is released.

gewusst: Red cabbage juice is a natural indicator; it turns red in acid and green to yellow in alkali.
A salt is formed in every neutralisation, but it is not always table salt.
Limescale in the kettle can be dissolved with vinegar or citric acid; this too is a reaction between an acid and an alkaline substance.

teile.einleitung: Richard R. Ernst was a Swiss chemist from Winterthur who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991. He made NMR spectroscopy, a method for looking inside molecules, much faster and more precise. His ideas are also the basis for magnetic resonance imaging in hospitals.
wichtigste: Richard R. Ernst was born in Winterthur in 1933.
For most of his career he was a professor at the ETH Zurich.
In 1991 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for high-resolution NMR spectroscopy.
At the company Varian Associates in California he developed pulsed Fourier NMR in the 1960s.
He used the Fourier transform to obtain a whole spectrum from a short pulse.
In the 1970s he put two-dimensional NMR spectroscopy into practice.
He collected and studied Tibetan scroll paintings.

abschnitte.text: **Richard Robert Ernst** was born in Winterthur on 14 August 1933. He studied chemistry at the **ETH Zurich** and also wrote his doctoral thesis there. After some years in the USA he returned to the ETH in 1968, where he later became a professor. He died in June 2021 in his home town of Winterthur.

In **NMR spectroscopy**, nuclear magnetic resonance, a sample is placed in a strong magnetic field. Certain atomic nuclei behave like tiny magnets in it and respond to radio waves. From these signals, chemists can read how a molecule is built up. Before Ernst, the slow **continuous wave method** was used, in which the frequency was swept step by step.

At the company **Varian Associates** in California, Ernst had a brilliant idea in the 1960s. Instead of scanning the frequencies one at a time, he sent a short, powerful radio frequency pulse to the sample. Using the mathematical **Fourier transform** and a computer, he calculated the whole spectrum at once from the response. This made the measurement much faster and more sensitive, often about a hundred times.

In the 1970s, at the ETH, Ernst put **two-dimensional NMR spectroscopy** into practice. The signals are spread over two frequency axes, rather like on a map. In this way even large, complicated molecules such as proteins can be studied. For this work he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1991.

Ernst’s methods are also the basis for **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI), which doctors use to look inside the body. Ernst also campaigned strongly for researchers to take responsibility in society. In his free time he collected **Tibetan scroll paintings**, so-called thangkas. With spectroscopic methods he studied their pigments and so found out what they were painted with and how.

begriffe.erklaerung: Studying substances with light or other waves.
Nuclear magnetic resonance, a measuring method that uses atomic nuclei in a magnetic field.
A calculation method that breaks a signal down into its individual frequencies.
A famous award for outstanding achievements in science and other fields.

gewusst: Richard R. Ernst learnt of his Nobel Prize on an aeroplane on the way to Moscow.
Kurt Wüthrich, another Swiss Nobel Prize winner, later used NMR to determine the shape of proteins.

teile.einleitung: Polyethylene, PE for short, is the plastic produced in the largest quantities in the world. Plastic bags, cling film, milk bottles and many toys are made from it. Chemically it is surprisingly simple, made only of carbon and hydrogen.
wichtigste: Polyethylene is made from the small molecule ethene.
The reaction in which many ethene molecules form a long chain is called polymerisation.
Polyethylene consists only of carbon and hydrogen.
It is the most produced plastic in the world.
Soft films and plastic bags are usually made of low-density polyethylene (LDPE).
Many shampoo and detergent bottles, for example, are made of hard HDPE.
Polyethylene floats on water because its density is lower than that of water.
Polyethylene was discovered rather by chance in England in 1933.

abschnitte.text: The basic building block is the gas **ethene** (formerly called ethylene), a small molecule made of two carbon and four hydrogen atoms. In **polymerisation**, the double bonds open up, and thousands of ethene molecules link together into a chain. This creates a huge molecule, a **polymer**. You can imagine it as a very long string of beads in which every bead looks the same.

In 1933 chemists at the English company ICI were experimenting with gases under very high pressure. By chance they found a white, waxy mass in their vessel, the first polyethylene. In the Second World War it was used as insulation for cables in radar equipment. In the 1950s the German chemist **Karl Ziegler** found a process for making polyethylene at low pressure too.

**LDPE** means low-density polyethylene; its chains are highly branched and lie loosely. Soft films, plastic bags and freezer bags are made from it. **HDPE** means high-density polyethylene; its chains are hardly branched and lie close together. It is harder and is used for shampoo bottles, cans, pipes and crates for drinks.

Polyethylene has a density of about 0.9 to 0.97 grams per cubic centimetre and therefore floats on water. It is waterproof, flexible, resistant to many chemicals and easy to shape. When warmed it becomes soft; it is a **thermoplastic**. But because it is so resistant, it hardly breaks down in nature and can turn into microplastics.

Ethene is obtained mainly from **crude oil** or natural gas. Worldwide, about 100 million tonnes of polyethylene are produced every year (as of around 2020). In Switzerland many shops collect plastic milk and shampoo bottles separately so that the material can be recycled. On packaging, HDPE can often be recognised by the recycling number 2 and LDPE by the number 4.

begriffe.erklaerung: A giant molecule made of many identical building blocks.
A reaction in which small molecules join into a long chain.
A small gas molecule from which polyethylene is built.
A plastic that becomes soft and mouldable when warmed.
The mass of a substance per volume; it decides whether it floats.

gewusst: Chemically, polyethylene is almost the same as candle wax, only with much longer chains.
Very strong polyethylene fibres are used for ropes and protective vests.

teile.einleitung: Hess’s law is a basic rule of thermochemistry. It states that in a chemical reaction the same amount of heat is always released or taken in overall, no matter which route the reaction takes. This makes it possible to calculate amounts of heat that can hardly be measured in the laboratory.
wichtigste: Hess’s law says: the enthalpy of reaction does not depend on the reaction route.
It was put forward by Germain Henri Hess, who was born in Geneva in 1802.
It is based on the fact that enthalpy is a state function.
If you reverse a chemical equation, the sign of ΔH is also reversed.
Chemical equations can be added and subtracted like sums.
This way the enthalpy of formation of carbon monoxide can be calculated, even though it can hardly be measured directly.
The Born-Haber cycle uses Hess’s law to determine lattice energies.

abschnitte.text: **Germain Henri Hess** was born in Geneva in 1802. As a small child he moved to Russia with his family. He studied medicine and later became a professor of chemistry in Saint Petersburg. Around 1840 he published the law named after him. He is therefore regarded as one of the founders of **thermochemistry**.

Hess’s law can be compared to a mountain walk. Whether you take the steep path or the long detour, the difference in height between the valley and the summit stays the same. In the same way, the **enthalpy of reaction** ΔH depends only on the starting and end states and not on the route in between. This is true because enthalpy is a **state function**, rather like height above sea level.

When carbon burns, some CO₂ is always formed too, so the enthalpy of formation of **carbon monoxide** can hardly be measured directly. But we know C + O₂ → CO₂ with ΔH = -393.5 kJ/mol and CO + ½ O₂ → CO₂ with ΔH = -283.0 kJ/mol. If you subtract the second equation from the first, you get C + ½ O₂ → CO with ΔH = -110.5 kJ/mol. If you reverse an equation, the sign changes: splitting 2 H₂O into hydrogen and oxygen needs +572 kJ.

The conversion of graphite into **diamond** can also be calculated this way. Graphite has an enthalpy of combustion of -393.5 kJ/mol, diamond of -395.4 kJ/mol. From this it follows that graphite to diamond has a ΔH of +1.9 kJ/mol. So diamond contains a tiny bit more energy than graphite, even though both consist of pure carbon.

The **Born-Haber cycle** breaks the formation of a salt such as sodium chloride down into many small steps. These include vaporising the metal, splitting the chlorine molecules and forming the ions. Because the sum of all the steps must equal the overall reaction, the **lattice energy** can be calculated in this way. Hess’s law is a forerunner of the law of conservation of energy, which was formulated a little later.

begriffe.erklaerung: The heat energy taken in or given off in a reaction at constant pressure.
A quantity that depends only on the state and not on how you got there.
The part of chemistry that deals with heat in chemical reactions.
The energy released when ions come together to form a crystal.

gewusst: Hess was born in Geneva but wrote his most important work in Russia, where he was also called German Ivanovich Hess.
Diamond is actually less stable than graphite, but at room temperature it practically never changes.
Hess’s law is also used to calculate the energy content of foods and fuels.

teile.einleitung: Condensation is the change of a substance from the gas state to the liquid state. The best-known example is water vapour that cools down and turns back into drops of water. This is how clouds, fog, dew and the wet windows on a cold morning form.
wichtigste: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid.
It happens when a gas cools down or is compressed.
Clouds consist of tiny drops of water and ice that have formed by condensation.
The drops that form on the grass early in the morning are called dew.
Water from the air settles on a glass containing an ice-cold drink.
Vapour trails behind aeroplanes form from the water vapour in the exhaust.
Heat is released during condensation.

abschnitte.text: Most substances can be solid, liquid or gas. If a gas is cooled so much that its particles slow down and cling together again, it becomes liquid. This process is called **condensation**. Its opposite is boiling or evaporation. The air around us also always contains invisible water vapour, which can condense.

Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. If moist air cools down, at some point it reaches the **dew point**, the temperature at which it cannot hold any more water vapour. Then the water condenses on cold surfaces or on tiny dust particles in the air. By the way, condensation releases the heat that was needed earlier for evaporation.

**Clouds** and fog form when moist air cools down, for example because it has to rise over a mountain. Then billions of tiny water droplets form, and at great heights ice crystals. On clear nights the ground cools down a lot, and in the morning **dew** glitters on the grass. In autumn, fog often lies over the Swiss Plateau for weeks while it is sunny in the mountains.

A glass containing an ice-cold drink gets wet on the outside because water vapour from the air condenses on the cold glass. If you come into a warm house in winter, your glasses steam up because the warm, moist air cools down on the cold lenses. For the same reason, the inside of the window panes is often wet on cold mornings. The bathroom mirror also steams up after a shower.

High up, aeroplanes draw **vapour trails** across the sky. They form because the water vapour from the hot engine exhaust condenses and freezes immediately in the ice-cold air. Air conditioners cool the air, and moisture condenses, dripping out of a hose as water. In fridges and heat pumps, a refrigerant is evaporated and condensed in turn to move heat.

begriffe.erklaerung: The state of a substance: solid, liquid or gas.
Water in gas form, which you cannot see.
The temperature at which moist air starts to release water.
Changing from liquid to gas below the boiling point.

gewusst: The white “steam” above a saucepan is actually already condensed water in tiny droplets.
In the Atacama Desert, people catch fog with large nets to obtain drinking water.
Without condensation there would be no rain and no snow.

teile.einleitung: Carbon is a chemical element with the symbol C and the atomic number 6. It is the building block of all life, because every plant, every animal and every person consists largely of carbon compounds. It can look as different as a black pencil and a sparkling diamond.
wichtigste: Carbon has the symbol C and the atomic number 6.
Diamond and graphite both consist of pure carbon.
The lead of a pencil consists mainly of graphite and clay.
When carbon burns completely, carbon dioxide is formed.
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
All living things are built from carbon compounds.

abschnitte.text: Carbon is in sixth place in the **periodic table**, so its nucleus has 6 protons. A carbon atom can form four bonds with other atoms. That is why it can form long chains, rings and huge molecules. No other element has so many different **compounds**, namely many millions.

Diamond is the hardest natural substance and consists of pure carbon in which every atom is firmly bonded to four neighbours. **Graphite** is also pure carbon, but the atoms lie in thin layers that slide easily over one another. That is why graphite is soft and black. Such different forms of an element are called **allotropes**.

The lead of a pencil is not made of lead but of **graphite** and clay. Charcoal for barbecues is almost pure carbon. Soot from a candle flame is also carbon. Steel contains a little carbon, which makes it harder than pure iron.

When carbon burns with enough oxygen, the gas **carbon dioxide** CO₂ is formed. If there is too little oxygen, poisonous carbon monoxide forms. Burning coal, oil and natural gas releases a lot of CO₂ into the air and strengthens the **greenhouse effect**. Plants take in CO₂ and use it with the help of sunlight to make sugar.

Proteins, fats, sugars and the genetic material DNA are all **carbon compounds**. The branch of chemistry that deals with them is called **organic chemistry**. With radioactive carbon-14, researchers can find out how old bones or wood are. This method is called radiocarbon dating and has also been used on finds from Swiss lake dwelling settlements.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance that consists of only one kind of atom.
A soft, black form of carbon from which pencil leads are made.
One of several forms in which an element can occur.
An invisible gas produced when things burn and when we breathe out.

gewusst: Almost a fifth of a person’s body weight is carbon.
Diamonds burn in air at very high temperatures because they are made of carbon.
Graphene, a layer of carbon only one atom thick, is one of the strongest materials known.

teile.einleitung: Neon is a colourless gas and one of the noble gases. In a glass tube it glows a strong reddish orange when electricity flows through it, and it has shaped the look of whole cities. Its name comes from Greek and means “the new one”.
wichtigste: Neon is a chemical element with the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
At room temperature neon is a gas.
Neon is a noble gas and forms almost no compounds.
In nature, neon occurs in small amounts in the air.
In a glowing tube, neon shines reddish orange.
Neon is not poisonous.
Glowing advertising signs made of gas tubes are called neon signs.

abschnitte.text: Neon was discovered in London in 1898 by the British chemists **William Ramsay** and Morris Travers. They cooled air so much that it became liquid and then let it slowly evaporate. In doing so they found a new gas that glowed brightly in a small glass tube. They named it after the Greek word **neos**, which means new. Ramsay received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904 for discovering the noble gases.

abschnitte.titel: A noble gas in the air
abschnitte.text: Neon belongs to the **noble gases**, together with helium, argon, krypton, xenon and radon. Noble gases have a full outer electron shell and therefore hardly react with other substances. Not a single stable compound of neon is known. In the air, neon makes up only a tiny share of about 0.0018 per cent. Today it is obtained in **air separation** plants, which liquefy air and split it into its components.

If you send electricity through a glass tube containing neon, the neon atoms are excited. When they give this energy off again, they send out light. With neon this light is **reddish orange**. Other gases glow in other colours: argon with a little mercury, for example, glows blue, and helium pink. That is why glowing tubes in other colours often contain no neon at all, even though they are still called neon tubes.

The French inventor **Georges Claude** presented the first neon tubes in Paris in 1910. Soon **neon signs** were glowing on cinemas, bars and shops in many cities around the world. The colourful lights of Las Vegas or Times Square in New York are famous. Today many illuminated signs are being replaced by more economical light-emitting diodes. But neon signs are popular again as art objects and decorations.

Liquid neon boils at about minus 246 degrees Celsius and is therefore used as a **coolant** for very low temperatures. Neon is also found in certain lasers, such as the red helium-neon laser that used to work in barcode scanners at the checkout. In glow lamps, for example in voltage testers, a small neon light shows whether electricity is flowing. Today the word **neon colours** simply means very bright, glowing colours, even when there is no neon in them at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas that hardly reacts with other substances, for example neon, helium or argon.
A glowing advertising sign made of bent glass tubes filled with gas.
A process in which air is liquefied and separated into its gases.
The number of protons in the nucleus; for neon it is 10.

gewusst: Neon is lighter than air, so a balloon filled with neon would slowly rise.
In a neon tube, the gas glows without anything burning.
Many so-called neon tubes in the kitchen are in reality fluorescent tubes without any neon at all.

teile.einleitung: A solvent is a substance, usually a liquid, in which other substances dissolve. The most important solvent on Earth is water. For fat, paint or nail varnish, however, you need other solvents such as alcohol, acetone or petrol.
wichtigste: Water is the most important solvent on Earth.
Water molecules are polar and can therefore dissolve salts such as table salt well.
At 20 degrees, about 36 grams of table salt dissolve in 100 grams of water.
Fat dissolves better in non-polar solvents such as white spirit.
Many nail varnish removers contain the solvent acetone.
A solution in which nothing more dissolves is called a saturated solution.
Many solvents other than water are highly flammable and their fumes can be harmful.

abschnitte.text: **Water** dissolves more different substances than almost any other liquid. In the sea, salts are dissolved; in the blood, sugar and minerals; in the soil, nutrients for plants. A water molecule has a slightly negative side at the oxygen and slightly positive sides at the hydrogen atoms. It is said to be **polar**. This allows water to surround the charged particles of a salt and separate them from one another.

In chemistry there is a simple rule of thumb: **like dissolves like**. Polar substances such as salt and sugar dissolve in polar solvents such as water. Non-polar substances such as fat, oil or wax dissolve in **non-polar** solvents such as petrol. That is why a grease stain is better removed with white spirit than with plain water. Soap and washing-up liquid help because their particles have a water-loving and a fat-loving side.

Nail varnish remover often contains **acetone**, which dissolves the dried varnish again. Alcohol, more precisely ethanol, dissolves fragrances in perfume and active ingredients in disinfectants. In paints and varnishes, solvents keep them liquid. After painting, the solvent evaporates and the paint becomes solid. Glues and felt-tip pens also often contain solvents.

Every solvent can only take up a certain amount of a substance. When this amount is reached, it is called a **saturated solution**. For water and table salt, the limit at 20 degrees is about 36 grams per 100 grams of water. Solid substances usually dissolve better when warm. Gases, on the other hand, dissolve worse when warm, which is why warm mineral water loses its fizz faster.

Many solvents are highly **flammable**, and their fumes can cause headaches or dizziness. That is why you should air the room well when working with them and keep them away from flames. Evaporated solvents also pollute the air and in sunshine contribute to the formation of summer smog. Switzerland has therefore charged an incentive tax on volatile organic solvents since 2000. Today there are many water-based paints that give off fewer harmful fumes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid in which another substance dissolves.
A particle is polar if it has a slightly positive and a slightly negative side.
A colourless, strong-smelling solvent that dissolves nail varnish, for example.
A solution that cannot take up any more of the substance at the same temperature.

gewusst: Because water dissolves so many substances, completely pure water is almost never found in nature.
In dry cleaning, solvents are used instead of water, so the clothes do not actually get wet.
Coffee can be decaffeinated with carbon dioxide, which acts as a solvent under high pressure.

teile.einleitung: Copper is a shiny reddish brown metal that people have used for thousands of years. It conducts electricity and heat extremely well and is found today in almost every electrical device. With the chemical symbol Cu, it is one of the most important metals of all.
wichtigste: Freshly polished copper is reddish brown.
Copper conducts heat very well, which is why some pans have a copper base.
If you mix copper with zinc, you get brass.
Copper is soft; a thin copper wire is easy to bend by hand.
In electric motors, many copper wires are wound into coils.
The outer skin of the Statue of Liberty in New York is made of copper.
The period when people first made tools from copper is called the Copper Age.

abschnitte.text: **Copper** is a chemical element with the symbol Cu and the atomic number 29. It is a fairly soft, easily shaped metal with a typical reddish colour. Copper melts at about 1085 °C. After silver, it is the metal that conducts electricity best, and it also conducts heat excellently.

Because copper conducts electricity so well, most **electric cables** are made of copper. In electric motors, generators and transformers, long copper wires are wound into coils. Computers, mobile phones and cars also contain a lot of copper. A modern electric car needs considerably more copper than a car with a petrol engine.

Copper mixes well with other metals. With zinc it forms golden yellow **brass**, from which door handles, screws and brass instruments such as the trumpet are made. With tin it forms **bronze**, which is used for bells, statues and medals. The Swiss 10 and 20 centime coins are also made of a mixture of copper and nickel.

Copper was one of the first metals people worked; the period that followed is called the **Copper Age**. The glacier mummy Ötzi, found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991, carried an axe with a copper blade. Later people learnt to mix copper with tin to make bronze, and the Bronze Age began. The name copper comes from the Latin “cuprum”, which goes back to the island of Cyprus, where a lot of copper was mined in ancient times.

Copper is often used for roofs, gutters and domes because it lasts a very long time. Over time a green layer forms on it, the **patina**, which protects the metal. The Statue of Liberty in New York was originally copper brown and only turned green because of the patina. The dome of the Federal Palace in Bern also wears a green coat of copper.

In the kitchen, cooks value copper pans because they spread the heat quickly and evenly. Water pipes in houses are often made of copper. Copper also works against many bacteria, which is why door handles in some hospitals are made of copper alloys. For the body, copper in small amounts is an important trace element, found for example in nuts and wholemeal products.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of two or more metals, for example brass.
A golden yellow alloy of copper and zinc.
An alloy of copper and tin, used in the past for weapons and tools.
A green protective layer that forms on copper over time.
The ability of a substance to carry electricity or heat.

gewusst: Copper can be melted down and recycled as often as you like without losing quality.
The blood of squid and lobsters is bluish because it contains a pigment with copper.
The copper sheet of the Statue of Liberty is only about 2.4 millimetres thick.

teile.einleitung: Marine pollution means that rubbish, oil, chemicals or too many nutrients get into the oceans and harm plants, animals and people there. Today plastic waste in particular is a big problem. Switzerland also contributes to it, even though it is not by the sea.
wichtigste: A large part of plastic waste reaches the sea via rivers.
Huge collections of floating plastic are called garbage patches.
The largest known garbage patch is in the Pacific.
A plastic bottle takes hundreds of years to break down in the sea.
Sea turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish.
Lost fishing nets drifting in the sea are called ghost nets.
Via the Rhine, rubbish from Switzerland can reach the North Sea.

abschnitte.text: Marine pollution includes many substances: **plastic waste**, crude oil, sewage, chemicals, heavy metals and fertiliser from farming. Noise from ships also disturbs animals, for example whales, which communicate with sounds. Most of the pollution does not come from ships but from the land. It gets into the sea via rivers, the wind or directly from the coasts.

Ocean currents collect floating rubbish in certain places. This creates huge **garbage patches**. The best known is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch between Hawaii and California. However, you should not imagine it as a solid island: a large part consists of small pieces of plastic drifting spread out in the water. Plastic only breaks down very slowly into smaller and smaller pieces; a plastic bottle takes hundreds of years.

For many sea creatures plastic is deadly. **Sea turtles** think floating plastic bags are jellyfish and eat them. Seabirds pick up colourful bits of plastic, which then fill their stomachs so that they starve even though their bellies are full. Seals, dolphins and fish get caught in **ghost nets**, that is lost or discarded fishing nets. These nets go on fishing for years without anyone hauling them in.

In accidents involving tankers or oil rigs, **crude oil** runs into the sea; this is called an **oil spill**. Well-known examples are the accident of the tanker Exxon Valdez off Alaska in 1989 and the explosion of the Deepwater Horizon oil rig in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010. Oil sticks birds’ feathers together so that they can no longer fly or keep warm. Too much fertiliser from fields makes algae grow strongly. When these die and are broken down, the water runs short of oxygen, and so-called **dead zones** are formed.

Switzerland has no coast, but its rivers flow into four seas. The **Rhine** takes water to the North Sea, the Rhône to the Mediterranean, the Inn via the Danube to the Black Sea and the Ticino via the Po to the Adriatic. So rubbish thrown into a stream in Switzerland can travel all the way to the sea. That is why it is important not to leave rubbish lying around, including on lake shores and riverbanks. Sewage treatment plants clean waste water before it flows into rivers and lakes.

The most effective thing is for rubbish not to get into the sea in the first place. You can use **reusable bottles** and cloth bags, dispose of rubbish properly and recycle plastic. Many countries have banned thin single-use plastic bags or made people pay for them. Volunteers collect rubbish on beaches and riverbanks during clean-up events. Researchers are also developing devices that fish floating rubbish out of rivers and seas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge collection of floating rubbish formed by ocean currents.
A lost fishing net that drifts in the sea and keeps catching animals.
Pollution of the sea and coast by leaked crude oil.
An area of sea with so little oxygen that hardly any animals can live there.

gewusst: A ghost net can drift in the sea for years, catching more and more fish, seals and turtles.
Plastic waste has even been found in the Mariana Trench, the deepest point of the oceans.
Swiss rivers flow into four different seas: the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and the Adriatic.

teile.einleitung: NMR spectroscopy is a method that lets you look inside molecules without destroying them. It uses the fact that some atomic nuclei behave like tiny compass needles in a strong magnetic field. In this way you can find out how the atoms in a molecule are joined to each other.
wichtigste: NMR stands for “nuclear magnetic resonance”.
Only atomic nuclei with a nuclear spin, such as ¹H or ¹³C, can be measured, but not ¹²C.
Tetramethylsilane serves as the reference with a chemical shift of zero.
The area under a signal shows how many protons belong to it.
Neighbouring protons split signals into several lines.
Felix Bloch, who was born in Zurich, received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952 with Edward Purcell for nuclear magnetic resonance.
Magnetic resonance imaging in hospitals is based on the same principle.

abschnitte.text: Many atomic nuclei have a **nuclear spin**; they behave like tiny magnets. In a very strong magnetic field they line up. With radio waves of the right frequency they can be flipped over; they then come into **resonance**. As they flip back, the nuclei themselves send out radio signals, which the instrument measures. The most common carbon isotope ¹²C has a nuclear spin of zero and is therefore invisible, so the rare ¹³C is measured instead.

Depending on its surroundings in the molecule, a nucleus feels the magnetic field a little differently. That is why the signals appear in different places, measured in ppm; this is the **chemical shift**. Tetramethylsilane, TMS for short, serves as the zero point. The proton of an aldehyde group, for example, appears at about 9 to 10 ppm. Anyone who knows the typical ranges can read from the spectrum which groups are in the molecule.

The **integral**, that is the area under a signal, gives the relative number of protons. Neighbouring protons influence each other and split signals. In ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, the signal of the CH₃ group is split into three lines by the two protons of the neighbouring CH₂ group.
