So that the solvent does not interfere, samples are dissolved in **deuterated** solvents such as CDCl₃, in which hydrogen has been replaced by deuterium.

NMR has strong roots in Switzerland. **Felix Bloch**, born in Zurich in 1905, received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952 together with Edward Purcell. Richard Ernst of the ETH Zurich greatly improved the method and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991. Kurt Wüthrich, also at the ETH, used NMR to determine the shape of proteins and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. In Fällanden near Zurich, the company Bruker still makes NMR instruments today.

abschnitte.titel: From the laboratory to the hospital
abschnitte.text: **Magnetic resonance imaging**, MRI for short, uses the same principle to make pictures of the inside of the body. It mainly measures the hydrogen nuclei in the water of the tissues. The stronger the magnetic field of an NMR instrument, the better the resolution and sensitivity, which is why instruments with 800 MHz are better than those with 300 MHz. The strongest magnets are cooled to very low temperatures with liquid helium.

begriffe.erklaerung: A property of some atomic nuclei that makes them behave like small magnets.
When something vibrates particularly strongly at exactly its matching frequency.
“Parts per million”, the unit of chemical shift.
Heavy hydrogen, whose nucleus contains one more neutron.

gewusst: No fewer than three Nobel Prizes for NMR went to researchers who were born in Zurich or worked at the ETH.
In MRI the word “nuclear” was left out of the name, because many people wrongly thought of radioactivity.
The magnets of large NMR instruments are hundreds of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: Carbonic acid forms when the gas carbon dioxide dissolves in water. In everyday life we usually mean the fizzy bubbles in sparkling mineral water and soft drinks. Chemically, carbonic acid is a weak acid that very easily breaks down again into water and gas.
wichtigste: The bubbles in sparkling mineral water consist of carbon dioxide.
Carbonic acid forms when carbon dioxide reacts with water.
Carbon dioxide stays dissolved longer in cold water than in warm water.
When you open a bottle of fizzy water, you hear a hiss because gas escapes.
If a bottle is left open for a long time, the gas escapes and the water tastes flat.
Some springs are naturally fizzy.
With a soda maker you can make tap water fizzy at home.

abschnitte.text: When **carbon dioxide** dissolves in water, a small part of it reacts with the water to form carbonic acid with the formula H2CO3. Most of the gas, however, simply stays dissolved as CO2. Carbonic acid is a weak **acid** and tastes slightly sour. That is why sparkling water tingles on the tongue and tastes a little different from still water.

In mineral water, a lot of gas is pressed into the bottle under **pressure**. As long as the bottle is closed, the gas stays dissolved. When you open it, the pressure drops, it hisses, and bubbles rise. Cold water can hold more gas than warm water, which is why warm sparkling water loses its fizz faster.

If you shake a bottle of fizzy water, many tiny gas bubbles form in the water. When you open it, they grow in a flash and carry the water upwards with them. That is why the contents spray out. If you wait a few minutes after shaking, the bubbles rise to the top and the bottle can be opened more calmly.

Deep in the Earth, carbon dioxide from the rock can get into the groundwater. When this water comes to the surface, it fizzes by itself; such springs are called **carbonated springs**. In Switzerland there are such springs, for example, in Scuol in the Lower Engadine. Most mineral waters in the shops, however, only get their fizz when they are bottled.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Geneva invents fizzy water
abschnitte.text: In the 18th century the Englishman Joseph Priestley showed how to add carbon dioxide to water. In 1783 the German-born watchmaker **Johann Jacob Schweppe** developed a process in Geneva for producing sparkling water in large quantities. This gave rise to the drinks brand Schweppes, which is still well known today. Today anyone can make sparkling water at home with a **soda maker**.

The sea also takes up carbon dioxide from the air, and carbonic acid forms. If the carbon dioxide content of the air rises, seawater becomes slightly more acidic; this is called **acidification**. It makes it harder for corals and mussels to build their shells. Rainwater also always has a little carbonic acid dissolved in it, which slowly dissolves limestone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A weak acid that forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in water.
A colourless gas made of carbon and oxygen, CO2.
A spring whose water naturally contains carbon dioxide.
A device that presses carbon dioxide from a gas cylinder into tap water.

gewusst: Pure carbonic acid as a substance can hardly be bottled, because it breaks down almost immediately into water and carbon dioxide.
The drinks brand Schweppes has its origins in Geneva.
Milk, fruit juice and tea normally have no fizz.

teile.einleitung: In a chemical reaction, the limiting reactant is the starting substance that is used up first. It decides how much product can be formed at most, rather like the number of rolls decides how many sandwiches you can make, even if there is still a lot of cheese left.
wichtigste: The limiting reactant is the reactant that is completely used up first in a reaction.
It determines how much product can be formed at most.
The other reactants are in excess; some of them is left over.
To find the limiting reactant, you compare the amounts of substance with the chemical equation.
In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O with 3 mol of hydrogen and 2 mol of oxygen, hydrogen is limiting.
In syntheses, a cheap reactant is often used in excess so that the expensive one reacts as completely as possible.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you want to make sandwiches and need two slices of bread and one slice of cheese for each. If you have 10 slices of bread and 8 slices of cheese, you can only make 5 sandwiches, and 3 slices of cheese are left over. Here the bread is the **limiting reactant**. It is exactly the same in chemistry: the substance that runs out first limits the amount of product.

abschnitte.titel: The chemical equation as a recipe
abschnitte.text: A **chemical equation** shows in what ratio substances react with one another. The numbers in front of the formulas give the amounts of substance in **moles**. In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, two parts of hydrogen always react with one part of oxygen. If 3 mol of hydrogen and 2 mol of oxygen are available, the hydrogen only needs 1.5 mol of oxygen, so hydrogen is limiting and 0.5 mol of oxygen is left over.

First you convert all the masses into amounts of substance using the molar mass. Then you divide each amount by the number in front of the substance in the chemical equation. The substance with the smallest result is limiting. Example: 16 g of methane is 1 mol, 48 g of oxygen is 1.5 mol; in CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O the oxygen is therefore limiting, and at most 0.75 mol or 33 g of carbon dioxide is formed.

In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ with 2 mol of nitrogen and 3 mol of hydrogen, the hydrogen is only enough for 1 mol of nitrogen, and at most 2 mol of **ammonia** is formed. If 56 g of iron, that is 1 mol, react with 40 g of sulphur, that is 1.25 mol, to form iron sulphide, 8 g of sulphur are left over. In Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ with 1 mol of zinc and 1 mol of hydrogen chloride, only 0.5 mol of hydrogen is formed. And in 2 Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃, 2 mol of the 4 mol of aluminium are left over if only 3 mol of chlorine are present.

abschnitte.titel: Importance in the laboratory and industry
abschnitte.text: In industry, the aim is to use expensive raw materials as completely as possible. That is why a cheap reactant, such as air or water, is used in **excess**. The expensive substance thus becomes the limiting reactant and reacts almost completely. The calculated maximum amount is also compared with how much product was actually formed; this is called the **yield**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A starting substance of a chemical reaction.
A substance formed in a chemical reaction.
The unit of amount of substance; it counts particles in very large packages.
The amount of a substance that is left over after the reaction.
The proportion of product actually formed, compared with the largest possible amount.

gewusst: A mole contains about 602 thousand billion billion particles.
When cooking from a recipe, the same principle applies: the ingredient that runs out first decides the number of portions.
The limiting reactant is not always the substance with the smallest mass.

teile.einleitung: Red cabbage, in Switzerland usually called “Rotkabis”, is a violet-red vegetable from the cabbage family. It is not only a popular winter vegetable but also a magic ingredient for experiments. Its pigment shows by its colour whether something is acidic or alkaline.
wichtigste: In Switzerland red cabbage is usually called “Rotkabis”, in southern Germany also “Blaukraut”.
It is a form of cabbage, like white cabbage and Savoy cabbage.
Its colour comes from pigments called anthocyanins.
Red cabbage juice is an indicator: its colour shows whether something is acidic.
In pure water the juice is violet, with acid red and with bicarbonate of soda blue.
A dash of vinegar when cooking makes sure that red cabbage stays nicely red.
Blueberry juice also changes colour with acid.

abschnitte.text: **Red cabbage** is a cultivated form of cabbage, like white cabbage, Savoy cabbage and cauliflower. It forms a firm, round head of leaves lying tightly on top of one another. Red cabbage contains a lot of vitamin C and keeps for a long time, which is why it used to be an important winter vegetable. In Switzerland, **Rotkabis** is part of the game dishes in autumn, together with chestnuts and Spätzli.

Red cabbage owes its colour to **anthocyanins**, natural pigments that are also found in blueberries, cherries and grapes. These pigments change their form depending on how acidic their surroundings are. With each form the colour changes too. That is why red cabbage juice is a natural **indicator**.

For the experiment, you chop red cabbage finely and pour hot water over it. After about ten minutes you pour off the violet juice. In pure water it stays violet. If you add lemon juice or vinegar, it turns red, because these are **acidic**. With bicarbonate of soda or soapy water it turns blue to green, because these substances are **alkaline**.

Red cabbage juice shows many colours depending on the **pH**. Very acidic substances turn it red, weakly acidic ones pink, neutral ones violet. Weakly alkaline substances make it blue, more strongly alkaline ones green and very strongly alkaline ones even yellow. So with a single vegetable you can make a whole rainbow of colours and sort household substances by their acidity.

When cooking, people often add a dash of vinegar or a sour apple. The acid makes sure that the red cabbage stays nicely red. If you cook it in hard water without acid, it can turn bluish. This also explains the different German names “Rotkohl” (red cabbage) and “Blaukraut” (blue cabbage): depending on how it is prepared, the same vegetable is red or blue.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance whose colour shows whether something is acidic, neutral or alkaline.
Red, violet and blue pigments in plants, for example in red cabbage and berries.
A number from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline something is.
The opposite of acidic, like soapy water or bicarbonate of soda.

gewusst: With red cabbage juice you can write secret messages on paper that appear red with lemon juice.
The same head of red cabbage can turn red or blue in the pan, depending on whether acid is added.
Hydrangeas also change their flower colour depending on the soil, and anthocyanins play a part in this too.

teile.einleitung: Soot is a fine black powder that forms when something burns with too little air. You can see it as a black thread of smoke above a candle or as a coating in the chimney. In the past people wrote with soot; today it makes car tyres black.
wichtigste: Soot consists mainly of carbon.
It forms especially when something burns with too little air.
Above a sooty candle, a thin black thread of smoke rises.
The yellow colour of a candle flame comes from tiny glowing soot particles.
If you hold a cold spoon in a candle flame, a black spot forms.
The chimney sweep cleans soot out of chimneys and is seen as a bringer of good luck.
In the past, black ink was made from soot.

abschnitte.text: Soot is a black powder made of tiny particles that consist almost only of **carbon**. It forms during **incomplete combustion**, that is when a fuel does not get enough oxygen. Then not all the carbon burns to carbon dioxide; part of it is left over as solid particles. That is why a candle with a wick that is too long smokes, as does a fire with damp wood.

In a candle flame, tiny **soot particles** are forming all the time. They get so hot that they glow bright yellow and give the flame its colour. Normally they burn completely at the edge of the flame. But if you hold a cold **spoon** in it, the particles cool down and stick as a black spot.

Soot builds up in chimneys and flue pipes and can even catch fire, leading to a dangerous **chimney fire**. That is why the **chimney sweep** regularly cleans chimneys and heating systems. In Switzerland this is compulsory in many cantons. The chimney sweep is seen as a bringer of good luck, because in the past a clean chimney protected against fires and meant warm rooms.

Thousands of years ago, people mixed soot with water and glue to make black **ink**. In China and Japan people still paint with ink sticks made of soot today. Today industry deliberately produces **carbon black**. It makes car tyres black and durable and is found in printing inks, toners and black plastics.

Tiny soot particles from diesel engines, wood fires and candles are part of **fine particulate matter**. They can get deep into the lungs and damage health. That is why modern diesel vehicles and construction machines have a **particulate filter**. Soot also plays a part on glaciers, because the dark powder absorbs sunlight and makes the ice melt faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical element of which soot, graphite and diamond are made.
Burning with too little oxygen, which produces soot.
A deep black colour for writing and painting.
A filter that holds back soot particles from exhaust gases.

gewusst: A large part of the mass of a car tyre can consist of carbon black.
Meeting a chimney sweep on New Year’s Day is considered particularly lucky.

teile.einleitung: The reaction order describes how strongly the rate of a chemical reaction depends on the concentrations of the starting substances. If you double a substance, the reaction can become equally fast, twice as fast or even four times as fast. The reaction order reveals which of these cases applies.
wichtigste: The reaction order is the exponent of the concentration in the rate law.
The overall order is the sum of all the exponents.
The reaction order must be determined by measurement; it cannot simply be read from the chemical equation.
In a zero-order reaction the rate stays constant, as in the breakdown of alcohol in the liver.
Radioactive decay follows a first-order rate law.
In first order, the half-life does not depend on the starting concentration.
After three half-lives, only 12.5 per cent is left.

abschnitte.text: The **reaction rate** shows how fast the concentration of a substance changes. It usually depends on how much of the starting substances is present. In the **rate law** this is written, for example, as: v = k·c(A)²·c(B). The exponents are called reaction orders, here second order with respect to A and first with respect to B. The overall order is the sum, that is 3.

In a **zero-order** reaction, the rate does not depend on the concentration. The same amount is always converted per unit of time, as if a machine were working to a beat. A well-known example is the breakdown of alcohol in the liver: the enzymes are working flat out and manage roughly the same amount every hour. Many reactions on the surfaces of catalysts also behave like this.

In **first order**, the rate is proportional to the concentration. A special feature is the **half-life**: it is always the same length, no matter how much you have at the start. After one half-life half is left, after two a quarter and after three 12.5 per cent. Radioactive decay follows this law. If you plot the natural logarithm ln c against time, you get a straight line.

In **second order** with respect to a substance A, the rate quadruples if you double c(A). This often happens when two identical particles have to collide. If one partner is present in very large excess, its concentration stays almost constant. Then the reaction appears to behave like first order; this is called **pseudo-first order**. One example is the splitting of sugar in a lot of water.

The reaction order can only be determined reliably by **experiment**. You measure how the concentration changes over time, for example through the colour, the pressure or the conductivity. Then you check which plot gives a straight line. This knowledge is needed, for example, to predict how long medicines or foods will keep.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast the amount of the substances changes in a reaction.
The number k in the rate law, which is different for every reaction and temperature.
The time after which only half of a substance is still present.
The small raised number that says how many times a number is multiplied by itself.

gewusst: The half-life of carbon-14 is used to find the age of mummies and old bones.
The reaction order can also be a fraction such as 1.5.
The expiry date of some medicines is also calculated with rate laws.

teile.einleitung: Hydrochloric acid is one of the best-known and strongest acids. It forms when the gas hydrogen chloride dissolves in water. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive and dangerous, but in dilute form it is even found in our own stomach.
wichtigste: Hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl) in water.
Concentrated hydrochloric acid contains about 37 per cent hydrogen chloride.
The acidic effect is caused by hydrogen ions, more precisely oxonium ions.
Base metals such as zinc dissolve in it, forming hydrogen gas.
Noble metals such as gold are not attacked by hydrochloric acid.
Its German name, “Salzsäure” (salt acid), comes from the fact that it can be made from table salt.
Our gastric juice contains dilute hydrochloric acid.

abschnitte.text: **Hydrogen chloride** HCl is a colourless, sharp-smelling gas. It dissolves very well in water, forming hydrochloric acid. The HCl molecules give their proton to water molecules, forming **oxonium ions** and chloride ions. The oxonium ions make the solution acidic. That is why blue litmus paper turns red in hydrochloric acid.

Commercial **concentrated hydrochloric acid** contains about 37 per cent hydrogen chloride. Above an open bottle you can often see white mist. It forms because hydrogen chloride escapes and forms fine droplets with the moisture in the air. These fumes are corrosive, which is why it is only handled in a fume cupboard and with safety goggles and gloves.

If you put a piece of **zinc** into dilute hydrochloric acid, gas bubbles form immediately. Hydrogen is produced, and the zinc slowly dissolves. Iron and magnesium react in the same way. **Noble metals** such as gold, silver or platinum, on the other hand, are not attacked by hydrochloric acid. Only a mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid, aqua regia, can dissolve gold.

In industry, hydrochloric acid is needed for cleaning metals, for making plastics such as PVC and for many chemicals. On **building sites**, dilute hydrochloric acid is used to remove cement and lime residues from tiles and stones. Some descalers also contain hydrochloric acid. Such products must never be mixed with cleaners containing chlorine, because poisonous chlorine gas can form.

In the **stomach**, special cells produce dilute hydrochloric acid. Gastric juice has a pH of about 1 to 2 and is therefore very acidic. The acid kills bacteria in food and helps to digest protein. A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from digesting itself. If stomach acid gets into the gullet, you feel it as heartburn.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that gives up protons in water and tastes sour or is corrosive.
A water molecule that has taken up an extra proton, formula H₃O⁺.
A metal such as gold or platinum that hardly reacts with other substances.
A dye that turns red with acid and blue with alkali.

gewusst: In the past, hydrochloric acid was called “spirit of salt”, because it was obtained from table salt.
Without hydrochloric acid in the stomach, many germs from food could get into the intestine.
The white mist above hydrochloric acid is not smoke but tiny droplets of acid.

teile.einleitung: Reaction kinetics is the part of chemistry that studies how fast chemical reactions take place. Some reactions take years, like the rusting of iron; others take only fractions of a second, like an explosion. Reaction kinetics explains what this speed depends on and how it can be influenced.
wichtigste: The reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit of time.
According to collision theory, particles must collide in order to react.
A collision only leads to a reaction if there is enough energy and the right orientation.
The highest-energy state on the reaction path is called the transition state.
A larger surface area, for example with a powder, speeds up a reaction.
According to the RGT rule, the rate rises two to four times with 10 K more.
In reactions with several steps, the slowest step decides the overall speed.
Catalysts speed up reactions without being used up themselves.

abschnitte.text: The **reaction rate** shows how much the concentration of a substance changes per unit of time. At the start of a reaction it is usually high, because many starting substances are present. These starting substances are called **reactants**, and the substances formed are called **products**. The more reactants have been used up, the slower the reaction usually goes.

According to **collision theory**, particles must collide for them to react. But not every collision is enough: the particles need enough energy and the right orientation to each other. The minimum energy is called the **activation energy**. On the way from the reactants to the products, the particles pass through a particularly high-energy state, the **transition state**.

At higher temperatures particles move faster and collide more often and more violently. The **Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution** shows that more particles then exceed the activation energy. A rule of thumb is the **RGT rule**: with 10 kelvin more, a reaction runs about two to four times as fast. That is why food goes off more slowly in the fridge.

The higher the **concentration** of the reactants, the more often the particles meet. Surface area also plays a big part. Zinc powder reacts much faster with hydrochloric acid than a piece of zinc of the same mass, because its **surface area** is much larger. For the same reason, fine flour dust in the air can burn dangerously fast.

A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction by making possible a route with lower activation energy. It is not used up in the process. In car exhausts, a catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. In our body, **enzymes** work as catalysts, for example in digestion.

Many reactions take place in several partial steps. The slowest step then decides the rate of the whole reaction; it is called the **rate-determining step**. It is like a checkout in a supermarket: the slowest station holds everyone up. In 1889 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius described mathematically how the rate depends on temperature.

begriffe.erklaerung: The minimum energy particles need for a reaction.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A starting substance of a chemical reaction.
The highest-energy moment on the way from reactant to product.
A protein in the body that acts as a catalyst.

gewusst: Without enzymes, digesting a meal in our body would take many years.
In theory a diamond turns into graphite, but so slowly that you never notice.
A match needs only a small push of energy; after that, burning carries on by itself.

teile.einleitung: Sulphur is a yellow chemical element with the symbol S. It is found at volcanoes, in minerals and even in our body. Many of its compounds smell unpleasantly of rotten eggs.
wichtigste: Pure sulphur is yellow and solid at room temperature.
Its chemical symbol is S, its atomic number 16.
In nature, sulphur is often found at volcanoes.
Sulphur burns with a blue flame.
Many sulphur compounds smell of rotten eggs.
The heads of many matches contain sulphur.
In Baden in the Aargau, warm thermal water containing sulphur bubbles up.

abschnitte.text: Pure **sulphur** is a yellow, brittle solid that does not dissolve in water. It is a **non-metal** and conducts neither electricity nor heat well. At about 115 degrees it melts into a yellow liquid. If you heat it further, the melt turns dark red and thick. Pure sulphur itself hardly smells; the typical stench comes from its compounds.

abschnitte.titel: Where it is found in nature
abschnitte.text: At **volcanoes**, gases containing sulphur rise up, and yellow sulphur crystals grow where they come out. The Ijen volcano in Indonesia is famous; there workers mine sulphur by hand. Sulphur is also found in many minerals, for example in shiny **pyrite**, “fool’s gold”. Crude oil and natural gas also contain sulphur compounds. Today most sulphur is obtained when crude oil and natural gas are purified.

The typical stench usually comes from the gas **hydrogen sulphide**. It forms when protein rots, because protein contains sulphur. Onions and garlic also owe their sharp smell to sulphur compounds. In thermal baths such as **Baden** in the Aargau, you can smell the sulphur in the warm water. The springs there were already popular with the Romans.

Sulphur burns with a weak **blue flame**. It combines with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide, a sharp-smelling gas. Sulphur dioxide in the air can lead to acid rain, which damages forests and buildings. That is why heating oil and fuels have to be desulphurised today. In the past, wine barrels were fumigated with sulphur to kill germs.

The most important sulphur compound is **sulphuric acid**, which is needed in large quantities in industry, for example for fertiliser. Sulphur is found in the heads of many matches and used to be an ingredient of gunpowder. In **vulcanisation**, natural rubber is turned into elastic rubber with sulphur, for example for car tyres. Our body also needs sulphur; it is built into hair, nails and many proteins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom.
A poisonous gas that smells of rotten eggs.
A sharp-smelling gas produced when sulphur burns.
Heating natural rubber with sulphur to make rubber.
A gold-coloured mineral made of iron and sulphur, also called fool’s gold.

gewusst: Jupiter’s moon Io is coloured yellow and orange because of its many sulphur volcanoes.
The human nose can smell hydrogen sulphide even in the tiniest amounts.
In Latin sulphur is called “sulfur”, which is where the symbol S comes from.

teile.einleitung: Carbon monoxide is an invisible and odourless gas with the formula CO. It is produced when something burns with too little oxygen, and it is very poisonous. At the same time it is an important raw material in industry, for example in making iron.
wichtigste: Carbon monoxide has the chemical formula CO.
It is produced in burning when there is too little oxygen.
The gas is colourless and odourless, which is why you do not notice it.
In the body it binds to the red blood pigment, about 200 to 300 times more strongly than oxygen.
A CO alarm warns of the dangerous gas in homes.
When carbon monoxide burns with oxygen, carbon dioxide is formed.
In the blast furnace, carbon monoxide removes the oxygen from the iron ore.

abschnitte.text: A **carbon monoxide** molecule consists of one carbon atom and one oxygen atom. It is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas that is a little lighter than air. It is flammable and burns with a blue flame to form carbon dioxide CO₂. So the difference from CO₂ is exactly one oxygen atom, but that makes a big difference.

Carbon monoxide is produced by **incomplete combustion**, that is when wood, coal, gas, petrol or heating oil burn with too little oxygen. Dangerous sources are badly adjusted gas boilers, blocked chimneys, charcoal barbecues indoors or engines running in garages. Cigarette smoke also contains carbon monoxide. In cars, the catalytic converter turns a large part of it into carbon dioxide.

In the blood, the red blood pigment **haemoglobin** carries oxygen to all the organs. Carbon monoxide binds about 200 to 300 times more strongly to haemoglobin than oxygen does and pushes it out. As a result the brain and heart get too little oxygen. The first signs are headaches, dizziness, nausea and tiredness; later you can lose consciousness.

Because you can neither see nor smell the gas, **CO alarms** make sense in rooms with fireplaces or gas appliances. Heating systems and chimneys should be checked regularly; in Switzerland this is done by the chimney sweep. If you suspect poisoning, you must immediately open the windows, leave the room and call the emergency number 144. In hospital, those affected are given pure oxygen, sometimes in a pressure chamber.

In the **blast furnace**, carbon monoxide is formed from coke and air. It reacts with the iron ore, removes its oxygen and so leaves liquid pig iron behind. Together with hydrogen, carbon monoxide forms synthesis gas, from which methanol and other chemicals are made. Chemistry also uses the gas to make acetic acid and plastics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Burning with too little oxygen, which produces poisonous CO.
The red blood pigment that carries oxygen in the blood.
A device that sounds an alarm when there is too much carbon monoxide in the air.
A huge furnace in which pig iron is obtained from iron ore.

gewusst: A smoke alarm does not detect carbon monoxide; you need a separate CO alarm for that.
Carbon monoxide also occurs in small amounts in space and helps astronomers map gas clouds.
In the past, the town gas used for cooking in many Swiss towns contained a lot of carbon monoxide.

teile.einleitung: Rust is the reddish brown, crumbly layer that forms on iron when it comes into contact with water and air. The metal turns into a completely new substance. Every year rust destroys bicycles, cars, bridges and machines, but you can protect against it.
wichtigste: Rust is reddish brown and forms only on iron and steel.
To rust, iron needs water and oxygen.
Rust is a new substance and no longer the same as iron.
Salt, such as road salt in winter, speeds up rusting a lot.
Iron that rusts for years becomes brittle and falls apart.
Painting, oiling or galvanising protect against rust.
Stainless steel contains chromium and therefore does not rust.

abschnitte.text: **Rust** forms when iron reacts with oxygen from the air and with water. This chemical reaction is an **oxidation**; the iron gives up electrons. A new substance made of iron, oxygen and water is formed, chemically mainly iron oxide hydroxide. Rust is reddish brown, porous and crumbly. Other metals such as copper or aluminium also change in air, but only with iron is it called rust.

A bicycle left outside in the rain rusts much faster than one in a dry cellar. Without water, iron hardly rusts; in dry desert air it lasts a long time. **Salt** speeds up rusting a lot, which is why cars rust faster in winter because of road salt. By the sea, too, metal parts rust particularly quickly because of the salty air.

Rust does not stick firmly to the iron but flakes off. Underneath there is fresh iron again, which can go on rusting. In this way rust eats into the metal layer by layer until it becomes brittle and falls apart. Rust also takes up more space than iron, which can crack the concrete of bridges in which steel bars are embedded. Worldwide, **corrosion** causes enormous damage every year.

The simplest way to protect iron is to keep water and air away. A garden gate is **painted**, and a bicycle chain is oiled regularly. Many parts are **galvanised**, that is coated with a thin layer of zinc, for example crash barriers along roads. Cars are given several protective layers of paint and wax.

**Stainless steel** contains, besides iron, at least about 10.5 per cent chromium. The chromium forms a wafer-thin, invisible protective layer on the surface. If it is scratched, it forms again by itself. Sinks, cutlery, saucepans and many devices in hospitals are made of such steel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical reaction in which a substance gives up electrons, often together with oxygen.
When a material such as metal is slowly destroyed by reactions with its surroundings.
Coating iron with a layer of zinc so that it does not rust.
A steel with chromium that hardly rusts.

gewusst: Mars looks red because its soil contains a lot of iron oxide, a kind of rust.
Rust is used as a brownish red pigment in paints and for polishing.
There is a special steel that deliberately forms a layer of rust, which then protects it from further rusting.

teile.einleitung: The molar volume shows how much space one mole of a substance takes up. The special thing: for gases it hardly depends on which gas it is. At 0 degrees and normal air pressure, one mole of any ideal gas fills about 22.4 litres.
wichtigste: The molar volume is the volume of one mole of a substance, given in litres per mole.
At 0 °C and 101.325 kPa an ideal gas has a molar volume of about 22.4 L/mol.
At 0 °C and 100 kPa it is about 22.7 L/mol, at 25 °C and 100 kPa about 24.8 L/mol.
If the pressure is doubled, the volume of a gas is halved.
Liquid water has a molar volume of only about 18 mL/mol.
Gases need so much more space because the distances between their particles are much larger than the particles themselves.
With the molar volume you can convert an amount of gas in litres into an amount of substance in moles.

abschnitte.text: The **molar volume** is the volume divided by the amount of substance. So it says how many litres one mole of a substance takes up. For solids and liquids it is different for every substance. For gases, on the other hand, it is almost the same for all gases, as long as temperature and pressure are the same. This makes it a practical tool in chemistry.

As early as 1811 the Italian scientist **Amedeo Avogadro** made a bold suggestion. Equal volumes of different gases contain the same number of particles at the same temperature and pressure. This rule is now called **Avogadro’s law**. It follows that one mole of hydrogen takes up as much space as one mole of oxygen or carbon dioxide. Only the number of particles matters, not their size or mass.

How large the molar volume is depends on **temperature** and **pressure**. At 0 °C and 101.325 kPa, the former standard pressure, it is about 22.4 litres per mole. If 100 kPa is used as standard pressure, it is about 22.7 litres per mole. At 25 °C and 100 kPa the gas expands to about 24.8 litres per mole. If you double the pressure to 202.65 kPa at 0 °C, the volume shrinks to about 11.2 litres.

Many problems can be solved with the molar volume. Three moles of an ideal gas take up about 67.2 litres at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa. 11.2 litres of carbon dioxide are half a mole, and because one mole weighs about 44 grams, that is 22 grams. To burn one mole of **methane** completely, you need two moles of oxygen, that is about 44.8 litres. In this way you can calculate how much air a gas cooker or a stove needs.

One mole of liquid **water** has a volume of only about 18 millilitres, about a tablespoon. As steam at 100 °C, the same amount takes up over 30 litres. The reason: in a gas, the distances between the particles are much larger than the particles themselves. That is why gases can be compressed, but liquids hardly at all. The **ideal gas** is a model in which the particles’ own volume is completely ignored.

begriffe.erklaerung: The volume of one mole of a substance, for example 22.4 litres for gases under standard conditions.
A model of a gas whose particles have no volume of their own and do not attract each other.
Fixed values for temperature and pressure so that measurements can be compared.
A unit of pressure; normal air pressure at sea level is about 101 kPa.

gewusst: 22.4 litres fit into a cube with sides of about 28 centimetres.
Real gases differ only slightly from the ideal gas, mainly at high pressure or low temperature.
One mole of hydrogen weighs only about 2 grams and one mole of carbon dioxide about 44 grams, and yet as gases both take up almost the same space.

teile.einleitung: Stomach acid is the acidic juice in our stomach, which contains mainly hydrochloric acid. It helps to digest protein and kills many germs. It is so strong that it could attack metal, and yet the stomach does not digest itself.
wichtigste: Stomach acid consists mainly of dilute hydrochloric acid.
It is produced in the stomach lining.
When the stomach is empty, gastric juice has a pH of about 1 to 2.
The acid kills many germs in food.
Together with the enzyme pepsin, it starts the digestion of protein.
A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.
In the duodenum, the acidic food pulp is neutralised again.

abschnitte.text: **Gastric juice** is produced by glands in the **stomach lining**. Its most important component is **hydrochloric acid**, which is released by special cells, the parietal cells. An adult produces about two to three litres of gastric juice a day. When the stomach is empty, the pH is about 1 to 2. That is acidic in a similar way to lemon juice, only much stronger.

The acid makes the **proteins** from food swell and loosens their structure. It also turns a precursor into the enzyme **pepsin**. Pepsin cuts the long protein chains into smaller pieces. Fats and carbohydrates, on the other hand, are mainly digested later in the intestine. The stomach kneads the food with the juice into a pulp.

Bacteria and other germs are constantly getting into the body with food. The strong acid kills many of them before they reach the intestine. So stomach acid is part of the body’s **defences**. One bacterium that can still survive in the stomach is called Helicobacter pylori. The researchers Barry Marshall and Robin Warren received the Nobel Prize in 2005 for showing that it can cause stomach ulcers.

abschnitte.titel: Why the stomach does not digest itself
abschnitte.text: The stomach wall is covered with a thick **layer of mucus**. This mucus contains alkaline substances that mop up the acid right at the wall. In addition, the cells of the stomach lining renew themselves very quickly, every few days. If this protection no longer works properly, inflammation of the stomach lining or an ulcer can develop.

If stomach acid gets up into the **gullet**, it burns behind the breastbone. This is called **heartburn**. For occasional heartburn, medicines that neutralise the acid help; they are called **antacids**. In the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine, the acidic food pulp is neutralised quite normally. This is done by hydrogen carbonate from the pancreas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strong acid made of hydrogen and chlorine, the main component of stomach acid.
An enzyme in the stomach that breaks proteins down into smaller pieces.
A number that shows how acidic or alkaline something is; 7 is neutral, smaller numbers are acidic.
Medicines that neutralise excess stomach acid.
The first section of the small intestine directly after the stomach.

gewusst: Stomach acid is so acidic that it could dissolve limestone and some metals.
The cells of the stomach lining are renewed about every three to five days.
Even the smell of food, or thinking about it, can make the stomach produce gastric juice.

teile.einleitung: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, PFAS for short, are a huge group of artificially made chemicals. They make pans, rain jackets and pizza boxes water- and grease-repellent. Because they are practically not broken down in nature, they are also called “forever chemicals”.
wichtigste: PFAS are carbon compounds in which many hydrogen atoms have been replaced by fluorine.
In perfluorinated chains, all the hydrogen atoms on the carbon have been replaced by fluorine.
The carbon-fluorine bond is extremely stable, which is why PFAS hardly break down.
PFAS are water- and grease-repellent and are therefore used for coatings.
The well-known fluoroplastic polytetrafluoroethylene was discovered in 1938 by Roy Plunkett.
Firefighting foam containing PFAS has polluted soil and groundwater in many places.
PFOS was added to the Stockholm Convention in 2009 and is therefore strongly restricted worldwide.

abschnitte.text: PFAS consist of chains of **carbon atoms** to which many **fluorine atoms** are attached instead of hydrogen. If they are called “perfluorinated”, every hydrogen atom on the chain has been replaced by fluorine; with “polyfluorinated” it is only many of them. The group includes many thousands of different substances. Well-known examples are perfluorooctanoic acid, **PFOA** for short, with 8 carbon atoms, and perfluorooctane sulphonic acid, PFOS for short.

Because PFAS make water, grease and dirt run off, they are found in many everyday products. They are in coated frying pans, outdoor jackets, carpets, baking paper and fast food packaging. The fluoroplastic **polytetrafluoroethylene** (PTFE) was discovered by chance in 1938 by the American Roy Plunkett and is known under the brand name **Teflon**. PFAS were also used for a long time in ski wax, cosmetics and in industry.

The bond between carbon and fluorine is one of the strongest bonds in organic chemistry. Neither sunlight nor bacteria can easily break it in nature. That is why PFAS stay in soils, waters and living things for decades or much longer. Some of them build up in the body and are suspected of damaging **health**.

In the past, particularly large amounts of PFAS got into the environment through **firefighting foam**, for example at airfields and fire brigade training grounds. From there they seeped into the groundwater. In Switzerland, too, polluted soils have been found at such places. Waterworks often remove PFAS with **activated carbon**, on whose huge surface the substances stick.

In 2009 PFOS was added to the **Stockholm Convention** on persistent organic pollutants. Later other PFAS such as PFOA followed. Many countries, including Switzerland, have set maximum levels for drinking water and food and ban certain uses. Experts are looking for substitutes, for example for firefighting foam and rainwear.

begriffe.erklaerung: The abbreviation for a large group of very stable fluorine chemicals.
A very reactive chemical element that forms extremely strong bonds with carbon.
Porous carbon with a huge surface that holds on to pollutants.
Water that collects underground in layers of rock.

gewusst: Today traces of PFAS can be detected in almost every person and even in animals in the Arctic.
PTFE was discovered because a gas cylinder seemed empty, but a white powder had formed inside it.

teile.einleitung: Leather is a durable, flexible material made from the skin of animals. So that the skin does not rot, it is tanned. Shoes, belts, bags, saddles and much more are made from leather.
wichtigste: Leather is made from animal skin.
Turning animal skin into leather is called tanning.
Most of the world’s leather comes from cattle.
Shoemakers make shoes and repair them.
Belts and horse saddles are often made of leather.
In the past, the outer cover of a football was made of leather.
Leather shoes are cared for with shoe polish so that they shine.

abschnitte.text: **Leather** is tanned animal skin. Most hides come from cattle, but also from sheep, goats and pigs. The hides are usually a by-product of meat production. Leather is tough, tear-resistant, flexible and lets air through, which is why it feels pleasant.

Untreated skin would quickly rot or become hard and brittle when it dries. In **tanning**, the protein fibres of the skin are treated with tanning agents so that they last permanently. In the past, mainly plant tanning agents from tree bark were used, for example from oaks. Today a large part of leather is tanned with chromium salts, which is quicker but can pollute the environment.

Someone who turns hides into leather is a **tanner** by trade. The **shoemaker** makes and repairs shoes, and the saddler makes saddles, bridles and bags. In many Swiss old towns, street names such as Gerbergasse (Tanners’ Lane) recall this old craft. Tanneries were usually by streams and rivers because they needed a lot of water.

Leather is one of humanity’s oldest materials. As early as the Stone Age, people wore clothing and shoes made of animal skins. The glacier mummy Ötzi, who lived over 5000 years ago, wore shoes made of leather and fur. Footballs also used to have a leather cover, which became heavy in the rain; today they are made of plastic.

abschnitte.titel: Leather in everyday life and care
abschnitte.text: Shoes, belts, purses, jackets, gloves and furniture covers are made of leather. When riding, the leather **saddle** lies on the horse’s back. So that leather stays nice for a long time, it is cared for with shoe polish or leather grease, which keeps it supple and protects it from wet. As an alternative, there is now artificial leather made of plastic and even materials made from plant fibres or fungi.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process that turns animal skin into durable leather.
A substance from plants or minerals that makes skin durable.
A craftsman who makes saddles, bags and other leather goods.
A plastic material that looks like leather.

gewusst: The oldest surviving leather shoes in the world were found in a cave in Armenia and are over 5000 years old.
Suede (“Wildleder” in German, literally “wild leather”) is not leather from wild animals but leather with a roughened surface.
In the old town of Fez in Morocco there are tanneries that have worked in almost the same way for centuries.

teile.einleitung: Polyethylene terephthalate, PET for short, is the plastic that most drinks bottles are made of. It is light, shatterproof and as transparent as glass. In Switzerland, PET bottles are collected diligently and made into new bottles or fibres.
wichtigste: PET is the abbreviation for polyethylene terephthalate.
It is made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, which come mainly from crude oil.
PET is a thermoplastic and becomes soft and mouldable when warmed.
Bottles are made by stretch blow moulding from small, thick-walled blanks.
In the recycling triangle, PET has the number 1.
As a textile fibre, PET is called polyester and is found in fleece jackets, for example.
In Switzerland in 2024, over 80 per cent of PET drinks bottles were recycled.

abschnitte.text: **Polyethylene terephthalate** is a plastic made of very long chain molecules, a **polymer**. It is formed when the starting substances ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid join into long chains. Both are obtained mainly from crude oil. PET was developed in England in the 1940s, at first for textile fibres.

PET is light, shatterproof and transparent, which is why it is well suited for **drinks bottles**. It also withstands the pressure of fizzy drinks. As a **thermoplastic**, PET becomes soft and mouldable when warmed and hardens again when it cools. A PET bottle weighs only a fraction of a glass bottle of the same size, which saves energy in transport.

First, small, thick-walled **blanks** are made that look like test tubes with a screw thread. At the bottling company they are warmed, put into a mould and stretched with a rod. Then compressed air blows them up until they take on the shape of the bottle. This process is called stretch blow moulding and takes only fractions of a second.

In Switzerland there are collection containers for PET drinks bottles at many points of sale. The organisation **PET-Recycling Schweiz** takes care of collecting and recycling. In 2024 the recycling rate was over 80 per cent. You should squash the bottles flat so that they take up less space in transport, and screw the lid back on. Only drinks bottles belong in the PET collection, not shampoo or oil bottles.

Collected bottles are turned into flakes, which are made into new bottles or into fibres. As a textile fibre, PET is called **polyester** and is used for fleece jackets, sportswear and rucksacks. In the recycling triangle on packaging, PET can be recognised by the number 1. Like all plastics, PET breaks down extremely slowly in nature, which is why it must never end up in the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge molecule made of many identical building blocks linked together.
A plastic that becomes soft when warmed and can be reshaped.
A small intermediate product from which the bottle is later blown up.
The name of PET when it is used as a fibre for fabrics.

gewusst: Fibres from several recycled PET bottles can be used for one fleece jacket.
New Swiss PET bottles often contain a large proportion of recycled PET.
A blank for a half-litre bottle is only about the size of a finger.

teile.einleitung: A polymer is a huge molecule made up of many identical or similar small building blocks. These building blocks are called monomers and are linked together like beads on a necklace. Plastics such as PET, but also natural substances such as cellulose, proteins and DNA, are polymers.
wichtigste: A polymer is a giant molecule made of many small building blocks.
A monomer is a small molecule that can join into long chains.
Polyethylene is made from ethene by polymerisation.
In the polycondensation of polyesters, water is split off.
In polyamides such as nylon, amide bonds link the building blocks.
PET stands for polyethylene terephthalate.
Cellulose is a natural substance made of glucose units.

abschnitte.text: The word polymer comes from Greek and means “many parts”. A **monomer** is a small molecule that can join with others into long chains. A polymer molecule can consist of thousands or even millions of monomers. Some chains are straight, others branched or **cross-linked** with each other.

In **polymerisation**, double bonds in the monomers open and the building blocks attach to one another; this is how polyethylene is made from ethene. In **polycondensation**, the monomers join and a small molecule is split off, usually water. This is how **polyesters** and polyamides are made. In polyamides such as nylon, **amide bonds** link the building blocks.

**Thermoplastics** become soft when warmed and can be reshaped; examples are polyethylene and PET. **Thermosets** are tightly cross-linked and cannot be melted; they are used, for example, for sockets and pan handles. **Elastomers** are loosely cross-linked and stretchy like rubber. Car tyres and rubber bands are made of elastomers.

Drinks bottles are usually made of PET, which stands for **polyethylene terephthalate**. Plastic bags and films are often made of polyethylene. Nylon is used for tights, ropes and toothbrushes. In Switzerland PET bottles have been collected separately for decades, and a large part of them is **recycled** into new bottles.

Nature also makes polymers. **Cellulose** consists of many glucose units and gives plants and wood their strength. Starch in potatoes and bread is also built from glucose. Proteins consist of amino acids, and **DNA** is a polymer made of nucleotides.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small molecule that serves as a building block for a polymer.
A reaction in which many monomers join into a long chain.
A plastic that becomes soft when warmed and can be reshaped.
A hard plastic that is tightly cross-linked and does not melt.

gewusst: Nylon was invented in the 1930s by the American Wallace Carothers.
Paper consists mainly of cellulose, that is of a natural polymer.
Nylon hook-and-loop fasteners go back to the Swiss engineer George de Mestral, who was inspired by burrs.

teile.einleitung: Plastic is a material that people make artificially, usually from crude oil. Plastics are light, easy to shape and versatile, which is why they are found in toothbrushes, bottles, clothes and cars. But because they break down very slowly in nature, they are also a big environmental problem.
wichtigste: In everyday life, synthetic materials are simply called plastic.
Plastic is made by people, usually from crude oil.
Plastics are light and easy to shape.
Many plastics become soft when they get very hot.
Plastic does not conduct electricity and therefore insulates electric cables.
Fleece jumpers are usually made of plastic fibres.
In nature, plastic breaks down very slowly and so becomes a problem.

abschnitte.text: Plastics consist of huge molecules, the **macromolecules**. They are formed when thousands of small building blocks, the **monomers**, join together like beads on a necklace. The finished chain is called a **polymer**. Depending on the building block and the shape of the chains, plastics are hard, soft, transparent or stretchy.

The most important raw material is **crude oil**, and also natural gas. In refineries and chemical plants, basic substances such as ethene are obtained from it and linked into polymers. As granules or powder they go to factories, where they are melted and injected into moulds or blown into films. Worldwide, about 400 million tonnes of plastic are produced every year (as of around 2022).

**Thermoplastics** become soft when heated and can be reshaped, for example PET in drinks bottles or polyethylene in carrier bags. **Thermosets** stay hard even when hot, for example sockets and pan handles. Elastomers are rubbery and stretchy, like bicycle inner tubes. That is why not every plastic is suitable for every job.

Toothbrushes, toys, bicycle helmets, rain jackets and packaging are usually made of plastic. Because plastic does not conduct electricity, it sheaths cables and protects us from electric shocks. Fleece jumpers are made of **polyester** fibres, often even from recycled PET bottles. In cars and aeroplanes, too, plastic replaces metal and makes them lighter.

Many plastics take hundreds of years to break down in nature. They crumble into tiny particles, **microplastics**. These have already been found in the sea, in Swiss lakes, in the soil and even in the snow of the Alps. Animals mistake pieces of plastic for food and can die from them.

In Switzerland, PET drinks bottles are collected separately, and a large part of them is made into new bottles. Other plastics usually end up in the waste incineration plant, where their energy is used for electricity and heating. The first fully synthetic plastic was **Bakelite**, made by Leo Baekeland in 1907. The chemist Hermann Staudinger, who did research at the ETH Zurich for a long time, explained that plastics consist of long chains and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1953.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge molecule made of many identical building blocks linked in a chain.
A small building block from which a polymer is put together.
A plastic that becomes soft when heated and can be reshaped.
Tiny plastic particles smaller than five millimetres.
The plastic most drinks bottles are made of.

gewusst: A fleece jumper can be made from several old PET bottles.
Plastics have only existed for just over a hundred years, and yet today they are found everywhere on Earth.
There are also plastics made from plants such as maize or sugar cane.

teile.einleitung: Molecular geometry describes the shape a molecule has in space. Molecules are not flat as they appear on paper, but three-dimensional structures with particular angles. Their shape decides how a substance smells, how it dissolves and how it reacts.
wichtigste: Molecules have a particular shape in space.
The methane molecule CH₄ is tetrahedral.
In the water molecule the H-O-H angle is about 104.5°.
Ammonia NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal, boron trifluoride BF₃ trigonal planar.
Sulphur hexafluoride SF₆ is octahedral.
CO₂ is linear and therefore non-polar, even though its bonds are polar.
The carbon atoms in ethene are sp² hybridised.

abschnitte.text: With the **valence shell electron pair repulsion model**, VSEPR model for short, you can predict the shape of a molecule. The idea is simple: electron pairs around a central atom repel each other. That is why they arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible. Both bonds and **lone pairs** count.

In methane CH₄ the four bonds point to the corners of a **tetrahedron**, and the angle is 109.5°. In ammonia NH₃ a lone pair occupies one corner, so the molecule is **trigonal pyramidal**. In water H₂O there are two lone pairs, and the molecule is bent at about 104.5°. Lone pairs need more space and squeeze the bonds together a little.

If a central atom has only three bonding partners and no lone pair, the molecule is flat and **trigonal planar**, like boron trifluoride BF₃. Two bonding partners without lone pairs give a **linear** shape, as in CO₂. Sulphur hexafluoride SF₆ has six fluorine atoms that point to the corners of an **octahedron**. All the angles there are 90°.

Whether a molecule is **polar** depends on its shape. In CO₂ the two C=O bonds are polar, but they point in exactly opposite directions. The **bond dipoles** therefore cancel out, and CO₂ is non-polar. Water is bent, so the dipoles do not cancel out, and water is strongly polar.

To explain the shapes more precisely, the model of **hybridisation** is used. In methane the orbitals of carbon are sp³ hybridised, which matches the tetrahedral shape. The carbon atoms in ethene C₂H₄ are **sp² hybridised**, and the molecule is flat. In ethyne C₂H₂ they are sp hybridised, and the molecule is straight like a rod.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid with four triangular faces, like a pyramid with a triangular base.
Two electrons on an atom that are not involved in any bond.
A molecule with a slightly positive and a slightly negative side.
The angle between two bonds on the same atom.

gewusst: Because water is bent and polar, water drops have surface tension, on which pond skaters can walk.
Molecules that are mirror images of each other, like left and right hands, can smell quite different.
The VSEPR model was worked out in the 1950s by Ronald Gillespie and Ronald Nyholm.

teile.einleitung: Extinguishing agents are substances used to fight a fire, for example water, foam, powder or carbon dioxide. Not every extinguishing agent suits every fire. Using the wrong one can even make a fire dangerously worse.
wichtigste: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat; if one of them is missing, it goes out.
Extinguishing agents cool the fire, smother it or interrupt the burning.
Fires are divided into fire classes: A, B, C, D and F.
Class A are solid materials that form embers, such as wood and paper; class B are flammable liquids such as petrol and alcohol.
Class F stands for burning cooking oil and cooking fat.
A burning pan of oil must never be put out with water.
In Switzerland the fire brigade can be reached on the emergency number 118.

abschnitte.text: For something to burn, three things are needed at the same time: a **fuel**, **oxygen** from the air and a high enough temperature. This is called the fire triangle. An extinguishing agent takes at least one of these three ingredients away from the fire. Water cools; a lid or a blanket keeps oxygen away. Powder also disrupts the chemical reactions in the flame.

So that the right extinguishing agent is chosen, fires are divided into **fire classes**. Class A are solid materials that form embers, such as wood, paper, fabric or straw. Class B are flammable liquids such as petrol, alcohol or varnish; class C are flammable gases such as propane or natural gas. Class D are burning metals such as magnesium, and class F are fires of cooking oil and fat in the kitchen. Every fire extinguisher shows which fire classes it is suitable for.

**Water** is the most important extinguishing agent, because it is cheap and cools very strongly. It is good for class A, that is for burning wood or paper. With burning petrol, however, water would sink to the bottom and the petrol would go on burning on top. Here **foam** helps: it lies over the liquid like a blanket and cuts it off from oxygen. That is why airport fire brigades have large foam tenders.

The **ABC powder extinguisher** works on fire classes A, B and C but leaves a lot of fine dust. A **carbon dioxide extinguisher** pushes away the oxygen and leaves no residue. That is why it is often used in computer rooms, laboratories or on electrical equipment. In small rooms, however, carbon dioxide is dangerous, because people there no longer get any oxygen either. Burning metals such as magnesium are put out with dry sand or special metal fire powder, because water would only fan the flames.

With a small pan fire, you simply put a suitable **lid** on the pan and switch off the hotplate. Without oxygen the fire goes out. A **fire blanket** is also good. Water on burning oil, on the other hand, is life-threatening: the water sinks into the hot oil, turns into steam in an instant and carries burning droplets of oil with it. A huge jet of flame results, which is called a **fat explosion**.

In a fire, the rule in Switzerland is: first raise the alarm, then rescue people, and only after that put out the fire. The fire brigade can be reached on the emergency number **118**. You should only use a fire extinguisher if the fire is still small and you are not putting yourself in danger. Many fire brigades in Switzerland are **volunteer fire brigades**, which means the firefighters have another job and turn out when the alarm goes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of fires with similar fuel, for example A for wood or B for petrol.
A portable device with an extinguishing agent that you can use yourself on small fires.
A fireproof blanket that is laid over a fire to smother it.
A dangerous jet of flame when water gets into burning oil.

gewusst: One litre of water turns into well over a thousand litres of steam when it evaporates, which is why water in hot oil is so dangerous.
Burning magnesium can even break water down and burn even more fiercely as a result.
In the past, fires were fought with bucket chains, in which many people passed buckets of water from hand to hand.

teile.einleitung: A tin can is an airtight metal container in which food keeps for years. The food is heated in the sealed can so that all germs die. The can was invented over 200 years ago, and still today almost every store cupboard holds cans of beans, tomatoes or tuna.
wichtigste: Tin cans make food last a long time.
They are usually made of sheet steel with a thin layer of tin against rust.
The food is heated in the sealed can so that germs die.
In a sealed can, food often stays good for several years.
Cans without a ring pull are opened with a tin opener.
A lid bulging outwards means that the contents may have gone off.
Steel cans can be separated from aluminium cans with a magnet.

abschnitte.text: Food goes off because bacteria and moulds grow in it. In a tin can, the food is filled in, the can is sealed airtight and then heated strongly. The germs die; this is called **sterilising**. Because no new germs can get in, the contents often stay edible for several years.

Most tin cans are made of **tinplate**, that is thin sheet steel with a very thin layer of tin. The tin protects the iron from rust. Inside, many cans also have a layer of lacquer so that acidic foods do not attack the metal. Drinks cans, on the other hand, are often made of **aluminium**.

Around 1810 the French cook Nicolas Appert discovered that food that is heated and sealed airtight keeps for a long time; he used glass bottles. In the same year the Englishman Peter Durand patented the tin can as a container. At first it was mainly soldiers and sailors who ate from cans. Strangely, the **tin opener** was only invented decades later; before that, cans were opened with a hammer and chisel.

If the lid of a can bulges outwards, which is called **blowing**, gases have formed inside. This can mean that bacteria have survived and the contents have gone off. Such cans must not be eaten but thrown away. You should also not use badly dented or rusty cans.

Empty tin cans are rinsed briefly and taken to the collection point for scrap metal. With a **magnet** you can check whether a can is made of steel, because aluminium is not attracted. The collected metal is melted down and made into new steel. This saves a lot of energy and raw materials.

In 1886 a cannery was founded in Lenzburg in the Aargau, from which the well-known brand Hero grew. There, vegetables, fruit and jam were produced in cans and jars. In the past, canned food was particularly important because there were no fridges yet. Even today, the federal government recommends keeping an **emergency supply** of long-life food at home.

begriffe.erklaerung: Food that has been made to keep, in a can or a jar.
Killing all germs by strong heating.
Thin sheet steel with a protective layer of tin.
A can lid bulging outwards, a warning sign that the contents have gone off.

gewusst: The tin opener was only invented about 50 years after the tin can.
On polar expeditions, cans were found whose contents had still not gone off after many decades.
A tin can can be recycled again and again without the metal losing quality.

teile.einleitung: A fire blanket is a fireproof blanket that can be used to smother small fires quickly. It often hangs within reach in the kitchen and is particularly helpful when a pan of oil catches fire. Used correctly, it can prevent a bigger fire.
wichtigste: A fire blanket is used to smother small fires.
It takes the air, and therefore the oxygen, away from the fire.
Fire blankets are often made of fireproof glass fabric.
You pull hard on the tapes to get the blanket out of its case quickly.
You keep your hands behind the blanket so that they are protected.
After covering the fire, you leave the fire blanket in place.
If there is no fire blanket, you can cover a burning pan with a suitable lid.

abschnitte.titel: How does a fire blanket work?
abschnitte.text: A fire needs three things: something that can burn, heat and **oxygen**. If one of them is missing, the fire goes out. The **fire blanket** lies over the flames and cuts off the supply of air. As a result the fire is smothered without any water being needed.

Modern fire blankets are usually made of fireproof **glass fabric**, which does not burn even at great heat. The blanket is stored folded in a case that hangs on the wall. Two tapes stick out at the bottom. If you pull hard on them, the blanket falls open into your hands immediately.

You hold the blanket by the tapes or the top corners and fold the top edge over your hands so that they are **protected** behind the blanket. Then you calmly lay the blanket over the burning pan, moving it away from you. Then you switch off the cooker and leave the blanket in place until everything has cooled down. If you lift it too early, the hot oil can flare up again with fresh air.

You must never put out burning oil or fat with water. The water sinks into the hot oil, turns into steam in an instant and carries burning droplets of oil with it, causing a dangerous **fat explosion**. That is why the fire blanket or a suitable lid is the best choice for a pan fire. If a person’s clothing catches fire, you can also wrap them in a fire blanket or have them roll on the ground.

In Switzerland, fire brigades and fire safety experts recommend having a fire blanket within reach in every kitchen. It should not hang directly above the cooker, but where you can reach it without reaching through the flames. If a fire cannot be put out immediately, you leave the flat, close the doors and call the fire brigade on **118**. A fire blanket is only meant for small fires and does not replace an emergency call.

begriffe.erklaerung: Putting out a fire by taking away its air.
Material made of fine glass fibres that does not burn.
A fire of hot oil or fat, for example in a pan.
A dangerous jet of flame when water hits burning oil.

gewusst: Even a glass of water on burning oil can produce a jet of flame several metres high.
Unlike a fire extinguisher, a fire blanket can be used straight away without practice.
Cooking oil can catch fire by itself from about 300 °C.

teile.einleitung: Acids are substances that taste sour and can attack other substances. You know them from the kitchen, for example in vinegar or lemon juice. Strong acids in the laboratory, on the other hand, are dangerous and must be handled carefully.
wichtigste: Acids taste sour, but in the laboratory you must never taste anything.
Acidic solutions contain particularly many oxonium ions (H3O+).
Blue litmus paper turns red in an acid.
Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which helps with digestion.
Acetic acid gives vinegar its sour taste.
Some ants spray formic acid to defend themselves.
When diluting, the rule is: first the water, then the acid.

abschnitte.text: An acid is a substance that gives up **hydrogen ions** in water. These combine with water to form **oxonium ions** (H3O+), which cause the acidic effect. The more of them there are in a solution, the more acidic it is. The opposite of acids are alkalis, also called bases.

How acidic a solution is, is shown by the **pH**. The scale usually runs from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral, like pure water. Values below 7 are acidic, values above 7 are alkaline. Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, and gastric juice is often even lower.

With **indicators**, acids can be made visible. Blue litmus paper turns red in an acid and stays blue in an alkali. Red cabbage juice also changes colour: in acid it turns red to pink. Universal indicator paper even shows the approximate pH with many colours.

Many acids are harmless and even useful. **Acetic acid** is in vinegar, citric acid in lemons and oranges, carbonic acid in mineral water. In the stomach, dilute **hydrochloric acid** helps to digest food and kill bacteria. Kettles are also descaled with vinegar or citric acid.

Some ants, such as the red wood ant, spray **formic acid** when they feel threatened. Stinging nettles also contain formic acid in their stinging hairs, which is why your skin burns. Because of exhaust gases, rain can become **acid rain**, which damages forests and buildings. In the 1980s the dying of forests was a big issue in Switzerland.

Strong acids such as sulphuric acid or concentrated hydrochloric acid burn skin and eyes. That is why in the laboratory you wear **safety goggles**, gloves and a lab coat. When diluting, you always add the acid to the water and not the other way round. A memory aid: “Always add acid to water, never water to acid.” Otherwise the mixture can heat up a lot and spit.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
A substance that shows by its colour whether something is acidic or alkaline.
The opposite of an acid, also called a base, for example soapy water.
When acid and alkali cancel each other out and salt and water are formed.

gewusst: Stomach acid is so strong that it can attack metal, but a layer of mucus protects the stomach wall.
Cola contains phosphoric acid and is therefore quite acidic.
The German word for acid, “Säure”, comes from the sour (“sauer”) taste that many acids have.

teile.einleitung: Molten salt electrolysis is a process in which a substance is melted and broken down with electricity. It is used to obtain base metals such as aluminium and sodium, which are difficult to make in other ways. The process needs a great deal of electricity, which is why Switzerland’s hydropower played an important part in it.
wichtigste: In molten salt electrolysis, a substance is melted instead of being dissolved in water.
Aluminium is obtained almost exclusively in this way today.
Hall and Héroult developed the process independently of each other in 1886.
Cryolite lowers the melting temperature of aluminium oxide.
The aluminium is deposited at the negative pole.
The anodes are made of carbon and are slowly used up.
Sodium is obtained in this way from molten table salt.
Making new aluminium needs a lot of electricity.

abschnitte.text: In **electrolysis**, a substance is broken down with electricity. If a salt is dissolved in water, with base metals hydrogen would often be formed instead of the metal. That is why the substance is melted, and the ions become mobile in the hot melt. So “molten salt” means that the substance is **melted** instead of being dissolved in water.

Two **electrodes** dip into the melt, and a voltage is applied to them. The positively charged metal ions move to the negative pole, the **cathode**, and take up electrons there. In this way they become metal atoms; in aluminium production, liquid aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell. The negative ions move to the positive pole, the **anode**, and give up electrons there.

The starting material is **aluminium oxide**, which is obtained from the ore bauxite. Pure aluminium oxide only melts at over 2000 degrees Celsius. If it is mixed with the mineral **cryolite**, a temperature of about 950 degrees Celsius is enough. The anodes are made of carbon, which reacts with the oxygen to form carbon dioxide, which is why they are slowly used up and have to be replaced.

In 1886 the American Charles Martin **Hall** and the Frenchman Paul **Héroult** invented the process independently of each other. Before that, aluminium was as expensive as silver or gold. As early as 1888 one of the first aluminium smelters was built in **Neuhausen am Rheinfall**, powered by the hydropower of the Rhine. Later aluminium was also produced in Valais, but today no new primary aluminium is produced in Switzerland any more.

**Sodium** is also obtained by molten salt electrolysis, from molten table salt. Chlorine gas is also produced at the positive pole. As early as 1807 the Englishman Humphry Davy was the first to make sodium and potassium by electrolysis of molten substances. Because the process needs an enormous amount of electricity, **recycling** is important: melting down old aluminium needs only a small fraction of the energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Breaking down a substance with electricity.
The negative pole, where particles take up electrons.
The positive pole, where particles give up electrons.
A mineral that greatly lowers the melting temperature of aluminium oxide.
A reddish rock from which aluminium is obtained.

gewusst: Hall and Héroult were both born in 1863 and both died in 1914.
Recycled aluminium needs only about 5 per cent of the energy needed for new aluminium.

teile.einleitung: Proteins are long chains of amino acids and are among the most important substances of life. They build muscles, hair and fingernails and work as enzymes, messengers and defence substances. Anyone who eats eggs, cheese, beans or meat takes in proteins.
wichtigste: Proteins consist of amino acids.
The human body uses about 20 different amino acids for its proteins.
The amino acids are linked to each other by peptide bonds.
All proteins contain nitrogen, whereas fats and sugars do not.
When an egg is boiled, the proteins denature, and the egg white becomes firm and white.
In the biuret test, proteins turn violet.
Hair and fingernails are made of the protein keratin.

abschnitte.text: Proteins are built from **amino acids**, which hang together like beads on a necklace. They are joined by **peptide bonds**. Humans use about 20 different amino acids, and even a short chain can form countless combinations from them. The finished chain folds into a very particular three-dimensional shape, and this shape decides the protein’s job.

**Enzymes** are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in the body, for example during digestion. Red **haemoglobin** in the blood carries oxygen, and the hormone insulin controls blood sugar. Antibodies recognise germs, and muscle proteins make it possible for us to move. Collagen makes skin, tendons and bones firm; keratin forms hair and nails.

Proteins are sensitive to heat, acids and salts. If their shape is destroyed, this is called **denaturation**. This is exactly what happens when an egg is boiled: the runny, clear egg white becomes firm and white. Proteins in the body can also be damaged by a very high temperature, which is why a very high fever is dangerous.

There is a lot of protein in meat, fish, eggs, milk and cheese and in pulses such as lentils, beans and chickpeas. During digestion the body breaks the proteins down into amino acids and builds its own proteins from them. Some amino acids cannot be made by the body itself; they are called **essential** and must come from food. In cheesemaking, the milk protein **casein** is made to curdle with rennet, an important step for Emmental or Gruyère.

With the **biuret test** proteins can be detected: a sample with copper sulphate in sodium hydroxide solution turns violet. Unlike fats and sugars, proteins always contain **nitrogen**, often sulphur too. The name protein was used around 1838 by the Dutch chemist Gerardus Mulder and comes from the Greek word for “the first”. This was meant to show how fundamental these substances are for life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block of which proteins consist.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in the body.
The destruction of a protein’s shape, for example by heat.
A tough protein in hair, nails and feathers.
The most important protein in milk, which curdles in cheesemaking.

gewusst: Collagen is the most common protein in the human body.
Spider silk is a protein and, for its weight, stronger than steel.

teile.einleitung: Lipids are a large group of natural substances that include fats, oils, waxes and cholesterol. What they have in common is that they dissolve poorly in water. They provide our body with a lot of energy and form the membranes of all cells.
wichtigste: Lipids dissolve poorly in water but well in non-polar solvents.
Fat has an energy value of about 37 kilojoules per gram.
In the small intestine, the enzyme lipase splits the fats from food.
Phospholipids have a water-loving head and a water-repelling tail; they are amphiphilic.
In water, phospholipids form a lipid bilayer by themselves.
Cholesterol belongs to the group of steroids.
LDL carries cholesterol from the liver to the body tissues.
In fat hardening, liquid vegetable oils become solid through catalytic hydrogenation.

abschnitte.text: **Lipids** are natural substances that hardly dissolve in water but dissolve well in non-polar solvents such as petrol. You notice this when oil floats on soup or when a grease stain cannot be washed out with water alone. Lipids include fats and oils, phospholipids, steroids such as **cholesterol** and waxes. Vitamins A, D, E and K are also fat-soluble.

Fats and oils consist mainly of **triglycerides**. In these, three fatty acids are joined with a glycerol molecule to form an ester.
