Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds and make fats such as butter solid. Unsaturated fatty acids with double bonds make oils such as olive oil or rapeseed oil liquid at room temperature.

**Phospholipids** have a water-loving head and two water-repelling tails, so they are amphiphilic. In water they arrange themselves into a **lipid bilayer**, in which the tails point inwards. The membranes that surround every cell are made of such bilayers. Cholesterol is built into these membranes and makes them more stable.

At about 37 kilojoules per gram, fat provides more than twice as much energy as carbohydrates or proteins. In the small intestine it is broken into small droplets with the help of bile and split by the enzyme **lipase**. In the blood, fats and cholesterol are transported in protein packages, the lipoproteins. LDL takes cholesterol from the liver to the tissues; HDL brings excess cholesterol back to the liver.

In **fat hardening**, liquid vegetable oils are treated with hydrogen and a catalyst. Double bonds are removed, and the oil becomes solid; this is how a lot of margarine used to be made. Fats and sodium hydroxide solution produce soap by saponification. Waxes such as beeswax protect leaves and feathers from wet in nature and are used for candles and care products.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fat molecule made of glycerol and three fatty acids.
A long carbon chain with an acid group at the end, a building block of fats.
Partly water-loving and partly water-repelling, like a phospholipid.
An enzyme that splits fats during digestion.
Lipids with four joined carbon rings, such as cholesterol.

gewusst: The human brain consists largely of lipids.
Camels store fat in their hump, not water.
Soap works because its molecules, like phospholipids, have a water-loving and a fat-loving part.

teile.einleitung: Acid rain is precipitation that is clearly more acidic than normal rain. It forms when exhaust gases from factories, heating systems and cars combine with water in the clouds to form acids. In the 1980s many people in Switzerland were very worried about their forests.
wichtigste: Rain is called acid rain from roughly a pH below 5.6.
Sulphur dioxide from burning coal and heating oil contributes particularly to acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides from car engines also make rain acidic.
In Switzerland in the 1980s, damage to forests in particular was discussed.
Marble statues weather badly because acid dissolves the lime.
Filters that remove sulphur from exhaust gases have greatly reduced acid rain in Europe.
The catalytic converter in a car reduces the emission of nitrogen oxides.

abschnitte.text: Even clean rain is slightly acidic, because some **carbon dioxide** from the air dissolves in it. Its pH is therefore about 5.6. If the rain is clearly more acidic, it is called **acid rain**. In heavily polluted areas, pH values around 4 and even lower used to be measured, that is more than ten times as acidic as normal rain.

When **coal** and **heating oil** burn, sulphur dioxide is produced, because these fuels contain sulphur. In hot engines and furnaces, **nitrogen oxides** are also produced. In the air, these gases react with oxygen and water to form sulphuric acid and nitric acid. The wind can carry the pollutants hundreds of kilometres before they come down with the rain.

Acid rain harms soils, plants and waters. In acidified lakes, fish can die because the water is too acidic; this was observed above all in Scandinavia. In Switzerland and Germany there was a heated debate about **forest dieback** in the 1980s. Statues and buildings made of **marble** and limestone weather particularly badly, because acids dissolve the lime.

Power stations and factories were given filters that remove sulphur from the exhaust gases; this is called **flue gas desulphurisation**. Heating oil and petrol now contain much less sulphur than before. From the end of the 1980s, new petrol cars in Switzerland were fitted with a **catalytic converter**, which converts nitrogen oxides. International agreements on clean air also helped to reduce pollution across borders.

Thanks to these measures, acid rain is much rarer in Europe today than 40 years ago. The sulphur dioxide content of the air has fallen sharply in Switzerland. Soils and lakes, however, recover only slowly; some need decades. In countries where a lot of coal is still burnt, acid rain remains a problem.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how acidic or alkaline a liquid is.
A sharp-smelling gas produced when fuels containing sulphur are burnt.
Gases made of nitrogen and oxygen, produced mainly in engines.
A process that removes sulphur from the exhaust gases of power stations.

gewusst: The Scottish chemist Robert Angus Smith already used the term “acid rain” in the 19th century.
Because of acid rain, some stone figures on old churches lost more of their facial features in a few decades than in the centuries before.

teile.einleitung: Paul Karrer was a Swiss chemist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1937. He researched vitamins and pigments such as carotene, which makes carrots orange. For four decades he taught and did research at the University of Zurich.
wichtigste: Paul Karrer was born in Moscow in 1889 to Swiss parents.
From 1919 to 1959 he was a professor at the University of Zurich.
In 1931 he was the first to work out the structure of vitamin A.
In 1937 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on carotenoids, flavins and vitamins A and B2.
In 1938 he succeeded in synthesising vitamin E, also called tocopherol.
His textbook of organic chemistry from 1927 became a widely used standard work.
Before that he worked with Alfred Werner in Zurich and with Paul Ehrlich in Frankfurt.

abschnitte.text: **Paul Karrer** was born on 21 April 1889 in **Moscow**, the son of Swiss parents. As a small child he returned with his family to Switzerland and grew up in the canton of Aargau. He studied chemistry at the University of Zurich. There he was a student and then an assistant of the Nobel Prize winner **Alfred Werner**. Karrer died in Zurich in 1971.

From 1912 to 1918 Karrer worked in the laboratory of the famous medical scientist **Paul Ehrlich** in Frankfurt am Main. With Salvarsan, Ehrlich had developed one of the first medicines against a dangerous infectious disease. Karrer researched organic **arsenic compounds** there, which were meant to serve as remedies. After Ehrlich’s death in 1915 he stayed in Frankfurt for a few more years. In 1918 he returned to Zurich.

In 1919 Karrer became professor of chemistry at the **University of Zurich** and remained so until 1959, that is for forty years. He headed the Chemical Institute and trained many researchers. In 1927 his **textbook of organic chemistry** appeared, which was translated into many languages. For decades it was one of the most important chemistry books at universities. Thanks to him, Zurich became a centre of vitamin research.

Karrer studied above all the **carotenoids**, yellow to red pigments that colour carrots, tomatoes and peppers, for example. He showed how they are linked to vitamin A, which our eyes need in order to see. In 1931 he was the first to work out the chemical structure of **vitamin A**. He also worked on the flavins, which include vitamin B2. In 1938 he succeeded in synthesising **vitamin E**, also called tocopherol.

In 1937 Paul Karrer received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for his investigations of carotenoids, flavins and vitamins A and B2. He shared the prize with the Briton Walter Norman Haworth, who had researched vitamin C. His teacher Alfred Werner had already received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913. His work helped to make vitamins artificially. Today vitamins are produced in large quantities, for example for food supplements and animal feed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance vital for life that the body must take in with food in small amounts.
Yellow to red pigments in plants, for example carotene in carrots.
Making a substance from simpler starting substances.
A famous prize awarded every year for outstanding achievements, including in chemistry.

gewusst: Paul Karrer was 70 years old when he retired after four decades as a professor.
The body can make vitamin A itself from the orange pigment in carrots.
With Paul Karrer and his teacher Alfred Werner, no fewer than two Nobel Prize winners in chemistry came from the University of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: The proton is a positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus. The number of protons determines which chemical element it is. Without protons there would be neither hydrogen nor stars, and acids also work thanks to them.
wichtigste: The proton is a positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The number of protons decides which element it is.
An iron atom has 26 protons in its nucleus.
A proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron.
It consists of two up quarks and one down quark.
Ernest Rutherford is regarded as the discoverer of the proton.
According to Brønsted, an acid is a proton donor.

abschnitte.text: Every atomic nucleus contains at least one **proton**. The proton has a positive electric charge exactly as large as the negative charge of an electron. It is about 1836 times heavier than an electron, which is why almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus. Together with the neutrons, it is held in the nucleus by the **strong nuclear force**.

The number of protons in the nucleus is called the **atomic number** and decides which element it is. Hydrogen has one proton, carbon six and iron 26. If an atom had one more proton, it would be a completely different element. The simplest nucleus of all, the nucleus of ordinary hydrogen, is a single proton.

The physicist **Ernest Rutherford** is regarded as the discoverer of the proton; he detected it around 1919 when he bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles. Later it was found that the proton itself consists of even smaller particles. It contains two **up quarks** and one down quark. These quarks are held together by particles called gluons.

In chemistry, protons play a big part in acids. According to the theory of the Danish chemist **Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted**, an acid is a **proton donor**, that is a substance that gives up protons. A base takes up protons. In water, a hydrogen ion H⁺ exists, in simple terms, as an **oxonium ion** H₃O⁺.

At **CERN** near Geneva, protons are brought almost to the speed of light in the LHC particle accelerator and made to collide. This is how the Higgs particle was discovered in 2012. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen uses protons for **proton therapy**, in which tumours are irradiated very precisely. In the Sun, protons fuse to form helium, releasing huge amounts of energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
A tiny particle of which protons and neutrons are made.
A substance that gives up protons, that is an acid.

gewusst: The word proton comes from Greek and means “the first”.
Protons are extremely stable; the decay of a proton has never been observed.
The LHC particle accelerator at CERN has a circumference of about 27 kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Salts are substances built from positively and negatively charged particles, the ions. The best-known salt is the table salt on our dining table, but there are thousands of others. Salts are found in gypsum, fertiliser, mineral water and even in our bones.
wichtigste: Salts are built from positive and negative ions.
Because of the strong attraction between the ions, salts usually have very high melting points.
The salts of hydrochloric acid are called chlorides, those of sulphuric acid sulphates.
Magnesium sulphate is known as Epsom salt.
Gypsum consists mainly of calcium sulphate.
Potassium chloride is used as fertiliser because it supplies plants with potassium.
Copper sulphate with water of crystallisation forms blue crystals.

abschnitte.text: A salt consists of **ions**, that is electrically charged atoms or groups of atoms. The positive ions are usually metal ions, for example sodium, potassium or calcium. The negative ions often come from acids, like the chloride ion from hydrochloric acid. In **table salt**, chemically sodium chloride, sodium and chloride ions alternate regularly.

The ions arrange themselves in a regular **ionic lattice**, which is why salts often form beautiful crystals. Table salt crystals, for example, are little cubes. Because the oppositely charged ions attract each other very strongly, salts only melt at high temperatures, table salt at about 800 degrees Celsius. As solids, salts do not conduct electricity, but they do when dissolved in water or molten.

The names reveal which acid a salt comes from. Salts of hydrochloric acid are called **chlorides**, salts of sulphuric acid **sulphates**, salts of nitric acid nitrates and salts of carbonic acid carbonates. Limestone, for example, is calcium carbonate, and gypsum is calcium sulphate. Salts are formed, for example, when an acid reacts with an alkali; this is called **neutralisation**.

Potassium chloride and other salts are spread on fields as **fertiliser** so that plants grow well. Magnesium sulphate, Epsom salt, is used in medicine and as a bath additive. Copper sulphate with built-in water of crystallisation forms bright blue crystals and is used in vineyards against fungal diseases. In winter salt is spread on roads so that the ice melts.

In Switzerland, table salt is obtained from salt layers deep underground. Water is pumped in, the salt dissolves, and the **brine** is then evaporated. The Swiss Saltworks operate plants at Riburg and Schweizerhalle on the Rhine and at Bex in the canton of Vaud. At Bex you can visit an old **salt mine** with kilometres of tunnels.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrically charged particle.
A regular arrangement of ions in a crystal.
The reaction of an acid with an alkali, which produces salt and water.
Salty water from which salt is obtained.
Water that is firmly built into the crystal of a salt.

gewusst: If you heat blue copper sulphate, it loses its water of crystallisation and turns white.
The word salary for wages probably comes from the Latin word for salt, because salt used to be very valuable.

teile.einleitung: Paracelsus was a famous Renaissance doctor, natural scientist and alchemist who came from the area around Einsiedeln. He turned the medicine of his time upside down by observing diseases closely and using chemically made remedies. Many see him as a pioneer of modern pharmacology.
wichtigste: Paracelsus’s real name was Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.
He was born in 1493 or 1494 near Einsiedeln in what is now the canton of Schwyz and died in Salzburg in 1541.
He is regarded as the founder of iatrochemistry, which introduced chemically made medicines into medicine.
In Basel in 1527 he is said to have publicly burnt the textbook Canon of Medicine by Avicenna.
According to his teaching, all substances consist of the three principles sulphur, mercury and salt.
He wrote one of the first works on the diseases of miners.
He is known for the principle that the dose alone decides whether a substance is a poison.

abschnitte.text: **Paracelsus** was born as Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim near **Einsiedeln**, the son of a doctor. Later the family moved to Villach in Carinthia, where he learnt a lot about mining and metals. He gave himself the name Paracelsus, probably in reference to the Roman doctor Celsus. He travelled as a wandering doctor through large parts of Europe, for example through Italy, France, Germany and Austria. He died in **Salzburg** in 1541.

In 1527 Paracelsus became **town physician** of Basel and was allowed to teach at the university. What was unusual was that he gave his lectures in German instead of Latin. He mocked the old textbooks and is said to have publicly thrown the **Canon of Medicine** by the Persian doctor Avicenna into the fire. With his sharp manner he made many enemies. As early as the beginning of 1528 he had to leave Basel again after a quarrel.

Paracelsus was convinced that chemistry should provide remedies and not gold. He is therefore regarded as the founder of **iatrochemistry**, the study of chemically made medicines. He used substances such as mercury, antimony and sulphur compounds deliberately as medicines. Traditionally he is also credited with the opium tincture **laudanum**. According to his teaching of the **tria prima**, all substances consist of the three principles sulphur, mercury and salt.

His most famous idea goes roughly like this: all things are poison, and nothing is without poison; only the **dose** makes a thing not a poison. By this he meant that a substance can heal in small amounts and harm in large amounts. This principle is still the basis of **toxicology**, the study of poisons, today. Even table salt or water can be dangerous in huge amounts. On the other hand, some poisons are used as medicines in tiny amounts.

Paracelsus wrote one of the first works on the **diseases of miners** and is therefore regarded as a pioneer of occupational medicine. He is said to have given the metal **zinc** its present name. In one of his writings on nature spirits, the earth spirit gnome appears, a word that became known through it. In Einsiedeln and Salzburg, monuments and memorials remind people of him. Most of his writings were only printed after his death.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study that uses chemistry to make medicines, from the Greek iatros for doctor.
The forerunner of chemistry, which among other things searched for gold and remedies.
The science of poisons and their effects.
The three basic principles sulphur, mercury and salt in the teaching of Paracelsus.

gewusst: Paracelsus gave lectures in German so that people who knew no Latin could understand him too.
The word gnome for a small earth spirit became known through a work by Paracelsus.
Paracelsus also wrote about healing springs, for example about the spa at Pfäfers in what is now the canton of St Gallen.

teile.einleitung: Mercury is a shiny silver metal that is liquid at room temperature. It is so heavy that even an iron screw floats on it. At the same time it is very poisonous, which is why it is hardly used in everyday objects any more today.
wichtigste: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
It has a silver colour and forms small round beads on the table.
An iron screw floats on mercury because mercury is much denser.
In the past, mercury was often found in clinical thermometers.
Mercury and its vapour are poisonous.
If a mercury thermometer breaks, you touch nothing and fetch adults.
The German name “Quecksilber” comes from an old word “queck”, meaning alive.
In English, mercury has the same name as the planet Mercury.

abschnitte.text: Mercury has the chemical symbol **Hg** and the atomic number 80. It melts at only about minus 39 degrees Celsius and is therefore liquid at room temperature. Because it has a very high **surface tension**, it breaks up into small, round beads that roll across the table. At about 13.5 grams per cubic centimetre it is more than 13 times as dense as water, which is why even iron floats on it.

The old German word **“queck”** means alive, because the metal seems to move by itself; that is where the German name “Quecksilber” comes from. The symbol Hg comes from the Latin hydrargyrum, which means “water silver”. In English it is called mercury, after the swift messenger of the gods and the planet Mercury. As early as ancient times, mercury was obtained from the red mineral **cinnabar**.

abschnitte.titel: Uses in the past and today
abschnitte.text: In the past, mercury was found in clinical thermometers, barometers and blood pressure monitors. Dentists used it for **amalgam** fillings, and small amounts are contained in old energy-saving light bulbs. Today mercury has been replaced almost everywhere by less dangerous substances, for example by digital thermometers. The worldwide **Minamata Convention** of 2013 aims to greatly reduce the use of mercury.

Even at room temperature, mercury gives off poisonous **vapour** that you cannot smell. If it is breathed in, it can damage the nerves, kidneys and brain. If an old thermometer breaks, you touch nothing, leave the room, open the windows and fetch adults straight away. You must never suck up the beads with a vacuum cleaner, because this spreads the mercury around the room.

If mercury gets into water, bacteria turn it into particularly poisonous compounds. These build up in fish, especially in large predatory fish such as tuna. In the Japanese town of **Minamata**, many people fell ill in the 1950s because a factory let waste water containing mercury into the sea. That is why waste containing mercury goes to the special waste collection in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that shines and conducts electricity well.
How heavy a substance is compared with its size.
A mixture of mercury with other metals, used in the past for dental fillings.
A red mineral from which mercury is obtained.

gewusst: One litre of mercury weighs about 13.5 kilograms, more than a full ten-litre bucket of water.
Apart from mercury, only the non-metal bromine is a liquid element at room temperature.

teile.einleitung: A coin is a piece of money made of metal, usually round. In chemistry, coins are interesting because they are made of alloys that have to be hard, durable and difficult to forge. In Switzerland all coins are minted in Bern.
wichtigste: Swiss coins are made by the Federal Mint, Swissmint, in Bern.
Making coins is called minting.
Since 2007 the smallest Swiss coin has been the golden yellow 5-centime piece.
The Swiss 1-franc piece is made of copper and nickel.
The ½, 1 and 2 franc coins show Helvetia.
In Switzerland the 5-franc piece is often called a “Fünfliber”.
When tossing a coin, the two sides are called heads and tails.

abschnitte.text: A **coin** is a piece of money made of metal that is issued by a state. One side usually shows the value, the other a picture or symbol. That is why, when tossing a coin, the sides are called **heads and tails**. The first coins were minted around 600 BC in the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey. They were made of electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver.

Coins are almost always made of **alloys**, that is mixtures of metals. The Swiss franc coins and the 10 and 20 centime pieces are made of **cupronickel**, a shiny silver alloy of copper and nickel. The 5-centime piece is made of aluminium bronze, a mixture of copper, aluminium and a little nickel, which is why it is golden yellow. Until 1967 the franc coins were made of silver. When the price of silver rose, the metal was worth more than the coin itself, and they switched to cupronickel.

First, round discs, the **blanks**, are punched out of a metal strip. Then a machine presses the blanks with great force between two hard steel dies. The picture is pressed onto both sides at the same time; this is called **minting**. In Switzerland this is done by the Federal Mint, **Swissmint**, in Bern. It also makes special coins and commemorative coins for collectors.

Today there are coins of 5, 10 and 20 centimes and of ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs in Switzerland. The 1-centime piece was withdrawn in 2007; since then the **5-centime piece** has been the smallest coin. The coins of ½, 1 and 2 francs show **Helvetia**, the female figure who represents Switzerland. The 5-franc piece, the **Fünfliber**, shows the head of an Alpine herdsman. On its edge is the Latin inscription Dominus providebit, which means “The Lord will provide”.

Forged money should be hard to make, which is why coins have exact weights, diameters and edge markings. Machines often test coins with magnetic fields, because each alloy conducts electricity differently. Copper tarnishes over time because it reacts with oxygen from the air. That is why old copper coins turn dark or get a greenish layer. Nickel and cupronickel, on the other hand, stay shiny for a long time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Making coins by pressing a picture into a metal disc with high pressure.
A mixture of several metals, for example copper and nickel.
The Federal Mint in Bern, which makes all Swiss coins.
The popular name for the Swiss 5-franc piece.

gewusst: The Swiss 10-centime piece has been minted with an almost unchanged design since 1879 and is one of the oldest coins in the world still in use.
The year on Swiss coins shows the year in which they were minted.
Because silver coins were collected and melted down, the old silver francs quickly disappeared from people’s purses after 1968.

teile.einleitung: Safety goggles protect the eyes from splashes, splinters, dust or glaring light. In chemistry lessons they are compulsory as soon as substances are being experimented with. Even a single drop of acid or alkali can seriously injure the eye; goggles prevent this.
wichtigste: In chemistry lessons you wear safety goggles during all experimental work.
Side shields keep out splashes that come from the side.
The lenses of many safety goggles are made of impact-resistant polycarbonate.
Goggles with a full seal fit closely to the face all round.
People who wear glasses put over-glasses on top of their own glasses.
Welding goggles have dark lenses against glaring light and UV radiation.
The mandatory sign “Wear eye protection” is a blue circle with a white goggles symbol.

abschnitte.text: **Safety goggles** are glasses that are not for seeing better but for protecting the eyes. They are part of **personal protective equipment**, like gloves, a helmet or ear protection. They are worn in the laboratory, in the workshop, on building sites or when mowing the lawn. Good safety goggles are tested to a standard. In Europe this is often shown by the marking EN 166 on the frame.

In the laboratory, acids, alkalis or hot liquids can suddenly splash. That is why the rule is: the goggles stay on during **all experimental work**, including tidying up. Contact lenses are unsuitable, because chemicals can get under the lens. Anyone who wears glasses puts **over-glasses** on top. If something does get into the eye, it is rinsed immediately for a long time with water, for example at an **eyewash station**.

**Safety spectacles** look like normal glasses and have side shields. **Sealed goggles** fit closely all round and also protect against fumes, dust and splashes from below. A face shield also protects the cheeks and chin. The lenses are often made of **polycarbonate**, a plastic that is much more impact-resistant than glass. Many models have a coating so that they steam up less.

Welding produces an extremely bright light with a lot of **UV radiation**. Without protection it can cause arc eye, which is very painful. That is why welding goggles and welding masks have heavily tinted lenses. There are also special laser safety goggles for working with lasers. Normal sunglasses are not enough for this.

The **mandatory sign** for eye protection is a blue circle with a white goggles symbol. Round blue signs always mean: you must do this. It is found on laboratory doors, in workshops and on machines. In Swiss schools, the safety rules state that safety goggles are worn when experimenting in chemistry lessons. Employers must provide their employees with suitable safety goggles.

begriffe.erklaerung: Clothing and devices that protect a person from hazards at work.
A transparent, very impact-resistant plastic.
Safety goggles that fit closely to the face all round.
Safety goggles worn over your own glasses.
A device for quickly rinsing the eye with water after an accident.

gewusst: Polycarbonate is so impact-resistant that it is also used for helmet visors.
If something splashes into the eye, rinsing with water for at least ten minutes is recommended.
Some safety goggles have small ventilation slots so that they do not steam up.

teile.einleitung: The test tube is a narrow glass tube that is open at the top and has a round bottom. It is one of the most important pieces of equipment in the chemistry laboratory. Small amounts of substances are mixed, heated and observed in it.
wichtigste: A test tube is a thin glass tube closed at the bottom with a round end.
Heat-resistant test tubes are usually made of borosilicate glass.
For heating, the test tube is held with a test tube holder.
For heating, it is filled at most to a third.
Over the flame it is held at a slant and shaken gently.
In bumping, an overheated liquid can suddenly spurt out.
Test tubes are put down in a test tube rack.

abschnitte.text: A test tube is a thin **glass tube**, often about as long as a pencil. At the bottom it is closed with a round end; at the top it is open. It is used to mix small amounts of substances and to observe whether they react with each other. In German it is called “Reagenzglas”, from **reagent**, the name for a substance used in a test reaction.

Good test tubes are made of **borosilicate glass**. This glass withstands great heat and rapid changes of temperature without cracking. That is why a test tube can be held directly over the flame of a Bunsen burner. For simple experiments without heat there are also test tubes made of ordinary glass or plastic.

For heating, you hold the test tube with a wooden or metal **test tube holder**, because it gets very hot. You fill it at most to a third and hold it at a slant over the flame. You shake it gently so that the liquid warms up evenly. The opening never points towards yourself or other people, and you wear safety goggles.

Sometimes a liquid is heated above its boiling point without boiling. Then suddenly a large bubble of vapour forms all at once and the liquid shoots out; this is called **bumping**. Shaking gently while heating prevents it. Small **anti-bumping granules** also help, because bubbles form evenly on them.

Several test tubes are put in a **test tube rack** so that they do not fall over and roll away. For cleaning, a narrow **test tube brush** that reaches to the bottom is used. Then the tubes are left to dry upside down. Broken glass belongs in a special container, never in the normal rubbish.

Test tubes are not only used in chemistry. In medicine, blood is put into similar tubes for testing, usually made of plastic. In biology, bacteria are grown in them on **culture media**. The phrase “in the test tube” is therefore often used generally for experiments in the laboratory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance used in the laboratory to detect other substances.
Sudden, violent boiling of an overheated liquid.
A particularly heat-resistant glass.
A gas burner used for heating in the laboratory.

gewusst: For experiments in the test tube, experts also say “in vitro”, which is Latin for “in glass”.
A round end spreads the heat better and is easier to clean than a corner.
A test tube rack often holds ten or more tubes side by side.

teile.einleitung: Oxygen is a chemical element without which people and animals could not live. We breathe it in with every breath, even though we can neither see nor smell it. Every fire also needs oxygen to burn.
wichtigste: Oxygen has the chemical symbol O and the atomic number 8.
Dry air consists of about 21 per cent oxygen.
Green plants make oxygen during photosynthesis.
By mass, oxygen is the most common element in the Earth’s crust.
People and animals need oxygen to get energy from food.
Without oxygen nothing can burn.
In the laboratory, oxygen is detected with the glowing splint test.

abschnitte.text: At room temperature oxygen is a colourless, odourless and tasteless **gas**. In the air it does not occur as single atoms, but as a **molecule** of two atoms with the formula O2. It only becomes liquid at about minus 183 degrees Celsius and is then pale blue. A special form is **ozone**, with three oxygen atoms, which protects against UV radiation high up in the atmosphere.

About 21 per cent of dry air is oxygen; most of the rest is nitrogen. But much more oxygen is in solid substances: by mass it is the most common element in the **Earth’s crust**. It is firmly bound in rocks such as quartz and granite. Water also consists largely of oxygen, because every water molecule contains one oxygen atom.

Green plants, algae and some bacteria make oxygen during **photosynthesis**. They use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to form sugar and give off oxygen. A large part of the oxygen comes from tiny algae in the sea, the **plankton**. Without these living things there would hardly be any free oxygen in the air.

When we breathe in, oxygen gets into the blood through the **lungs**. The red blood cells carry it to all the cells with the pigment haemoglobin. There the food is “burnt” with the help of oxygen so that the body has energy. This produces carbon dioxide, which we breathe out again. In hospital, some patients are given extra oxygen from a cylinder.

Oxygen does not burn itself, but it helps other substances to burn. In pure oxygen, things burn much more fiercely than in normal air. This property is used in the **glowing splint test**: a glowing wooden splint bursts into a bright flame again in oxygen. In welding, oxygen is mixed with gas to produce very hot flames.

Oxygen was discovered in the 1770s, independently of each other, by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Sweden and Joseph Priestley in England. The French chemist **Antoine Lavoisier** realised that burning is a reaction with oxygen. He also gave the element its name, which means something like “acid former”. The German word “Sauerstoff” (sour substance) is a translation of it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance that cannot be broken down any further chemically.
The process in which plants make sugar with sunlight and give off oxygen.
A special form of oxygen with three atoms that protects against UV rays high up.
A test: a glowing wooden splint bursts into flame again in oxygen.

gewusst: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is attracted by magnets.
On the summit of Mount Everest the air is so thin that many mountaineers take oxygen cylinders with them.
More than two billion years ago there was almost no free oxygen in the Earth’s atmosphere.

teile.einleitung: Solubility shows how well a substance dissolves in a liquid. Sugar disappears in tea, but sand stays at the bottom. The chemistry of solutions explains why this is so and how much can be dissolved at most.
wichtigste: A mixture in which a substance is completely dissolved in a liquid is called a solution.
The liquid in which a substance dissolves is called the solvent.
Dissolved substances break up into tiny particles that can no longer be seen.
Salt water and sugar water stay transparent.
A dissolved substance has not disappeared; its weight remains in the solution.
Many solid substances dissolve better in warm water than in cold.
Gases such as carbon dioxide, on the other hand, dissolve better in cold water.

abschnitte.text: If you put sugar into water and stir, a **solution** forms. The sugar is the solute, and the water is the **solvent**. The sugar particles spread out so finely between the water particles that you cannot see them any more, even with a magnifying glass. That is why the solution stays transparent. Tea is also a solution: water in which colours and flavours from the tea leaves have dissolved.

If you dissolve salt in a glass of water, the glass becomes heavier by exactly the weight of the salt. So the salt is still there, only spread out in tiny particles. You can prove this by letting the water evaporate. Then the **salt crystals** are left behind again. This is also how sea salt is obtained in shallow pools on the coast.

You cannot dissolve an unlimited amount of a substance. At 20 degrees, about 36 grams of table salt dissolve in 100 grams of water. Much more table sugar fits in, about 200 grams. When the limit is reached, it is called a **saturated solution**. Anything you add after that sinks to the bottom as **sediment**.

A sugar cube dissolves even in cold water without stirring, but only slowly. **Stirring** and **warmth** speed up dissolving, because the particles move faster. For many solid substances, more also dissolves in hot water than in cold. With gases it is the other way round: warm mineral water loses its fizz faster. Fish notice this too, because there is less oxygen dissolved in warm water.

Some substances hardly dissolve in water at all, for example sand, oil or chalk. Oil floats as a layer on top of the water. Sand or soil make the water cloudy and settle later; this is called a **suspension**. Such mixtures can be separated with a filter, but a true solution cannot. Squash, by the way, is a sugar solution, which is why it mixes easily with water.

Rainwater contains a little dissolved carbon dioxide and can therefore slowly dissolve **limestone**. Over a very long time, caves form in this way. A well-known example in Switzerland is the Hölloch in the Muotatal in the canton of Schwyz, one of the longest cave systems in the world. Where the water in the cave evaporates, the limestone is deposited again and forms stalactites and stalagmites.

begriffe.erklaerung: A transparent mixture in which a substance is spread out very finely in a liquid.
The liquid in which another substance dissolves, for example water.
A solution in which no more of the substance dissolves at the same temperature.
The part of a substance that no longer dissolves and stays at the bottom.

gewusst: So much salt is dissolved in the Dead Sea that people float on top almost by themselves.
At room temperature, one litre of water can dissolve about two kilograms of sugar.
Rock candy forms when large crystals slowly grow out of a saturated sugar solution.

teile.einleitung: Hydrocarbons are chemical compounds that consist only of carbon and hydrogen. They are the main components of natural gas, crude oil, petrol and candle wax. Depending on the structure of their molecules, they are divided into families, for example alkanes, alkenes and aromatics.
wichtigste: Hydrocarbons consist only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
Alkanes have only single bonds and the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Alkenes have at least one C=C double bond.
Methane is the main component of natural gas.
Benzene, with the formula C₆H₆, is the best-known aromatic compound.
Hydrocarbons are important fuels and raw materials for plastics.

abschnitte.text: Hydrocarbons contain only the elements C and H. The carbon atoms form chains or rings to which the **hydrogen atoms** are attached. Small molecules such as methane and propane are gases, medium ones such as octane are liquids and large ones such as paraffin wax are solid. The most important source is **crude oil**, which is separated into its components in refineries.

**Alkanes** have only single bonds and follow the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. The first ones are called methane, ethane, propane and butane. The unbranched alkane with eight carbon atoms is called **octane**; it is an important part of petrol. Alkanes are rather unreactive, but in light they react with chlorine by **free radical substitution**.

**Alkenes** have at least one C=C double bond; the simplest is ethene C₂H₄. The double bond makes them reactive. If you add ethene to brown bromine water, it turns colourless because an **electrophilic addition** takes place. Alkynes such as ethyne even have a triple bond; ethyne is used in welding.

Benzene has the formula C₆H₆ and forms a ring of six carbon atoms. Its electrons are spread over the whole ring, which makes it particularly stable. Such substances are called **aromatics**, because many of them have a strong smell. Benzene is poisonous and causes cancer, which is why it is handled carefully in the laboratory.

**Methane** is the main component of natural gas, with which many houses in Switzerland are heated. Propane and butane are filled into gas bottles for barbecues and camping. The plastic polyethylene is made from ethene. Burning hydrocarbons produces CO₂, which strengthens **climate change**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hydrocarbon with only single bonds, for example methane.
A hydrocarbon with at least one double bond between two carbon atoms.
A formula that shows how many atoms of each kind a molecule has.
A reaction in which particles attach to a double bond.

gewusst: Methane is also produced in the stomachs of cows and is released when they burp.
The octane number at the petrol station shows how resistant a petrol is to knocking.
On Saturn’s moon Titan there are whole lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

teile.einleitung: Why does a cork float while a stone goes straight down? Whether something floats or sinks depends on how heavy it is in relation to its size and how strongly the water pushes it upwards. This force is called upthrust and explains why even huge ships made of steel do not sink.
wichtigste: Water pushes every object upwards with a force called upthrust.
An object floats if it is lighter than the water it displaces.
What matters is density: substances with a lower density than water float.
Corks, wood and apples float; stones and metal balls sink.
Large steel ships float because they are full of air inside.
In the very salty Dead Sea you can lie on the surface almost without moving.
Many fish use their swim bladder to control whether they rise or sink.

abschnitte.text: When an object goes into water, it displaces water. The water pushes it upwards with a force called **upthrust**. This force is exactly as large as the weight of the water displaced. This was discovered by the Greek scholar **Archimedes** over 2000 years ago. You can feel upthrust when you try to push a ball under water.

If an object is heavier than the water it displaces, it sinks. If it is lighter, it floats on the surface. If both weigh the same, it hovers in the water. What matters is **density**, that is how much mass there is in a certain volume. Water has a density of about 1 g/cm³, a cork much less, a stone much more.

A piece of steel sinks immediately, but a huge **steel ship** floats. This is because the hull of the ship is full of air inside. It displaces so much water that the upthrust carries the whole weight. An experiment with modelling clay shows the same thing: a ball of clay sinks, but if you shape it into a flat little boat, it floats. A submarine fills tanks with water to dive and blows them empty with air to rise.

Salt water has a higher density than fresh water and therefore carries better. In the **Dead Sea**, the water is so salty that you can lie on the surface almost without moving. An egg that sinks in tap water floats in very salty water. In the sea, too, you float a little more easily than in a Swiss lake.

abschnitte.titel: Floating aids in nature and everyday life
abschnitte.text: Many **fish** have a swim bladder, which they fill with gas or empty in order to hover in the water. Children learning to swim wear **armbands** with air in them. On a boat you wear a life jacket, which keeps your head above water. In Basel many people let themselves drift in the Rhine in summer and pack their clothes in a waterproof bag, the Wickelfisch, which also acts as a floating aid.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes objects upwards.
How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
To push water aside because an object takes its place.
A gas-filled organ in many fish that helps them hover.

gewusst: Ice floats because frozen water has a lower density than liquid water.
According to legend, Archimedes cried “Eureka” when he discovered the principle of upthrust in the bath.
An apple floats because there is a lot of air inside it.

teile.einleitung: Dissolving means that a substance spreads out so finely in a liquid that you can no longer see it. Sugar in tea or salt in seawater are good examples. But the substance has not disappeared; you can often still taste it.
wichtigste: When something dissolves, it spreads out in tiny particles in a liquid.
Sugar and salt dissolve well in water; sand does not dissolve.
Sugar dissolves faster in warm water than in cold water.
Stirring helps a substance dissolve faster.
You cannot see dissolved substances, but you can often taste them.
Seawater tastes salty because salt is dissolved in it.

abschnitte.text: If you put sugar into warm tea and stir, it has disappeared after a short time. In reality it has split up into tiny particles that are spread out between the water particles. The liquid that dissolves something is called the **solvent**, and the substance that is dissolved is called the **solute**. Together they form a **solution**, which looks clear.

In warm water the particles move faster, which is why sugar dissolves more quickly there than in cold water. **Stirring** also helps, because fresh water keeps reaching the sugar. Small grains dissolve faster than one big lump, because they have more **surface**. That is why icing sugar dissolves faster than a sugar cube.

Not every substance dissolves in water. **Sand** stays at the bottom as grains even after a lot of stirring. Oil does not dissolve in water either; it floats on top. Fat does dissolve in other liquids such as petrol, which is why you often need special **stain removers** for greasy stains.

You cannot see dissolved salt, but you notice it because the water tastes salty. Seawater contains about 35 grams of dissolved salt per litre. If you let salt water **evaporate**, the salt is left behind as a white crust. At some point water cannot take up any more salt; then the solution is **saturated** and the rest stays at the bottom.

An **effervescent tablet** fizzes in water and dissolves; the fizz comes from the gas carbon dioxide. Squash is a solution of sugar and water with flavouring. Mineral water from Swiss springs has minerals such as calcium and magnesium dissolved in it. Gases can dissolve too; this is how the fizz gets into sparkling water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A clear liquid in which another substance is invisibly spread out.
The liquid in which something dissolves, usually water.
When nothing more can dissolve in a solution.
When a liquid slowly turns into gas and disappears.

gewusst: Water is sometimes called the “universal solvent” because so many substances dissolve in it.
So much salt is dissolved in the Dead Sea that people float on its surface without any effort.
Caves such as the Hölloch in the Muotatal formed because water dissolved limestone over a long time.

teile.einleitung: Paper is a thin material made of finely matted plant fibres. We write, draw and print on it, wrap things in it and use it as tissues. Chemically, paper consists mainly of cellulose, a substance that plants form in their cell walls.
wichtigste: Paper is usually made from wood.
It consists mainly of cellulose fibres that are closely matted together.
Paper was invented about 2000 years ago in China.
Before paper was invented, the ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus.
Thick, firm paper for boxes is called cardboard.
New paper can be made from waste paper.
Paper catches fire easily and must therefore not be placed close to a burning candle.

abschnitte.text: Paper consists mainly of **cellulose**, the building material of plant cell walls. These fibres are long and thin and catch on each other like felt. They usually come from wood, for example from spruces, pines or beeches. In the past, old rags of linen or cotton were also used. Fillers such as chalk are added, which make the paper whiter and smoother.

First, wood is chopped up and boiled with water and chemicals until the fibres come free. This produces a pulp, the **wood pulp**. This fibre pulp is greatly diluted and poured onto a fine screen. The water drains away, and the fibres are left behind as a thin layer. Large paper machines press and dry this web and so produce many hundreds of metres of paper in a minute.

The ancient Egyptians wrote on **papyrus**, which was made from the stems of a marsh plant on the Nile. Our word paper comes from this word. In the Middle Ages people in Europe often wrote on parchment made from animal skin. Real paper was invented in **China**; the official Cai Lun improved how it was made around the year 105. The knowledge reached Europe via the Arab world, and with Gutenberg’s printing press around 1450 paper became very important.

There are many kinds of paper: writing paper, drawing paper, newsprint, tissue paper or photo paper. How thick it is, is given by the weight of one square metre, the **grammage**. Normal printer paper usually weighs 80 grams per square metre. If paper is much thicker and firmer, it is called card or cardboard. The best-known size is A4, measuring 21 by 29.7 centimetres.

New paper can be made from **waste paper**, which needs fewer trees, less water and less energy. In Switzerland, people tie up newspapers and cardboard in bundles and put them out by the road on collection days. The fibres can be reused several times, but they get shorter each time. Paper is **flammable** and catches fire quickly. That is why it never belongs near a burning candle or a hot hotplate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance made of long fibres, of which plant cell walls are made.
A writing material of the ancient Egyptians made from a marsh plant.
The weight of one square metre of paper; it shows how thick the paper is.
Reusing used materials to make something new from them.

gewusst: If you fold an A4 sheet in half, you get exactly the next smaller size, A5.
In Basel there is a museum in an old paper mill where you can make a sheet of paper yourself.
Banknotes are not only made of wood fibres; they are often made of cotton or plastic.

teile.einleitung: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the compounds of carbon. These include substances such as sugar, fats, alcohol, vinegar, plastics and medicines. Because carbon can form countless chains and rings, it is the largest field of chemistry.
wichtigste: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from an inorganic substance.
Functional groups determine the properties of organic substances.
Alcohols have a hydroxyl group -OH, aldehydes a group -CHO.
Carboxylic acids carry the carboxyl group -COOH; the acid in vinegar is called ethanoic acid.
A carboxylic acid and an alcohol form an ester.
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but a different structure.

abschnitte.text: In the past it was believed that organic substances could only be made by living things, thanks to a special **life force**. In 1828 the German chemist **Friedrich Wöhler** made urea from the inorganic substance ammonium cyanate. Until then urea had only been known from urine. This showed that organic substances can also be made in the laboratory.

Organic molecules have a framework of carbon atoms to which certain groups of atoms are attached. These **functional groups** determine how a substance behaves. Alcohols have the **hydroxyl group** -OH, like ethanol in wine. Aldehydes have the group -CHO, and ketones such as acetone in nail varnish remover have a C=O group in the chain.

Substances with the **carboxyl group** -COOH are called carboxylic acids. The acid in vinegar is systematically called **ethanoic acid**, and in everyday life acetic acid. When a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, an **ester** is formed with the loss of water. Many esters smell fruity and are used as flavourings for sweets and drinks.

Several substances can have the same **molecular formula** and still be different. Such compounds are called **isomers**. In **structural isomers** the atoms are joined in a different order. Butane and isobutane both have the formula C₄H₁₀, but one is a straight chain and the other is branched.

Organic chemistry is of great importance for medicines, dyes, plastics and fragrances. In **Basel**, an important chemical and pharmaceutical industry grew out of dye manufacturing in the 19th century. Today, pharmaceutical companies active worldwide, such as Roche and Novartis, have their headquarters there. Companies for flavours and fragrances such as Givaudan in Vernier near Geneva also work with organic chemistry.

begriffe.erklaerung: In chemistry: a compound that contains carbon.
A group of atoms in a molecule that determines its properties.
A substance made from an acid and an alcohol, often with a fruity smell.
Substances with the same molecular formula but a different structure.

gewusst: The smell of bananas comes largely from an ester called isoamyl acetate.
Over a hundred million different carbon compounds are known.
Carbon dioxide and limestone do contain carbon, but they usually count as inorganic chemistry.

teile.einleitung: A lava lamp is a decorative lamp in which colourful blobs of wax slowly rise and fall in a liquid. The show looks like flowing lava and works without any motor, using only heat. You can even build a simple version yourself from water, oil and an effervescent tablet.
wichtigste: The heat of the lamp makes the blobs of wax rise.
At the top the wax cools down and sinks again.
After switching it on, it takes a while because the wax first has to warm up.
You should not shake a warm lava lamp, otherwise it turns cloudy.
The inventor of the lava lamp came from Great Britain.
The lamp got its name because the blobs look like lava.
In a home-made lava lamp, an effervescent tablet makes the bubbles rise.

abschnitte.text: A **lava lamp** consists of a glass container standing on a base with a light bulb. In the glass there is a clear or coloured liquid and a coloured **wax**. The two substances do not mix with each other. At room temperature the wax is solid and a little heavier than the liquid, which is why it lies at the bottom.

The bulb in the base warms the wax from below. Warm wax expands, becomes less dense than the liquid and rises. At the top it is cooler, the wax contracts, becomes heavier again and sinks down. This creates a constant cycle called **convection**.

After switching it on, it usually takes more than an hour for the lamp to bubble properly. This is because the wax first has to melt and get warm enough. You should not shake a warm lava lamp, otherwise the wax breaks into tiny droplets and the liquid turns **cloudy**. It should also not be left running for hours unattended, because the glass gets hot.

The lava lamp was invented by the Briton **Edward Craven Walker** and first sold in 1963. He is said to have got the idea from an egg timer with wax and liquid that he saw in a pub. In the 1960s and 1970s the lamp became a cult object. To this day it is a popular retro decoration in many children’s bedrooms.

For a simple version, fill a glass about a quarter full with water and pour cooking oil on top. The oil floats on top because it is lighter than water. A few drops of **food colouring** sink through the oil and colour only the water, because the colouring does not dissolve in oil. If you drop in an effervescent tablet, bubbles of carbon dioxide form, which carry coloured drops of water upwards, where they burst and sink down again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how heavy a substance is compared with its size.
A flow in which warm material rises and cold material sinks.
A substance that becomes soft and liquid when warm and solid again when it cools.
A tablet that fizzes in water and releases carbon dioxide.

gewusst: Manufacturers keep the exact recipe of the wax and liquid in real lava lamps secret.
The same principle as in the lava lamp also makes hot air rise above a radiator.
The first lava lamps were called “Astro Lamp”.

teile.einleitung: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which electrons pass from one substance to another. Two processes always take place at the same time: an oxidation and a reduction. Batteries, rusting, burning and even our breathing are redox reactions.
wichtigste: In a redox reaction, electrons are transferred.
In the broader sense, oxidation means the loss of electrons.
Reduction means the gain of electrons.
An oxidising agent takes up electrons and is reduced in the process.
Oxidation numbers are used to follow which atoms give up or take up electrons.
In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is oxidised.
When iron rusts, oxygen acts as the oxidising agent.

abschnitte.text: In the past, oxidation was understood only as reaction with oxygen. Today it is defined more generally: an **oxidation** is the loss of electrons, a **reduction** the gain of electrons. Because electrons do not simply disappear, the two always take place together. The name redox is made up of **reduction** and oxidation.

An **oxidising agent** takes up electrons and is itself reduced in the process. A **reducing agent** gives up electrons and is oxidised in the process. If you dip a zinc sheet into a blue copper sulphate solution, reddish brown copper is deposited. In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc gives up electrons and is oxidised, while the copper ions are reduced.

With **oxidation numbers** you can follow exactly who gives up electrons and who takes them up. Oxygen usually has the number -2 and hydrogen +1, but in hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂ oxygen has the number -1. In potassium permanganate KMnO₄ manganese has the oxidation number +7, and in sulphuric acid H₂SO₄ sulphur has +6. If the oxidation number rises, an atom has been oxidised; if it falls, it has been reduced.

In a **battery**, redox reactions take place separately at two terminals. The electrons flow through a wire from one terminal to the other, and that is electric current. Around 1800 the Italian **Alessandro Volta** built the first battery, the voltaic pile. In **electrolysis**, redox reactions are driven the other way with electricity; this is how aluminium is obtained, for example.

abschnitte.titel: Redox in nature and everyday life
abschnitte.text: When iron **rusts**, oxygen acts as the oxidising agent and the iron is oxidised. Every kind of burning, for example of wood or petrol, is also a redox reaction. In **photosynthesis**, plants build up sugar, and in breathing we break it down again; both are redox processes. In Valais, aluminium was produced by electrolysis in Chippis from 1908, thanks to hydropower from the Alps.

begriffe.erklaerung: The loss of electrons by a particle.
The gain of electrons by a particle.
A substance that takes electrons from others and is reduced in the process.
An imagined charge used to follow where electrons move to.
A redox reaction driven by electricity.

gewusst: A memory aid: oxidation is losing electrons, reduction is gaining electrons.
The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after Alessandro Volta.
The glow of fireflies is also based on a redox reaction.

teile.einleitung: The mole is the unit for the amount of substance, that is for how many particles there are in a portion of a substance. One mole contains about 602 thousand billion billion particles, a number with 24 digits. Chemists need the mole so that they can calculate easily with unimaginably large numbers of atoms.
wichtigste: The mole is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units, SI.
One mole contains about 6.022·10²³ particles; this number is called the Avogadro constant.
Since 2019 the mole has been defined by an exactly fixed value of the Avogadro constant.
From 1971 to 2019 the mole was defined by 12 grams of carbon-12.
The chemist Wilhelm Ostwald coined the name mole in 1893.
The name probably comes from the Latin word moles for mass or load.
Chemistry fans celebrate Mole Day on 23 October.

abschnitte.text: Just as a **dozen** always means 12 items, a **mole** stands for a very particular number of particles. This number is huge: about 602,214,076,000,000,000,000,000. It is called the **Avogadro constant**, after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro. Atoms and molecules are so tiny that even a sip of water contains an unimaginable number of them. With the mole, these amounts can be expressed in handy numbers.

Every substance has a **molar mass**, which is the mass of one mole. One mole of carbon-12 weighs exactly 12 grams. One mole of water weighs about 18 grams, which is about one big sip. One mole of table salt weighs about 58 grams. In this way you can use scales to measure out how many particles you need for a reaction.

The German chemist **Wilhelm Ostwald** introduced the name mole in 1893. The word probably comes from the Latin moles, which means mass or load. In 1971 the mole was added as the seventh base unit to the **SI**, the International System of Units. At that time it was defined by 12 grams of carbon-12. Since the big reform of 2019, the Avogadro constant has instead been fixed at an exact value.

A thousandth of a mole is called a **millimole**, mmol for short. So 0.25 mol is 250 mmol. In medicine, for example, blood sugar is measured in millimoles per litre. One mole of nitrogen molecules contains about 6·10²³ molecules. Because each N₂ molecule consists of two atoms, that is about 1.2·10²⁴ atoms.

On **23 October**, school classes and chemistry fans in many countries celebrate Mole Day. The date was chosen because of the Avogadro constant, which begins 6.02 times 10 to the power of 23. In American date writing, 10/23 gives 23 October. Traditionally it is celebrated from 6.02 in the morning until 6.02 in the evening. On this day there are often experiments, puzzles and cakes in the shape of a mole, the animal, because the words are the same in English.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that shows how many particles are in a portion of a substance, measured in moles.
The number of particles in one mole, about 6.022·10²³.
The mass of one mole of a substance, for example 18 grams for water.
The International System of Units, with seven base units such as the metre, kilogram and mole.

gewusst: If you spread a mole of grains of sand, each one cubic millimetre in size, over the whole surface of the Earth, the sand would be over a metre deep.
One mole of water is only about 18 millilitres, a little more than a tablespoon, and yet it contains about 602 thousand billion billion molecules.
Besides the mole, the base units include the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and candela.

teile.einleitung: The molar mass shows how much one mole of a substance weighs. A mole is a huge but exactly fixed number of particles. With the molar mass, chemists can weigh out how many atoms or molecules they need for a reaction, even though they could never see them individually.
wichtigste: The molar mass is the mass of a substance divided by its amount of substance.
It is usually given in grams per mole (g/mol) and has the symbol M.
One mole contains about 6.022 times 10 to the power of 23 particles; this is the Avogadro constant.
The value of the molar mass in g/mol practically equals the molecular mass in u.
Water has a molar mass of about 18 g/mol, glucose of about 180 g/mol.
It is calculated by adding up the atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula.

abschnitte.text: Atoms and molecules are so tiny that they cannot be weighed individually. That is why they are counted in packages, **moles**, just as eggs are counted in dozens. One mole contains about 602 thousand billion billion particles. The **molar mass** says how many grams such a package weighs. One mole of water weighs about 18 g, which fits in a tablespoon.

For the molar mass, you add up the **atomic masses** of all the atoms in a molecule. Hydrogen has about 1, carbon 12, oxygen 16, sulphur 32 and calcium 40 g/mol. Sulphuric acid H₂SO₄ thus comes to 2 + 32 + 64 = 98 g/mol. Calcium carbonate CaCO₃ has about 100 g/mol and glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ about 180 g/mol.

Between mass m, amount of substance n and molar mass M, the rule is: m = n times M. If you want 0.25 mol of sodium hydroxide (M about 40 g/mol), you have to weigh out 10 g. If you divide the molar mass by the Avogadro constant, you get the mass of a single particle. A water molecule thus weighs only about 3.0 times 10 to the power of minus 23 grams.

For gases there is a practical rule: one mole of any gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 °C and normal air pressure; this is the **molar volume**. If one litre of a gas weighs 1.25 g, it has a molar mass of 1.25 times 22.4, that is about 28 g/mol. That matches nitrogen, the main component of air. In this way unknown gases can be identified by weighing.

The molar mass of chlorine is about 35.45 g/mol and is not a whole number. This is because natural chlorine is a mixture of **isotopes**: about three quarters chlorine-35 and a quarter chlorine-37. The average gives the odd value. It is similar for copper or magnesium, whose values are given in every periodic table.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit for amount of substance, a package of about 6.022 times 10 to the power of 23 particles.
The number of particles in one mole, named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro.
How heavy an atom of an element is, given in the unit u.
Shows how many particles a portion of a substance contains, measured in moles.

gewusst: If you spread a mole of grains of sand over Switzerland, there would be a layer many kilometres high over the whole country.
Since 2019 the mole has been defined directly by an exactly fixed number of particles.
One mole of sugar weighs about 342 g, about as much as a small jar of jam.

teile.einleitung: Melting is when a solid substance becomes liquid through heat. You see it every day, for example when an ice cream drips in the sun or butter melts in the pan. In spring, huge amounts of snow even melt in the mountains.
wichtigste: When something melts, a solid substance becomes a liquid substance.
A substance melts when it gets enough heat.
Ice melts into water at 0 degrees Celsius.
A small ice cube melts faster than a big one.
Butter becomes liquid in a hot pan.
When a candle burns, the wax melts.
The opposite of melting is solidifying.

abschnitte.text: All substances consist of tiny **particles**. In a solid substance they are fixed in place and only shake a little. When the substance is warmed, the particles move more and more. At some point they can leave their places and slide past each other; then the substance is **liquid**.

The temperature at which a substance melts is called the **melting point**. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, chocolate already at about 30 to 35 degrees, which is why it melts in your mouth. Candle wax melts at about 50 to 60 degrees, depending on the type. Iron, on the other hand, needs over 1500 degrees, and tungsten, the metal in old light bulbs, even over 3400 degrees.

Butter in a hot pan quickly becomes liquid. With a burning candle, the **wax** around the wick melts and is then drawn up by the wick. An ice cube in a warm hand melts because the hand gives it heat. A small ice cube melts faster than a big one, because it has less ice and, in proportion, more surface.

In spring the snow melts in the Swiss mountains; this is called the **snowmelt**. Then streams and rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhône carry much more water. The **glaciers** are melting too, and because it is getting warmer, they have been getting smaller and smaller for decades. In summer, the meltwater also fills the reservoirs used to produce electricity.

When a liquid substance cools down, it becomes solid again; this is called **solidifying**. With water it is also called freezing. Melting and solidifying happen at the same temperature. These transformations are called changes of state; the substance itself stays the same.

People have been melting metals for thousands of years, for example copper and tin for bronze. Liquid metal is poured into moulds; this is how bells are made, for example. Glass is also melted at very high temperatures and then shaped. In **recycling**, old bottles and cans are melted down to make new things from them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a solid substance becomes liquid.
Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas.
When a liquid substance becomes solid through cooling.
The time in spring when a lot of snow melts.

gewusst: Salt on the road makes ice melt even below 0 degrees.
Mercury has already melted at about minus 39 degrees and is therefore liquid at room temperature.
Ice floats on water because it is lighter than liquid water.

teile.einleitung: Corrosion is the slow destruction of a material, usually a metal, by chemical reactions with its surroundings. The best-known example is the brown rust on iron. Every year corrosion causes huge damage to cars, bridges and machines.
wichtigste: Simply put, rust consists of hydrated iron(III) oxide.
Iron rusts when water and oxygen are present at the same time.
A local cell is a short-circuited galvanic cell on a metal surface.
Salt solution conducts ions better, which is why cars rust faster on salted roads.
If two different metals touch in damp conditions, the less noble one corrodes more.
Aluminium resists corrosion thanks to a dense oxide layer.
Stainless steel contains at least about 10.5 per cent chromium.

abschnitte.text: The word **corrosion** comes from the Latin “corrodere”, which means to gnaw away. Metals react with oxygen, water, acids or salts from their surroundings. Base metals such as iron, zinc or aluminium corrode more easily than noble metals such as gold or platinum. Concrete and plastics can also be attacked, but in everyday life we usually mean metals.

Iron only rusts when **water** and **oxygen** come together. The iron gives up electrons and becomes iron ions, while the oxygen takes up the electrons. In the end **rust** is formed, simply put hydrated iron(III) oxide. Rust is loose and porous, which is why moisture can get deeper and deeper into the metal.

Often a metal surface acts like a tiny battery, a so-called **local cell**. If two different metals touch in a damp environment, the less noble metal is dissolved. A steel screw in an aluminium sheet therefore makes the aluminium corrode more. In tin-plated iron, tinplate, a scratch rusts particularly quickly because tin is more noble than iron.

Salt dissolves in water to form ions, which conduct electricity well. That is why cars rust faster on salted roads in winter, and seawater is also very aggressive. Warmth and acidic air, for example from exhaust gases, also speed up corrosion. In dry air, on the other hand, iron hardly rusts.

Aluminium is a base metal but hardly corrodes in everyday life. In air it immediately forms a very thin, dense **oxide layer** that protects the metal underneath. Stainless steel, which contains at least about 10.5 per cent chromium, works in a similar way. Against rust on ordinary iron, **hot-dip galvanising** helps, for example, in which steel parts are dipped into liquid zinc.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reddish brown, loose layer that forms when iron reacts with water and oxygen.
A metal that reacts easily with oxygen, for example iron or zinc.
A tiny, short-circuited battery on a metal surface that causes corrosion.
A thin layer of metal and oxygen on the surface of a metal.

gewusst: Rust takes up more space than the iron it came from and can even crack concrete.
Gold practically does not corrode, which is why gold treasures thousands of years old still shine today.
Corrosion damage costs industrial countries many billions of francs every year.

teile.einleitung: The octet rule is a rule of thumb in chemistry: many atoms form bonds in such a way that they then have eight electrons in their outermost shell. The particularly stable noble gases also have eight outer electrons. With the rule you can predict how many bonds an atom forms or which ions it makes.
wichtigste: According to the octet rule, atoms aim for eight electrons in their outer shell.
In this way they reach the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas.
A sodium atom gives up 1 electron, a calcium atom 2 electrons.
An oxygen atom takes up 2 electrons to have a full outer shell.
A nitrogen atom shares 3 electrons with bonding partners.
Hydrogen is an exception and aims for only two electrons.
The number of outer electrons of a main group element can be seen from the number of its main group.

abschnitte.text: Atoms consist of a nucleus and a shell of electrons arranged in shells. For chemical behaviour, what matters most is the outermost shell with the **outer electrons**. The **noble gases** such as neon and argon have eight electrons there and hardly react. Other atoms try to reach eight too by forming bonds. Eight in Latin is octo, hence the name **octet**.

For main group elements, the **main group number** reveals the number of outer electrons. Sodium is in main group one and has one outer electron; calcium in group two has two. Nitrogen in group five has five, oxygen in group six has six, chlorine in group seven has seven. From this you can read how many electrons an atom is missing for an octet or has too many.

Metals readily give up electrons. A **sodium atom** gives up its only outer electron and becomes the sodium ion Na⁺ with the arrangement of neon. Calcium gives up two electrons and becomes Ca²⁺. Non-metals, on the other hand, take up electrons: oxygen takes up two, chlorine one. The **chloride ion** Cl⁻ then has the same electron arrangement as the noble gas argon, and together with Na⁺ it forms table salt.

Non-metals can also reach their octet by **sharing** electrons. This creates a covalent bond. A nitrogen atom shares three electrons, for example with three hydrogen atoms in ammonia NH₃. An oxygen atom shares two, for example in the water molecule H₂O, and carbon shares four, for example in methane CH₄. In the **Lewis structure**, each electron pair is drawn as a line, so you can count the octet.

The octet rule is a rule of thumb and does not always apply. **Hydrogen** aims for only two electrons, as many as the noble gas helium has; this is called the duet rule. In **boron trifluoride** BF₃, the boron atom has only six outer electrons around it. Elements from the third period onwards, for example sulphur and phosphorus, can have more than eight electrons around them. The rule applies most reliably to carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine.

The idea was developed around 1916, independently of each other, by the German **Walther Kossel** and the American **Gilbert Newton Lewis**. Kossel used it to explain how ions form, Lewis to explain bonding by shared electron pairs. The American Irving Langmuir made the rule well known and coined the name octet. To this day pupils in Switzerland learn to write formulas with this rule.

begriffe.erklaerung: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom, also called valence electrons.
A stable electron arrangement like that of a noble gas, usually with eight outer electrons.
An electrically charged particle formed by giving up or taking up electrons.
A line formula in which electron pairs are drawn as lines.

gewusst: Because noble gases already have an octet, they were long thought to be completely unreactive, until the first xenon compound was made in 1962.
With its four bonds, carbon forms millions of different compounds, the basis of all life.
The word octet is also known from music, where it means a group of eight musicians.

teile.einleitung: Growing crystals means letting crystals grow on purpose, in a jar at home just as in huge industrial plants. A crystal is a solid whose particles are arranged in a strictly regular way, which is why it has smooth faces and sharp edges. With salt, sugar and a bit of patience, any child can grow their own crystals.
wichtigste: At home you can easily grow crystals with salt or sugar in water.
You dissolve the salt in warm water, because more salt dissolves in it.
The crystals grow particularly nicely on a hanging thread.
The jar should stand in a quiet place, and growing takes several days.
Rock candy consists of large sugar crystals.
A snow crystal has six arms.
In Switzerland, crystal hunters search the mountains for rock crystals, which are made of quartz.

abschnitte.text: In a **crystal**, atoms, ions or molecules are arranged in a regular pattern that repeats again and again. This pattern is called a **crystal lattice**. Because the building blocks are arranged so neatly, smooth faces and straight edges are formed. Table salt, for example, forms little cubes, while rock crystal forms six-sided columns with points.

You dissolve as much salt or sugar in warm water as you can, until nothing more dissolves. Such a solution is called **saturated**. Then you hang a thread in it and put the jar in a quiet place. As the water slowly evaporates or the solution cools, the particles settle on the thread, and after a few days crystals have grown.

Warm water can dissolve more salt or sugar than cold water. When the solution cools, suddenly more is dissolved than would actually be possible; it is **supersaturated**. The extra particles look for a place where they can settle, such as a small starter crystal, the so-called **seed crystal**. The slower this happens, the bigger and more beautiful the crystals become.

Snowflakes are also crystals; they grow in clouds from water vapour and always have six arms. Deep in the rock of the Alps, **rock crystals** grew in cracks and cavities over millions of years. In Switzerland, **crystal hunters** search the mountains for such crystals. From 2005, particularly large rock crystals were discovered at the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri; some of them are on display in the Natural History Museum in Bern.

Computer chips need extremely pure **silicon crystals**. They are grown using a process discovered by the Pole Jan Czochralski in 1916: a seed crystal is slowly pulled out of molten silicon while turning. This produces crystal rods that can be over two metres long. Artificial rubies and sapphires, for example for watch bearings in the Swiss watch industry, are also grown.

**Rock candy** consists of large sugar crystals that are grown on threads or sticks. It is used mainly to sweeten tea. Salt from salt works such as those at Bex or Schweizerhalle also consists of many small crystals. Even in honey, sugar crystals form over time, and it then becomes solid.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid whose particles are arranged regularly.
A solution in which no more of a substance can dissolve.
A small starter crystal on which a larger crystal goes on growing.
A person who searches the Swiss mountains for crystals (in Swiss German “Strahler”).
A common mineral made of silicon and oxygen; rock crystal is pure quartz.

gewusst: Every quartz watch contains a tiny quartz crystal that keeps the time.
In the Naica mine in Mexico there are gypsum crystals over ten metres long.
No two snowflakes look exactly the same, even though they all have six arms.

teile.einleitung: The mass number shows how many protons and neutrons together are in the nucleus of an atom. It is always a whole number. It can be used to tell apart different kinds of the same element, the isotopes.
wichtigste: The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons in the atomic nucleus.
It is written at the top left of the element symbol.
An atom with 11 protons and 12 neutrons has the mass number 23.
If you subtract the number of protons from the mass number, you get the number of neutrons.
Uranium-238 has 92 protons and 146 neutrons.
Atoms of an element with different mass numbers are called isotopes.
The atomic mass in the periodic table is an average of the isotopes and is therefore often not a whole number.

abschnitte.text: An atom consists of a tiny **atomic nucleus** and a shell of electrons. In the nucleus are **protons** and **neutrons**, which together are called nucleons.
