The mass number simply counts all the nucleons. It has this name because almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus. An electron, after all, is almost 2000 times lighter than a proton.

The calculation is simple: mass number equals number of protons plus number of neutrons. A sodium atom with 11 protons and 12 neutrons therefore has the mass number 23. A fluorine atom has 9 protons and the mass number 19, so 10 neutrons. Chlorine-35 has 17 protons and therefore 18 neutrons. If an atom has the mass number 27 and 14 neutrons, it has 13 protons, so it is aluminium.

In **nuclide notation**, the mass number is at the top left and the atomic number at the bottom left of the element symbol. Often the mass number is simply written with a hyphen after the name, for example carbon-12 or uranium-238. Uranium-238 has 92 protons, so 238 minus 92 equals 146 neutrons. In this way everything about the nucleus can be read from the notation.

Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but not necessarily the same number of neutrons. Such variants are called **isotopes**. Hydrogen, for example, exists with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3; the heavy kinds are called deuterium and tritium. For carbon there are carbon-12, carbon-13 and radioactive carbon-14. Carbon-14 can be used to find the age of old bones or wood.

In the periodic table, chlorine has an **atomic mass** of about 35.5 u, even though there is no atom with half a neutron. The reason: in nature, chlorine consists of a mixture of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. The number in the periodic table is the average, weighted by how common each isotope is. The mass number, on the other hand, always applies to a single isotope and is a whole number. The neutron itself was only discovered in 1932 by the Englishman James Chadwick.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny centre of the atom, where the protons and neutrons are.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A kind of atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons.
A kind of atom defined exactly by its number of protons and neutrons.

gewusst: The most common hydrogen atom has no neutron at all; its mass number is 1.
Uranium-235 and uranium-238 differ by only three neutrons, but behave quite differently in a nuclear power station.
Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element.

teile.einleitung: Recycling means that new raw materials and products are made again from used things. An old drinks can can become a new can, and waste paper new paper. This protects nature and saves a lot of energy.
wichtigste: Recycling means reusing waste.
A recyclable is waste that is reused, for example glass, paper, PET or metal.
Recyclables are collected separately to save raw materials and energy.
The well-known recycling symbol consists of three arrows in a circle.
Many drinks cans are made of aluminium, which can be melted down almost any number of times.
At a collection point you can hand in glass, cans, used oil and other recyclables.
Switzerland is one of the countries that collect particularly large amounts of waste separately.

abschnitte.text: The word **recycling** comes from English and means something like “bringing back into the cycle”. Waste is collected, sorted and processed so that **raw materials** are produced again. Factories make new products from these raw materials. In this way waste becomes a **recyclable**, that is something that still has a value.

Each material is processed differently. Glass is sorted by colour, crushed and melted into new glass at very high heat. **Aluminium** from cans is melted down; this needs only a small part of the energy that would be needed for new aluminium from ore. Waste paper is broken down with water into a pulp, cleaned and pressed into new paper or **cardboard**. PET bottles are shredded into flakes, from which new bottles or fibres for clothes are made.

In many Swiss municipalities, **waste paper** is tied in bundles and handed in at the paper collection, often on certain days outside the front door. Cardboard boxes, squashed flat and tied together, go into the cardboard collection. Glass, cans, used oil and batteries are taken to the **collection point** or the municipal depot. PET bottles can be thrown into special collection containers in most shops. Anyone who does not separate their rubbish pays more, because in most municipalities there is a **bag charge** for rubbish bags.

The well-known symbol with the **three arrows in a circle** was designed in 1970 by the American student Gary Anderson for a competition. The arrows stand for the steps collecting, processing and using again. Today it is found on many packages worldwide. It shows that a material is recyclable or is made of recycled material.

The Earth has only limited **raw materials** such as crude oil, ores or wood. Anyone who recycles means less of these have to be newly extracted, and so protects forests, landscapes and animals. Recycling usually also saves energy and therefore greenhouse gases. In addition, fewer things end up in the waste incineration plant or in nature.

Even better than recycling is not making any rubbish at all, for example with a **reusable bottle** or a cloth bag. Things that are still good can be given away, mended or sold on. When sorting, it helps to have different containers at home for paper, glass, PET and cans. What matters is that only clean and correctly sorted recyclables go into the collection.

begriffe.erklaerung: Waste that can be reused, for example glass or paper.
A material from nature from which things are made, for example wood or ore.
A place where you can hand in glass, cans, used oil and other recyclables.
Money that you pay in many municipalities for each rubbish bag.
Packaging that can be used many times.

gewusst: Aluminium can be melted down again and again without getting worse.
Collected PET bottles can even be made into fleece jumpers.
Glass can be melted down as often as you like and shaped into new bottles.

teile.einleitung: The squeaky pop test is a simple experiment used in chemistry lessons to detect hydrogen. You hold a test tube containing the gas to a flame and listen carefully: if it whistles or barks, there was oxyhydrogen in it.
wichtigste: Oxyhydrogen is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.
Oxyhydrogen reacts most violently in a volume ratio of 2 to 1 of hydrogen to oxygen.
When oxyhydrogen reacts, water is formed.
For the test, you hold the test tube with the opening facing downwards.
A whistling or barking sound shows a positive test.
If there is almost pure hydrogen in the tube, you only hear a quiet “pop”.
In the school laboratory, hydrogen is often made from zinc and hydrochloric acid.

abschnitte.text: **Oxyhydrogen** is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen. It can also form when hydrogen mixes with air, because air contains about 21 per cent oxygen. If a flame or a spark comes along, the two gases react with each other in a flash. Water is formed, and a great deal of energy is released, which causes the bang. The reaction is most violent with two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen.

First you collect the gas in a **test tube**. Because hydrogen is much lighter than air, you hold the tube with the opening facing downwards so that the gas does not escape. Then you quickly bring the opening to a burner flame. You always wear safety goggles, and the teacher shows exactly how it is done.

A whistling or barking sound means that there was a mixture of hydrogen and air in the tube. If, on the other hand, there is almost pure hydrogen in the tube, you only hear a quiet “pop”, and the gas burns away calmly. If everything stays silent, there was no hydrogen. After the test you sometimes see a fine film of water in the test tube, the product of the reaction.

In the school laboratory, hydrogen is usually obtained by pouring dilute **hydrochloric acid** over **zinc**. Hydrogen gas bubbles up and zinc chloride forms. Hydrogen can also be obtained by electrolysis, that is by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. The squeaky pop test then shows that hydrogen really has been produced.

Hydrogen can be dangerous if it mixes with air unnoticed. In 1937 the hydrogen-filled airship **“Hindenburg”** burnt as it was landing at Lakehurst in the USA. Since then, airships and balloons have been filled with non-flammable helium. Used in a controlled way, however, the reaction of hydrogen and oxygen provides valuable energy, for example in rocket engines and fuel cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen that reacts with a bang when ignited.
The lightest chemical element, a colourless, flammable gas.
An experiment used to check whether a particular substance is present.
Splitting a substance with the help of electricity.

gewusst: The exhaust of a hydrogen fuel cell is pure water.
Hydrogen is about 14 times lighter than air.
At about 245 metres long, the Hindenburg was one of the largest aircraft ever built.

teile.einleitung: A balloon is a thin, stretchy skin, usually made of rubber, that is filled with air or helium. It is a popular toy and decoration for parties. At the same time it is wonderful for simple experiments on heat, pressure and electricity.
wichtigste: Most balloons are made of rubber, more precisely natural rubber.
In the fridge a blown-up balloon gets a little smaller because the air cools down.
In the hot sun the air expands, and a tight balloon can burst.
An open balloon whizzes away because the air rushing out pushes it.
If you rub a balloon on your hair, it becomes electrically charged and sticks to the wall.
Helium balloons go limp because the gas slowly escapes through the skin.
Balloon remains in nature are dangerous because animals can eat them.

abschnitte.text: Most balloons are made of **latex**, the milky sap of the rubber tree. To make them, moulds are dipped into liquid latex, which is left to dry before the skin is pulled off. This rubber skin is very stretchy and contracts again. Shiny **foil balloons**, on the other hand, are made of a metal-coated plastic film and hold helium much longer.

Air expands when it is warmed and contracts when it cools. That is why a balloon shrinks a little if you put it in the fridge. In the hot sun, on the other hand, it gets bigger and can **burst** if it was already blown up tight. Physicists described this link between temperature and volume more than 200 years ago.

If you let go of a blown-up, open balloon, the air rushes out of the back. It pushes the balloon in the opposite direction, and the balloon whizzes through the room. This is the same principle as in a rocket; it is called **recoil**. Because the air comes out unevenly, the balloon flies in a zigzag.

If you rub a balloon on your hair or on a woolly jumper, it picks up electrons. As a result it becomes **electrically charged**; this is called static electricity. If you then hold it against the wall, it sticks there. Your hair sometimes stands on end because the hairs repel one another.

The air in a blown-up balloon is under **pressure**, and the rubber skin is stretched tight. If you prick it with a needle, the skin tears open in a flash. The air escapes all at once and creates a pressure wave, which we hear as a bang. With a piece of sticky tape on the skin, you can sometimes prick it without it bursting.

The first rubber balloon was made by the English scientist **Michael Faraday** in 1824 for experiments with hydrogen. Soon afterwards balloons became popular as toys. Today we know that balloon remains that fall into nature after balloon races are dangerous for animals, because they eat them or get tangled in them. That is why some Swiss municipalities and festivals no longer release balloons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The milky sap of the rubber tree, from which rubber is made.
A force that pushes an object forwards when something rushes out of the back.
An electric charge created by rubbing that stays in place.
A shiny balloon made of coated plastic film.

gewusst: A latex balloon filled with helium often floats for only about a day.
Weather balloons grow as big as a house in the stratosphere before they burst.
Before there were rubber balloons, children blew up dried pigs’ bladders.

teile.einleitung: The periodic table is a table in which all the chemical elements are arranged according to their structure. It shows at a glance which elements behave in a similar way. It hangs in almost every chemistry room and is one of the most important tools of natural science.
wichtigste: In the periodic table all the chemical elements are arranged by their atomic number.
Dmitri Mendeleev published a periodic table of the elements in 1869.
The horizontal rows are called periods, the vertical columns groups.
Hydrogen is in first place.
Helium, neon and argon belong to the noble gases.
Lithium, sodium and potassium are alkali metals; fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are halogens.
As of 2026, 118 elements are known and officially named.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many chemists were looking for a way to arrange the known elements. In 1869 the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev** published a periodic table; at almost the same time the German Lothar Meyer was also working on a similar table. Mendeleev boldly left gaps for elements that nobody knew yet. He predicted their properties, and when gallium and germanium were discovered later, his **predictions** were amazingly accurate.

The elements are arranged by their **atomic number**, that is by the number of protons in the atomic nucleus. In first place is **hydrogen** with one proton, followed by helium with two. The horizontal rows are called **periods**; there are seven of them. The vertical columns are called **groups**, and elements in the same group behave similarly in chemistry.

On the far left are the **alkali metals** lithium, sodium and potassium, soft metals that react violently with water. On the far right are the **noble gases** helium, neon and argon, which hardly ever react. To their left are the **halogens** fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine, which form salts with metals. In the middle are the transition metals such as iron, copper and gold.

abschnitte.titel: What you can read from it
abschnitte.text: Each box shows the **element symbol**, the atomic number and usually the atomic mass. The metals are on the left, the non-metals at the top right. The period reveals how many electron shells an atom has. The group says how many electrons there are in the outermost shell, and that determines chemical behaviour.

As of 2026, 118 elements are known and officially named. About 90 of them occur in nature; the rest were made artificially in laboratories. The heaviest elements exist for only fractions of a second before they decay. Element 118 is called **oganesson** and was officially named in 2016.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one kind of atom.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus; it determines the place in the periodic table.
A horizontal row in the periodic table.
A vertical column of elements that behave similarly.

gewusst: The element mendelevium, with the atomic number 101, was named in honour of Mendeleev.
The United Nations declared 2019 the International Year of the Periodic Table, 150 years after Mendeleev’s publication.
The element helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun before it was found on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Microplastics are tiny plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres. They form when larger pieces of plastic break down, or are made this small on purpose. Today microplastics are found almost everywhere on Earth, in the sea, in lakes, in the soil and even in the air.
wichtigste: Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres.
Very small particles can only be seen with a microscope.
A plastic bag that lies in sun and water for a long time breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces.
In Switzerland a lot of microplastic comes from the wear of car tyres.
Fleece clothes lose particularly many synthetic fibres in the wash.
Microplastics have been found in the sea, in lakes and in the soil.
Clothes made of natural fibres help to produce less microplastic from the washing machine.

abschnitte.text: **Microplastics** are plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres, that is about the size of a grain of rice or much smaller. Some can just be seen with the naked eye; others can only be recognised under the **microscope**. Even smaller particles, below a thousandth of a millimetre, are called nanoplastics. Microplastics can take the form of beads, splinters or fibres.

There are two kinds. **Primary microplastics** are made small on purpose, for example as beads in some exfoliating scrubs or as plastic pellets for factories. **Secondary microplastics** form when larger pieces of plastic break down through sunlight, waves and rubbing. A plastic bag becomes brittle over time in this way and crumbles into tiny pieces. Most microplastic in the environment is secondary.

One of the biggest sources is **tyre wear**: every time a car brakes and pulls away, tiny particles rub off its tyres. In Switzerland it is regarded as the most important source of microplastics in the environment. Washing clothes made of synthetic fibres such as **fleece** also releases many fine fibres. Other sources are artificial pitches, coats of paint and carelessly discarded rubbish that slowly breaks down.

Researchers have found microplastics in all the oceans, from the sea floor to the ice of the Arctic. Swiss lakes such as Lake Geneva and rivers such as the Rhine also contain microplastic particles. It can even be detected in the soil of fields, in mountain snow and in the air. Animals such as mussels, fish and worms take in the particles with their food. In this way microplastics can enter the **food chain**.

Everyone can help to produce less microplastic. Clothes made of **natural fibres** such as cotton or wool do not lose plastic fibres. Full washing machines, lower temperatures and special wash bags reduce fibre loss. Rubbish belongs in the bin or in recycling and not in nature. Anyone who drives less also causes less tyre wear.

Exactly how dangerous microplastics are for people is still being researched. What is certain is that plastic hardly breaks down in nature and therefore builds up. Pollutants can also attach themselves to the particles. Experts are therefore calling for less plastic to get into the environment. In 2023 the European Union decided to ban intentionally added microplastics in many products step by step.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres.
Fine particles that rub off car tyres when driving.
A fibre made of plastic, for example polyester in fleece jumpers.
A series of living things in which each is eaten by the next.

gewusst: In a single wash, thousands of tiny fibres can come off a fleece jumper.
Microplastics have already been found in samples from Antarctica and in the snow of high mountains.
Tiny plastic particles also come off shoe soles and artificial grass over time.

teile.einleitung: The neutron is a tiny particle in the atomic nucleus that has no electric charge. Together with the protons it forms the nucleus of almost all atoms. Neutrons play an important part in nuclear power stations, in research and in dating finds.
wichtigste: The neutron is an electrically neutral particle in the atomic nucleus.
It was discovered in 1932 by James Chadwick.
Isotopes of an element differ in their number of neutrons.
Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, uranium-235 has 143 neutrons.
A free neutron decays after about 15 minutes on average.
In beta-minus decay, a neutron turns into a proton.
The Paul Scherrer Institute operates the SINQ neutron source.

abschnitte.text: The atomic nucleus consists of **protons** and **neutrons**; together they are called nucleons. The neutron is about as heavy as the proton but has no charge. It consists of three even smaller particles, one up quark and two down quarks. The **strong nuclear force** holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.

For a long time only protons and electrons were known. As early as 1920 Ernest Rutherford suspected that there must also be a neutral particle in the nucleus. The British physicist **James Chadwick** proved it in 1932. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics in 1935.

All atoms of an element have the same number of protons, but the number of neutrons can differ. Such variants are called **isotopes**. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons, 14 particles in the nucleus altogether. Uranium-235 has 92 protons and 143 neutrons, because 235 minus 92 gives 143.

Outside the nucleus a neutron is not stable and decays after about 15 minutes on average. In **beta-minus decay**, a neutron turns into a proton, producing an electron and an antineutrino. If a neutron hits a uranium-235 nucleus, the nucleus can break apart; this is called **nuclear fission**. New neutrons are released, which set off a **chain reaction**, as used in nuclear power stations such as Gösgen or Leibstadt.

Neutrons can penetrate deep into materials and show how they are built up inside. For this, the **Paul Scherrer Institute** in Villigen in the canton of Aargau operates the spallation neutron source **SINQ**. There neutrons are produced by firing fast protons at a metal target. Researchers use them to study batteries, medicines and old works of art, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: A collective name for protons and neutrons in the atomic nucleus.
A kind of atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons.
When a heavy atomic nucleus breaks into two smaller parts.
A process that keeps driving itself on.

gewusst: Neutron stars are the remains of exploded stars; a teaspoon of their material would weigh billions of tonnes.
Ordinary hydrogen is the only atom whose nucleus contains no neutron at all.
The radioactive carbon-14 used for dating is formed high in the atmosphere when neutrons from cosmic radiation hit nitrogen atoms.

teile.einleitung: Air is the invisible mixture of gases that surrounds our Earth like a shell. Without air we could not breathe, birds could not fly and we would not hear any sound. Although you cannot see it, air has weight and takes up space.
wichtigste: Air is invisible, but it is still there and takes up space.
Air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen.
About 21 per cent of air is oxygen, which we need to breathe.
A blown-up balloon is filled with air.
High up on mountains the air gets thinner.
The Earth’s layer of air is called the atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: You cannot see air, but you can feel it, for example as wind. When you blow up a balloon, you fill it with air. If you push an empty glass upside down into water, the **air** stays in the glass and the water cannot get in. This shows that air takes up **space**.

Air is a **mixture** of different gases. The largest part, about 78 per cent, is **nitrogen**. About 21 per cent is **oxygen**, and just under one per cent is the noble gas argon. There are also small amounts of carbon dioxide and water vapour.

When we breathe in, our body takes **oxygen** from the air. The blood takes it to all the cells, where it releases energy from food. When we breathe out, we give off **carbon dioxide**. Plants do the opposite: they take in CO₂ and give off oxygen.

The higher you climb, the less air there is above you, and the air gets **thinner**. On the Jungfraujoch, at 3454 metres above sea level, you breathe in noticeably less oxygen with each breath than on the Swiss Plateau. That is why you get tired more quickly walking there. Mountaineers who climb very high peaks can get **altitude sickness**.

The whole layer of air above us presses down on the Earth; this is called **air pressure**. One litre of air weighs about 1.2 grams. Air pressure is measured with a barometer, and its changes help with weather forecasting. When air moves, **wind** is created, which turns wind turbines and drives sailing boats.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
The gas in the air that people and animals need to live.
The gas that makes up most of the air.
The weight of the air pressing on everything.

gewusst: An adult breathes in and out about 10,000 to 12,000 litres of air a day.
Without air there would be no sound, which is why it is completely silent in space.
The sky is blue because air scatters blue sunlight more strongly than red.

teile.einleitung: A smoke alarm is a small device on the ceiling that beeps loudly as soon as it detects smoke. It warns people early of a fire, even in the middle of the night. This leaves enough time to leave the flat safely.
wichtigste: A smoke alarm beeps loudly when it detects smoke.
It is fitted on the ceiling because smoke rises.
Most smoke alarms need a battery.
With the test button you check whether the smoke alarm works.
In the bedroom it is particularly important, because you cannot smell smoke while asleep.
If it goes off and there is a fire, you leave the flat immediately.
A short beep every few minutes often means that the battery is almost flat.
A smoke alarm should be checked regularly.

abschnitte.titel: What does a smoke alarm do
abschnitte.text: A smoke alarm is a **warning device** that detects smoke in the air. As soon as enough smoke gets into it, it gives off a very loud, shrill **alarm tone**. This tone is so loud that it wakes up sleeping people too. This is important because people cannot smell smoke while asleep and would often not notice a fire.

Most smoke alarms for homes work with light and are called **optical smoke alarms**. In a dark measuring chamber, a small lamp sends out a beam of light that normally does not hit a sensor. If smoke particles get into the chamber, the light is scattered by them and reaches the **sensor**. Then the device sets off the alarm; this is called the scattered light principle.

Smoke rises, so a smoke alarm belongs on the **ceiling**, as close as possible to the middle of the room. Smoke alarms are particularly important in bedrooms, children’s rooms and the hallway leading to the exit. In the kitchen or the bathroom, steam easily causes false alarms, so other alarms or none are used there. In Switzerland smoke alarms are usually not compulsory in flats, but fire safety experts strongly recommend them.

Most smoke alarms run on a **battery**; some models have a built-in battery that lasts about ten years. If the battery is almost flat, the device gives a short beep every few minutes. With the **test button** you check regularly, for example once a month, whether the alarm works. After about ten years the whole alarm should be replaced, because the sensor ages.

If the smoke alarm goes off and there is a fire, you leave the flat immediately and take nothing with you. You close the doors behind you so that fire and smoke spread more slowly. Then you call the fire brigade from outside on **118**. You never use the lift in a fire, always the stairs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that sounds a loud alarm when there is smoke.
A part that measures or detects something, such as light or smoke.
An alarm even though there is no fire, for example because of steam.
All the measures that prevent fires or reduce their effects.

gewusst: A smoke alarm can give you a head start of several minutes, and it is often these very minutes that save lives.
There are smoke alarms for deaf people that warn with a flashing light or a vibrating pad.

teile.einleitung: Compost is dark, fertile soil that is made from garden and kitchen waste. Countless tiny creatures such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms break down leaves, grass cuttings and apple cores. In this way waste becomes food for new plants again.
wichtigste: A compost heap turns into fertile soil.
Apple cores, vegetable peelings and leaves belong on the compost.
Cooked meat does not belong on the garden compost.
Tiny fungi and bacteria break down the waste.
Earthworms help a great deal with composting.
It takes a few months for garden waste to turn into compost.
In Switzerland, garden and kitchen waste is collected as green waste.

abschnitte.text: Compost forms when plant waste rots in the air. In the end a crumbly, dark soil is left that smells like forest floor. This soil contains a lot of **humus** and nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Gardeners mix it into beds so that plants grow better.

Most of the work is done by **bacteria** and fungi that are so small that you cannot see them. After them come larger animals such as woodlice, springtails and above all **earthworms**. They eat the remains and leave behind nutrient-rich crumbs. All these creatures need air and moisture, so the compost should neither dry out nor get too wet.

When the tiny creatures are at work, heat is produced. Inside a large fresh compost heap it can get hotter than 60 °C. This heat kills many weed seeds and germs. After a few weeks the heap cools down, and mature **compost** slowly forms.

Fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, tea bags, eggshells, leaves, grass cuttings and small branches belong on the compost. Cooked food, meat and bones do not, because they attract rats and smell bad. Plastic, glass, metal and cat litter do not belong there either. A good compost is a **mixture** of moist and dry, coarse and fine waste.

Many municipalities in Switzerland collect **green waste** with a separate collection or have collection points. It is turned into compost in large composting plants. Part of it goes to **biogas plants**, where bacteria turn it into gas without oxygen. This biogas is used to produce electricity and heat, and the remains serve as fertiliser.

About a third of our household waste consists of scraps that can be composted. If they are composted, they do not end up in the waste incineration plant. The nutrients return to the soil, and less artificial fertiliser is needed. You also learn a lot about the **cycle** of nature from your own compost heap.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fertile soil made from rotted plant waste.
The dark, fertile part of the soil made of broken-down plant and animal remains.
Garden and kitchen waste that is collected separately in Switzerland.
A flammable gas that bacteria produce from waste without oxygen.
Living things that break down dead plants and animals.

gewusst: A handful of mature compost contains more tiny living things than there are people on Earth.
There are special worm bins in which compost worms can process kitchen waste even in a flat.

teile.einleitung: Sodium chloride is the chemical name for table salt, the salt we use every day for seasoning. It consists of sodium and chlorine, two substances that are dangerous on their own but together form a salt that is vital for life. Besides in the kitchen, it is needed for road salt, in industry and in medicine.
wichtigste: Sodium chloride has the formula NaCl and is known in everyday life as table salt.
It consists of sodium ions and chloride ions in a ratio of 1 to 1.
In the crystal, each sodium ion is surrounded by 6 chloride ions, which produces cube-shaped crystals.
Sodium chloride only melts at about 801 °C and has a density of about 2.2 g/cm³.
At 20 °C about 360 grams of table salt dissolve in one litre of water.
The WHO recommends that adults eat less than 5 grams of salt a day.
In Switzerland, salt is obtained in mines and salt works, for example in Bex and on the Rhine near Basel.

abschnitte.text: **Sodium chloride** is a salt made of the elements sodium and chlorine. Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, forming hydrogen. Chlorine is a poisonous greenish yellow gas. When they combine, harmless white table salt is formed, which we eat every day. In nature it occurs as the mineral **halite**, also called rock salt.

In table salt, positively charged sodium ions and negatively charged chloride ions are arranged as in a three-dimensional chessboard. Each sodium ion has 6 chloride ions as direct neighbours and vice versa. This **ionic lattice** is held together by strong electrical forces. That is why salt is hard, brittle and only melts at about 801 °C. Under a magnifying glass you can see that grains of salt are often little cubes.

If you put salt into water, it dissolves. The **water molecules** surround the individual ions and spread them throughout the water. At 20 °C about 360 grams of salt dissolve in one litre of water; then the solution is saturated. Salt water conducts electricity because the charged ions can move. It also only freezes below 0 °C.

Switzerland has its own salt from prehistoric seas, which lies deep underground. In the **Bex salt mine** in the canton of Vaud, salt has been extracted for centuries, and today visitors can tour it. Large salt works stand at Schweizerhalle and Riburg on the Rhine. There, water is pumped into the salt layers and the resulting brine is then evaporated.

Our body needs sodium and chloride, for example for the nerves, the muscles and the water balance. Too much salt, however, can raise blood pressure. The WHO recommends that adults eat less than 5 grams a day, about a teaspoon. A lot of salt is hidden in bread, cheese, sausage, crisps and ready meals. Many Swiss table salts also contain iodine and fluoride to help prevent disease.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrically charged particle, for example the sodium ion Na⁺ or the chloride ion Cl⁻.
A regular arrangement of positive and negative ions in a crystal.
The name for table salt when it occurs as a mineral in nature.
Water in which a great deal of salt is dissolved.

gewusst: In winter salt is spread on roads because salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than pure water.
The word “salary” for wages comes from the Latin word for salt, because salt used to be very valuable.
In Switzerland iodine was added to table salt from as early as 1922 to prevent goitre.

teile.einleitung: A nucleophile is a particle with a lone pair that, in a reaction, looks for a positively charged or positively polarised atom as a partner. The word literally means nucleus-loving. Nucleophiles play a leading role in organic chemistry, for example when an alcohol is made from a halogenoalkane.
wichtigste: A nucleophile has a lone pair and attacks positively polarised centres.
Nucleophile literally means nucleus-loving.
Typical nucleophiles are the hydroxide ion, water, ammonia and halide ions.
In the Lewis acid-base concept, a nucleophile is a Lewis base.
In a halogenoalkane, the nucleophile attacks the carbon atom that carries the halogen.
The hydroxide ion is a stronger nucleophile than water because it is negatively charged.
Among the halide ions, iodide is the strongest nucleophile in water.

abschnitte.text: A **nucleophile** is a particle that has a lone pair and makes it available for a new bond. For this it looks for an atom that needs electrons because it is positively charged or positively polarised. The word is made up of the Latin nucleus for kernel and the Greek philos for friend. So it means a particle that loves the positively charged atomic nucleus. Its counterpart is the **electrophile**, the electron-loving particle.

Many nucleophiles are negatively charged ions, such as the **hydroxide ion** OH⁻, the cyanide ion or halide ions such as chloride and iodide. But neutral molecules can also be nucleophiles if they have a lone pair. In **ammonia** NH₃ this electron pair is on the nitrogen atom. In water the oxygen atom even carries two lone pairs. Charged particles are usually stronger nucleophiles, which is why OH⁻ reacts much faster than H₂O.

An important reaction is **nucleophilic substitution**, that is replacement by a nucleophile. In a halogenoalkane such as bromomethane, the halogen atom pulls electrons towards itself. As a result the neighbouring carbon atom becomes slightly positive. A hydroxide ion attacks exactly this carbon atom, and the bromide ion is pushed out. In this way the halogenoalkane becomes an **alcohol**, here methanol.

How well a particle acts as a nucleophile is called its **nucleophilicity**. A negative charge usually makes a particle more nucleophilic. In water, size also plays a part: the large iodide ion is the strongest nucleophile among the halide ions there. This is because small ions such as fluoride are surrounded and shielded by a dense shell of water molecules. The solvent can therefore change the order.

According to the acid-base concept of the American chemist **Gilbert Newton Lewis**, a base is a particle that donates an electron pair. So a nucleophile is a **Lewis base**. The difference lies in the point of view: you speak of basicity when it is about equilibrium, and of nucleophilicity when it is about the speed of a reaction with a carbon atom. The terms nucleophile and electrophile were introduced by the British chemist Christopher Ingold in the 1930s.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two electrons of an atom that are not involved in a bond.
A particle that seeks electrons, the counterpart of the nucleophile.
A reaction in which an atom or a group is replaced by another.
A particle that donates an electron pair for a bond.
A hydrocarbon in which a hydrogen atom has been replaced by a halogen such as chlorine or bromine.

gewusst: In our body, too, enzymes work with nucleophiles to split or build molecules in a targeted way.
Whether a particle reacts as a base or as a nucleophile often depends on which partner it meets.
Chemists use arrows to draw how the nucleophile’s electron pair moves to the reaction partner.

teile.einleitung: A chemical equation is the shorthand of chemistry used to describe what happens in a chemical reaction. On the left are the starting substances, on the right the products, and in between an arrow. With it you can even calculate how much of a substance is formed.
wichtigste: A chemical equation shows the starting substances, the arrow and the products of a reaction.
There must be the same number of atoms of each kind on both sides.
According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass stays the same in a reaction.
One mole of a substance contains about 6.022 · 10²³ particles.
The molar mass of CO₂ is about 44 g/mol.
4 g of hydrogen give 36 g of water if they react completely.

abschnitte.text: To the left of the arrow are the **reactants**, that is the starting substances. To the right are the **products** formed in the reaction. One example is 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, which means: hydrogen and oxygen react to form water. The numbers in front of the formulas are called **coefficients** and show how many particles are involved.

In a chemical reaction no atoms are lost and no new ones are added; they are only joined in new ways. This is described by the **law of conservation of mass**, which the Frenchman **Antoine Lavoisier** confirmed in the 18th century by careful weighing. The total mass of the substances therefore stays the same. That is why a chemical equation must have the same number of atoms of each kind on both sides.

When **balancing**, you look for the right coefficients. For the burning of propane, C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O applies, because on the right there are 6 plus 4, that is 10 oxygen atoms. For the rusting of iron, the balanced equation is 4 Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃. You may only change the coefficients, never the small numbers in the formulas.

Because atoms are so tiny, they are counted in packages called **moles**. One mole contains about 6.022 · 10²³ particles; this number is called the **Avogadro constant**. The **molar mass** shows how much one mole of a substance weighs; for CO₂ it is about 44 g/mol. So 117 g of sodium chloride, with a molar mass of about 58.5 g/mol, corresponds to 2 mol.

With a chemical equation you can predict how much product is formed. 4 g of hydrogen is 2 mol of H₂, and according to the equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, this gives 2 mol of water. Because one mole of water weighs about 18 g, 36 g of water are formed. Such **stoichiometric** calculations are needed in industry, at the pharmacy and in the laboratory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A starting substance that is used up in a reaction.
A substance newly formed in a reaction.
A number in front of a formula that shows how many particles react.
The unit of amount in chemistry, a package of about 6 · 10²³ particles.
Calculating with amounts of substance and masses in chemical reactions.

gewusst: The Avogadro constant is so large that a mole of grains of sand would cover the whole of Switzerland kilometres deep.
Lavoisier is regarded as one of the founders of modern chemistry.
Even with a candle no mass is lost; afterwards the mass of the wax is in the carbon dioxide and water vapour in the air.

teile.einleitung: The metallic bond is the way in which the atoms in a metal hold together. The metal atoms give up some of their electrons, which then move freely through the whole metal. These mobile electrons explain why metals shine, conduct electricity and can be bent.
wichtigste: In a metal, positively charged atom cores form a regular lattice.
The outer electrons move freely between the atom cores; this is called the electron gas.
Because of the freely moving electrons, metals conduct electricity and heat very well.
Metals can be hammered and bent because the layers slide past each other without the bond breaking.
The metallic shine is also caused by the mobile electrons.
A mixture of two or more metals is called an alloy.
Brass consists of copper and zinc, bronze of copper and tin.

abschnitte.text: Metal atoms have only a few electrons in their outermost shell and give them up easily. What is left are positively charged **atom cores**, which arrange themselves into a regular **metal lattice**. The electrons that have been given up no longer belong to any particular atom. They move back and forth like a gas between the atom cores, which is why this is called the **electron gas model**. The negative electrons and the positive cores attract each other and hold the metal together.

If you apply a voltage to a metal wire, the free electrons move in one direction. This is **electric current**. Silver conducts best, closely followed by copper, which is why electric cables are usually made of copper. The mobile electrons also pass on heat quickly. That is why a metal railing feels much colder in winter than a wooden railing, even though both are equally cold.

If you hit a piece of metal with a hammer, whole layers of atom cores shift. The electron gas adjusts immediately, and the bond holds. That is why metal is **malleable** and does not break like glass or a salt crystal. Blacksmiths have used this for thousands of years to shape tools, horseshoes or bells. Gold can even be beaten into wafer-thin **gold leaf**.

When light hits a metal surface, the free electrons vibrate with it and send the light back almost completely. That is why metals shine and are suitable as **mirrors**. In the past, mirrors were often made of polished bronze; today there is usually a thin layer of silver or aluminium behind the glass. Gold and copper absorb some of the blue light and therefore shimmer yellowish or reddish.

If you mix molten metals, an **alloy** is formed after cooling. There too, the metallic bond holds the atoms together. **Bronze**, made of copper and tin, was so important that a whole era, the Bronze Age, is named after it. Brass, made of copper and zinc, is used for door handles, screws and brass instruments such as trumpets. Steel is an alloy of iron with a little carbon, so not only of metals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The positively charged remainder of an atom after it has given up its outer electrons.
The freely moving electrons between the atom cores of a metal.
A mixture of two or more metals, for example bronze or brass.
The property of a substance that lets it be bent or hammered without breaking.

gewusst: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Gold leaf can be hammered so thin that light shines through it with a greenish glow.
Swiss church bells are usually made of bell bronze, an alloy of copper and tin.
